assets.name: autosave
assets.summary: Wraps a save function so a burst of edits saves only the last draft, once the edits pause, and every call gets that save's Result.
assets.useWhen: an editor, a settings form or a canvas saves as the user types, and each keystroke must not become a request. Every call in a burst waits for the one save of the last draft and gets its Result, so a failed save can be shown next to whichever edit is on screen, and no call is left with a rejected promise nobody handles.
signatures: export function autosave<D, T>( save: (draft: D) => Promise<T>, options: AutosaveOptions, ): (draft: D) => Promise<Result<T, AutosaveError>>

assets.name: batchedWrite
assets.summary: Splits items into batches and writes them one batch at a time, stopping at the first batch that fails.
assets.useWhen: a bulk insert or import goes through an API or database with a limit per request, such as 100 rows per call, and a rate limit between calls. Batches run in order, never at once. On failure, `written` says how many items are already stored, so the job can resume with `items.slice(written)` instead of starting over.
signatures: export async function batchedWrite<T, U>( items: readonly T[], write: (batch: readonly T[]) => Promise<U>, options: BatchedWriteOptions, ): Promise<Result<U[], BatchedWriteError>>

assets.name: circuitBreaker
assets.summary: Wraps an async call so that after enough failures in a row it fails fast for a cooldown, instead of hitting a service that is down.
assets.useWhen: a dependency such as a payment provider, a search cluster or an internal service goes down, and every request waiting on its timeout would pile up and slow the whole app. While the circuit is open, calls return `CIRCUIT_OPEN` at once, with how long until the next try. After the cooldown, one trial call decides: success closes the circuit, failure opens it again. Make one breaker per dependency and share it.
signatures: export function circuitBreaker<A extends readonly unknown[], T>( call: (...args: A) => Promise<T>, options: CircuitBreakerOptions, ): (...args: A) => Promise<Result<T, CircuitBreakerError>>

assets.name: fetchAllByOffset
assets.summary: Fetches every page of an offset-and-limit API and returns all the items in one array.
assets.useWhen: an API or a SQL query pages with `offset` and `limit` (or `skip` and `take`), such as a REST admin endpoint or a table export, and the caller needs every row. A page shorter than `pageSize` ends the loop, so when the total is an exact multiple of the page size, one extra, empty page is fetched to find the end.
signatures: export async function fetchAllByOffset<T>( fetchPage: (offset: number, limit: number) => Promise<readonly T[]>, options: FetchAllByOffsetOptions, ): Promise<Result<T[], FetchAllByOffsetError>>

assets.name: fetchAllPages
assets.summary: Follows a cursor through every page of a paginated API and returns all the items in one array.
assets.useWhen: an API such as Stripe, Slack, GitHub GraphQL or DynamoDB returns a page of items and a cursor for the next one, and the caller needs all of them. `fetchPage` gets `None` for the first page and `Some(cursor)` after that. Pages are fetched one at a time, since each cursor comes from the page before it.
signatures: export async function fetchAllPages<T>( fetchPage: (cursor: Option<string>) => Promise<FetchAllPagesPage<T>>, options: FetchAllPagesOptions = {}, ): Promise<Result<T[], FetchAllPagesError>>

assets.name: findAsync
assets.summary: Checks items one at a time with an async check and returns the first that passes, without checking the rest.
assets.useWhen: each check costs a call and the first match is enough, such as the first free username among candidates, the first healthy endpoint, or the first file that exists. Checks run in order and stop at the first match: `Ok(Some(item))`. No match is `Ok(None)`; a check that throws is an Err, since the answer is then unknown.
signatures: export async function findAsync<T>( items: readonly T[], check: (item: T, index: number) => Promise<boolean>, ): Promise<Result<Option<T>, FindAsyncError>>

assets.name: hedgedCall
assets.summary: Starts a second copy of a slow async task after a delay, and takes whichever attempt succeeds first.
assets.useWhen: a read is idempotent and its latency has a long tail, such as a search query, a cache read or an object-store GET, and an occasional slow replica shouldn't make the caller wait. Most calls finish before `hedgeAfterMs` and never start a second attempt. Only use it for reads: the task can run twice.
signatures: export async function hedgedCall<T>( task: () => Promise<T>, options: HedgedCallOptions, ): Promise<Result<T, HedgedCallError>>

assets.name: latestOnly
assets.summary: Wraps an async function so only the newest call's answer is kept, and older calls that finish later come back as None.
assets.useWhen: requests can come back out of order and only the latest matters, such as search-as-you-type, a filter panel or switching tabs, where a slow answer for `"a"` must not replace the answer for `"ab"`. Every call still runs; an older call resolves to `None` once a newer one has started, so the caller just ignores it. The newest call's outcome comes back as `Some(Ok(value))` or `Some(Err(error))`.
signatures: export function latestOnly<A, T>(task: (input: A) => Promise<T>): (input: A) => Promise<Option<Result<T, unknown>>>

assets.name: mapAtRate
assets.summary: Maps items with an async function one at a time, never faster than a number of calls per second.
assets.useWhen: each item needs a call to an API with a strict rate limit, such as a geocoder allowing 10 requests per second or a mail provider allowing 2, and going over the limit gets the key blocked. Each call starts `1000 / perSecond` ms after the previous one finished, so the rate is never exceeded even when calls are fast. It stops at the first failure.
signatures: export async function mapAtRate<T, U>( items: readonly T[], fn: (item: T, index: number) => Promise<U>, options: MapAtRateOptions, ): Promise<Result<U[], MapAtRateError>>

assets.name: mapSettled
assets.summary: Maps every item with an async function and keeps going past failures, returning the values and the failures apart.
assets.useWhen: a bulk job should do as much as it can and report the rest, such as sending a batch of emails, resizing uploaded images or syncing records, where one bad item must not stop the others. `mapAsync` stops at the first failure; this never does, and each failure keeps its index and item so the caller can retry or report exactly those.
signatures: export async function mapSettled<T, U>( items: readonly T[], fn: (item: T, index: number) => Promise<U>, options: MapSettledOptions = {}, ): Promise<MapSettledOutcome<T, U>>

assets.name: mapWithRetry
assets.summary: Maps items with an async function, retrying each item on its own, and fails with the first item that never succeeded.
assets.useWhen: each item is an independent call that sometimes fails for a moment, such as uploading files, fetching thumbnails or calling a webhook per record. One retry of the whole list would redo every item; this retries only the item that failed. Every item runs to the end even after another gives up, and the first failure in list order comes back.
signatures: export async function mapWithRetry<T, U>( items: readonly T[], fn: (item: T, index: number) => Promise<U>, options: MapWithRetryOptions, ): Promise<Result<U[], MapWithRetryError<T>>>

assets.name: parallelRecord
assets.summary: Runs a record of async tasks in parallel and returns a record of their values, or the first task that failed.
assets.useWhen: a handler needs several unrelated things before it can answer, such as the user, their settings and their permissions, and any one of them missing means the request fails. Each value keeps its own type under its key, unlike a tuple from `parallel`, and the error names the key that failed.
signatures: export async function parallelRecord<Tasks extends Record<string, () => Promise<unknown>>>( tasks: Tasks, options: ParallelRecordOptions = {}, ): Promise<Result<ParallelRecordValues<Tasks>, ParallelRecordError>>

assets.name: partitionAsync
assets.summary: Splits items in two with an async check: the items that pass, then the items that don't.
assets.useWhen: deciding needs a lookup per item and both groups matter, such as which emails can receive mail and which bounce, which SKUs are in stock, or which users exist in another system. Both groups keep the input order. A check that throws fails the whole split, since the item would belong to neither group.
signatures: export async function partitionAsync<T>( items: readonly T[], check: (item: T, index: number) => Promise<boolean>, options: PartitionAsyncOptions = {}, ): Promise<Result<[T[], T[]], PartitionAsyncError>>

assets.name: pollJob
assets.summary: Polls a background job's status until it finishes or fails, and stops as soon as either happens.
assets.useWhen: an API starts work and hands back a job to check, such as a video transcode, a CI run, a bulk import or a model fine-tune. A job that reports failure ends the wait at once with its status, instead of being polled until attempts run out. `classify` maps the API's own states, such as `succeeded`, `errored` and `in_progress`, to these three.
signatures: export async function pollJob<S>( check: () => Promise<S>, options: PollJobOptions<S>, ): Promise<Result<S, PollJobError<S>>>

assets.name: pollUntil
assets.summary: Calls an async check at a steady interval until its value passes a test, and returns that value.
assets.useWhen: waiting for something another system is doing, such as an export file being ready, a deployment answering, or a payment reaching `succeeded`. Any value can pass, including `0` and `''`, unlike `poll`, which treats falsy values as "not yet". A check that throws stops the wait at once with `CHECK_FAILED`.
signatures: export async function pollUntil<T>( check: () => Promise<T>, isReady: (value: T) => boolean, options: PollUntilOptions, ): Promise<Result<T, PollUntilError<T>>>

assets.name: raceToSuccess
assets.summary: Starts every async task at once and returns the first one that succeeds.
assets.useWhen: several equivalent sources can answer and the fastest working one should win, such as the same file on three CDNs or a lookup against several resolvers. A failure doesn't end the race; only when every task has failed does an Err come back, with all the errors. The losing tasks keep running, because a promise can't be cancelled.
signatures: export async function raceToSuccess<T>( tasks: ReadonlyArray<() => Promise<T>>, ): Promise<Result<T, RaceToSuccessError>>

assets.name: retryOnCodes
assets.summary: Retries an async task only when it fails with one of the listed error codes, and fails at once on any other error.
assets.useWhen: some failures are temporary and others never go away, such as `ECONNRESET` and `ETIMEDOUT` against `EACCES`, or a service's `RATE_LIMITED` against `INVALID_INPUT`. Plain `retry` would retry a validation error three times before reporting it. The code is read from the thrown value's `code` property; a value without one isn't retried.
signatures: export async function retryOnCodes<T>( task: () => Promise<T>, options: RetryOnCodesOptions, ): Promise<Result<T, RetryOnCodesError>>

assets.name: retryResult
assets.summary: Retries an async task that reports failure by returning an Err, until it returns Ok or attempts run out.
assets.useWhen: the task already speaks Result, such as a client wrapped in `tryCatchAsync` or a service function that returns `Err({ code })`. Receta's `retry` only retries when the task throws, so an Err would count as success there. Pass `isRetryable` to stop at once on an error that another attempt can't fix, such as a declined card.
signatures: export async function retryResult<T, E>( task: () => Promise<Result<T, E>>, options: RetryResultOptions<E>, ): Promise<Result<T, RetryResultError<E>>>

assets.name: retryTransientHttp
assets.summary: Retries an HTTP call that fails with a temporary status (408, 425, 429, 5xx gateway errors) or a network error.
assets.useWhen: calling a third-party API through fetch, axios, got or an SDK, where 429 and 503 pass and 400, 401, 404 and 422 never will. The status is read from the thrown error's `status`, `statusCode` or `response.status`. An error with no status at all, such as a reset connection, counts as a network failure and is retried; any other status fails at once.
signatures: export async function retryTransientHttp<T>( task: () => Promise<T>, options: RetryTransientHttpOptions, ): Promise<Result<T, RetryTransientHttpError>>

assets.name: retryUntilValid
assets.summary: Retries an async read with backoff until the value it returns passes a check, treating a stale value like an error.
assets.useWhen: reading right after a write to a system that catches up a moment later, such as a search index, a read replica, an eventually consistent store or a webhook that lands after the redirect. Both a value that fails `isValid` and a thrown error get another attempt, after a growing delay. The error says which of the two the last attempt was.
signatures: export async function retryUntilValid<T>( task: () => Promise<T>, isValid: (value: T) => boolean, options: RetryUntilValidOptions, ): Promise<Result<T, RetryUntilValidError<T>>>

assets.name: retryWithTimeout
assets.summary: Runs an async task with a time limit on each attempt, and retries attempts that fail or hang.
assets.useWhen: calling a flaky dependency such as an HTTP API, a queue or a database, where one hung call must not hold the caller and a fresh attempt often succeeds. The task is called again for each attempt, so pass a function, not a promise.
signatures: export async function retryWithTimeout<T>( task: () => Promise<T>, options: RetryWithTimeoutOptions, ): Promise<Result<T, RetryError>>

assets.name: runSteps
assets.summary: Passes a state through async steps that each return a Result, and stops at the first step that fails.
assets.useWhen: a workflow is a list of steps that each build on the last, such as checkout (reserve stock, charge, create the shipment) or onboarding (create the account, the workspace, the first project). `pipeAsync` would hand an Err to the next step; this stops there and returns the state the failed step started from, so the caller knows what already happened and can undo or resume it.
signatures: export async function runSteps<S, E>( initial: S, steps: ReadonlyArray<RunStepsStep<S, E>>, ): Promise<Result<S, RunStepsError<S, E>>>

assets.name: runWithRollback
assets.summary: Runs async steps in order, and when one fails, undoes the steps that finished, newest first.
assets.useWhen: one action spans several systems with no shared transaction, such as signing a user up in the auth provider, the database and the billing system, and a failure halfway must not leave half an account behind. Each step brings its own `undo`, which gets what its `run` returned. `ROLLBACK_FAILED` means some undo failed too, and lists which.
signatures: export async function runWithRollback<const Values extends readonly unknown[]>(steps: { readonly [K in keyof Values]: RunWithRollbackStep<Values[K]> }): Promise<Result<Values, RunWithRollbackError>>

assets.name: settleRecord
assets.summary: Runs a record of async tasks at once and returns each one's Result under its own key.
assets.useWhen: a page or a report loads several independent parts, such as a dashboard's profile, feed and notifications, and each part should show its data or its own error without the others failing with it. Nothing is thrown; each key holds `Ok(value)` or `Err(reason)`, typed from its task.
signatures: export async function settleRecord<Tasks extends Record<string, () => Promise<unknown>>>( tasks: Tasks, ): Promise<SettleRecordOutcome<Tasks>>

assets.name: timeBox
assets.summary: Gives an async task a time limit, and returns None when it runs past the limit or fails.
assets.useWhen: the value is an optional extra, such as recommendations, a weather badge or a link preview, and the page should go ahead without it instead of waiting or showing an error. The task keeps running after the limit, because a promise can't be cancelled; its result is ignored. Use `withTimeLimit` when the caller needs to know what went wrong.
signatures: export async function timeBox<T>(task: () => Promise<T>, limitMs: number): Promise<Option<T>>

assets.name: tryInOrder
assets.summary: Runs async tasks one at a time, in order, and stops at the first one that succeeds.
assets.useWhen: the same thing can come from several sources ranked by preference, such as a list of mirrors, a primary database then a replica then a snapshot, or one LLM provider after another. A task starts only after the one before it failed, so later sources cost nothing while an earlier one works. An empty list fails with no errors.
signatures: export async function tryInOrder<T>( tasks: ReadonlyArray<() => Promise<T>>, ): Promise<Result<T, TryInOrderError>>

assets.name: withDeadline
assets.summary: Runs async steps one after another under one deadline for all of them, and starts no step once it has passed.
assets.useWhen: a request has one budget for several calls in a row, such as 2 seconds to check auth, read the database and render, and a per-call timeout would let three slow calls add up to three times the budget. When the deadline passes, the caller gets an Err at once; the step that was running keeps running, because a promise can't be cancelled, but the steps after it never start.
signatures: export async function withDeadline<T>( steps: ReadonlyArray<() => Promise<T>>, deadlineMs: number, ): Promise<Result<T[], WithDeadlineError>>

assets.name: withFallback
assets.summary: Runs a primary async task, and a fallback task only when the primary one throws or rejects.
assets.useWhen: a value has a preferred source and a backup, such as a live price API and a cached copy, or a primary region and a replica. The fallback starts only after the primary has failed, so it costs nothing while the primary works, and it receives the primary's error so it can log it or decide what to serve. When both fail, both errors come back.
signatures: export async function withFallback<T>( primary: () => Promise<T>, fallback: (primaryError: unknown) => Promise<T>, ): Promise<Result<T, WithFallbackError>>

assets.name: withTimeLimit
assets.summary: Gives an async task a time limit, and returns a Result that tells a timeout apart from a failure.
assets.useWhen: a request must answer within a budget, such as a payment authorisation or a health check, and the caller reacts differently to "too slow" and "broken". Receta's `timeout` rethrows a rejection and reports a timeout as a class instance; this returns both as plain errors with a `code`. The task keeps running after the limit, because a promise can't be cancelled.
signatures: export async function withTimeLimit<T>( task: () => Promise<T>, limitMs: number, ): Promise<Result<T, WithTimeLimitError>>

assets.name: batchedLoader
assets.summary: Collects the keys asked for at about the same time into one batched load, and gives each caller its own value.
assets.useWhen: code asks for records one at a time but the source can return many in one go, such as GraphQL resolvers loading each post's author, or a loop calling a "get user" that has a "get users" endpoint. N lookups become one call: the N+1 query problem. `loadMany` gets each key once and may return the values in any order; `keyOf` matches them back, and a key with no value is `Ok(None)`. Answers are kept for the loader's life, so make one loader per request. A failed batch isn't kept.
signatures: export function batchedLoader<K extends string | number, V>( loadMany: (keys: readonly K[]) => Promise<readonly V[]>, keyOf: (value: V) => K, options: BatchedLoaderOptions = {}, ): (key: K) => Promise<Result<Option<V>, BatchedLoaderError<K>>>

assets.name: cacheWithStats
assets.summary: Wraps a Receta Cache so it counts hits and misses, to measure whether a cache's size and expiry are right.
assets.useWhen: tuning a cache or reporting on one, such as sending the hit rate of a user cache to metrics every minute, or checking in a test that a memoized call was really served from the cache. Pass the wrapped cache to `memoize`, `memoizeBy` or `memoizeAsync` as `cache`. A miss is a `has` or `get` that finds nothing, a hit is a `get` that finds a value, which is how memoize asks.
signatures: export function cacheWithStats<K, V>(cache: Cache<K, V>): CacheWithStats<K, V>

assets.name: cachedLoader
assets.summary: Caches an async loader by string key, with invalidation by key or by key prefix for when the data changes.
assets.useWhen: values are cached under structured keys such as `user:42:profile` and `user:42:orders`, and a write must drop a whole group, such as everything about user 42, without clearing the rest. Concurrent loads of one key share a request, and a failed load isn't kept, so the next call tries again.
signatures: export function cachedLoader<T>(load: (key: string) => Promise<T>, options: CachedLoaderOptions = {}): CachedLoader<T>

assets.name: cachedLookup
assets.summary: Caches an async lookup that may find nothing, keeping what it found and what it didn't find for different times.
assets.useWhen: lookups often miss, such as accounts by email at sign-in, short links, or SKUs from a scanner, and every miss going to the database is the expensive part. A miss is kept briefly, so a flood of lookups for a missing key costs one query, and a key created a moment later still shows up soon. A failed lookup isn't kept at all.
signatures: export function cachedLookup<V>( lookup: (key: string) => Promise<Option<V>>, options: CachedLookupOptions, ): (key: string) => Promise<Result<Option<V>, CachedLookupError>>

assets.name: cachedUntilExpiry
assets.summary: Keeps one async value, such as an access token, until shortly before the expiry it carries, then loads a new one.
assets.useWhen: a value says when it stops working, such as an OAuth access token, signed URL, temporary cloud credentials or a session, and every call should reuse it until then. `marginMs` replaces it a little early, so a request never leaves with a token that dies on the way. Concurrent calls that find it expired share one load, and a failed load isn't kept.
signatures: export function cachedUntilExpiry<T>( load: () => Promise<T>, options: CachedUntilExpiryOptions<T>, ): () => Promise<Result<T, CachedUntilExpiryError>>

assets.name: getOrCompute
assets.summary: Returns the cached value for a key, or computes it, stores it and returns it: the cache-aside read for a Receta Cache.
assets.useWhen: code holds a cache directly instead of memoizing one function, such as one `lruCache` shared by several call sites, or a per-request cache where the computation closes over the request. Works with any Receta `Cache`, so `ttlCache` and `lruCache` keep their expiry and eviction. `compute` runs only on a miss.
signatures: export function getOrCompute<K, V>(cache: Cache<K, V>, key: K, compute: (key: K) => V): V

assets.name: getOrLoad
assets.summary: Returns the cached promise for a key, or starts the load and caches its promise, and drops it again if it fails.
assets.useWhen: an async read goes through a cache the code holds directly, such as a `ttlCache` of sessions shared by several handlers. The promise is stored before it settles, so concurrent callers share one load instead of each starting their own. A failed load is removed, so the next caller tries again, unless the entry was already replaced by then.
signatures: export async function getOrLoad<K, V>( cache: Cache<K, Promise<V>>, key: K, load: (key: K) => Promise<V>, ): Promise<Result<V, GetOrLoadError<K>>>

assets.name: invalidateAfter
assets.summary: Wraps an async write so that, once it succeeds, the memoized reads it makes stale are invalidated.
assets.useWhen: reads are memoized and writes change what they return, such as `getUser` cached while `renameUser` and `deleteUser` change users, or a cached list that any create must refresh. A failed write invalidates nothing, since the data didn't change. Each target names a memoized function and the keys of the write's arguments; a target without `keys` is cleared entirely, which suits lists and searches.
signatures: export function invalidateAfter<A extends readonly unknown[], T>( write: (...args: A) => Promise<T>, targets: readonly InvalidateAfterTarget<A>[], ): (...args: A) => Promise<Result<T, InvalidateAfterError>>

assets.name: loadOnce
assets.summary: Loads a value on first use and shares it with every later call, trying again after a failure.
assets.useWhen: something should be set up once, lazily, such as a database pool, an SDK client, remote config or a compiled schema, and calls during startup must share the one load instead of racing to make several. A failed load isn't kept, so the next call tries again; `reset()` forgets a good value too, such as after a config change.
signatures: export function loadOnce<T>(load: () => Promise<T>): LoadOnce<T>

assets.name: lruTtlCache
assets.summary: Creates a Receta Cache with both a size limit that drops the least recently used entry and an expiry per entry.
assets.useWhen: memoized data must stay both bounded and fresh, such as exchange rates, user permissions or rendered fragments, where `lruCache` alone keeps old values forever and `ttlCache` alone grows without limit. `memoize`'s own `maxSize` plus `ttl` drops the oldest entry instead of the least used one. Pass it as `cache` to `memoize`, `memoizeBy` or `memoizeAsync`.
signatures: export function lruTtlCache<K, V>(options: LruTtlCacheOptions): Cache<K, V>

assets.name: memoizeByArgs
assets.summary: Memoizes a function on all of its arguments, compared as JSON, with an optional LRU size limit.
assets.useWhen: a pure function takes several arguments, such as `shippingCost(country, weight)` or `price(sku, currency, quantity)`. `memoize` keys on the first argument only, so a second call with the same first argument would return the first call's answer. Arguments must be JSON data: functions, symbols and class instances don't survive, and `undefined` and `null` count as the same inside the key.
signatures: export function memoizeByArgs<A extends readonly unknown[], T>( fn: (...args: A) => T, options: MemoizeByArgsOptions = {}, ): MemoizedFunction<A, T>

assets.name: memoizeByVersion
assets.summary: Memoizes a function and forgets every result as soon as a version it reads changes, such as a locale or a data revision.
assets.useWhen: results depend on something global besides the arguments, such as translations that depend on the current locale, prices that depend on a rate table's revision, or permissions that depend on the role table's version. `versionOf` is read on every call; when it differs from the last call's (by `!==`), the cache is cleared first. The key defaults to the first argument; pass `keyOf` when the function takes more than one.
signatures: export function memoizeByVersion<A extends readonly unknown[], T>( fn: (...args: A) => T, versionOf: () => unknown, keyOf: (...args: A) => unknown = (...args) => args[0], ): (...args: A) => T

assets.name: memoizeLatest
assets.summary: Remembers only the last call, and returns its result again while the arguments stay equal.
assets.useWhen: an expensive function is called over and over with the same arguments, such as a chart layout recomputed on each render or a validation run on each keystroke, and remembering every past call would only grow memory. Arguments are compared deeply by default, so a new array with the same items still counts as the same; pass `isSameArgs` to compare another way, such as by identity.
signatures: export function memoizeLatest<A extends readonly unknown[], T>( fn: (...args: A) => T, isSameArgs: (previous: A, next: A) => boolean = (previous, next) => R.isDeepEqual(previous, next), ): (...args: A) => T

assets.name: memoizeOkOnly
assets.summary: Memoizes a function that returns a Result, keeping Ok results and computing an Err again on the next call.
assets.useWhen: a lookup or computation can fail for a reason that may pass, such as a rate not loaded yet, a template not registered yet, or a quota that resets, while a success stays true. Plain `memoize` would keep returning the first Err forever. The key defaults to the first argument; pass `keyOf` when the function takes more than one. The result has the memoized function's `cache` and `clear`.
signatures: export function memoizeOkOnly<A extends readonly unknown[], T, E>( fn: (...args: A) => Result<T, E>, keyOf: (...args: A) => unknown = (...args) => args[0], ): MemoizedFunction<A, Result<T, E>>

assets.name: memoizeSomeOnly
assets.summary: Memoizes a function that returns an Option, keeping what it found and looking again next time when it found nothing.
assets.useWhen: a lookup against data that fills up over time, such as a directory being synced, a registry plugins add to, or a store being hydrated, where "not there" now may be "there" in a second but a value found stays valid. Plain `memoize` would keep the first `None` forever. The key defaults to the first argument; pass `keyOf` when the function takes more than one. The result has the memoized function's `cache` and `clear`.
signatures: export function memoizeSomeOnly<A extends readonly unknown[], T>( fn: (...args: A) => Option<T>, keyOf: (...args: A) => unknown = (...args) => args[0], ): MemoizedFunction<A, Option<T>>

assets.name: memoizedSelector
assets.summary: Builds a selector that derives a value from state, and recomputes only when the inputs it picks out change.
assets.useWhen: a component or a subscriber derives data from a store, such as visible todos from the todos and the filter, and the derived value must stay the same object while its inputs do, so React and friends skip the re-render. `select` picks the inputs as a tuple; they are compared one by one by identity, the way immutable stores change. `combine` runs only when one of them changed. It remembers only the last inputs.
signatures: export function memoizedSelector<S, const I extends readonly unknown[], T>( select: (state: S) => I, combine: (...inputs: I) => T, ): (state: S) => T

assets.name: singleFlight
assets.summary: Wraps an async loader so calls with the same key made while one is running share it, and nothing is kept once it settles.
assets.useWhen: many callers ask for the same thing at the same moment, such as every request on a cold start reading one config row, or a burst of renders fetching one profile, but the answer must be fresh on the next call. `memoizeAsync` keeps the answer; this keeps it only while the request is in flight, so it removes duplicate requests without ever serving stale data. A rejection reaches every caller that shared it.
signatures: export function singleFlight<A extends readonly unknown[], T>( load: (...args: A) => Promise<T>, options: SingleFlightOptions<A> = {}, ): (...args: A) => Promise<T>

assets.name: staleIfError
assets.summary: Caches an async loader for a while, and when a reload fails, serves the last value that loaded, marked stale.
assets.useWhen: old data beats no data during an outage, such as prices, a catalog, a weather widget or remote config, and the screen can say "may be out of date". Values are reused for `ttlMs`; after that the next call reloads and waits. If the reload fails, the last good value comes back with `stale: true`. Only a key that never loaded fails.
signatures: export function staleIfError<T>( load: (key: string) => Promise<T>, options: StaleIfErrorOptions, ): (key: string) => Promise<Result<StaleIfErrorValue<T>, StaleIfErrorError>>

assets.name: staleWhileRevalidate
assets.summary: Serves a cached value at once even when it is old, and reloads it in the background so the next call gets a fresh one.
assets.useWhen: speed matters more than the last few seconds of freshness, such as a product page, exchange rates on a dashboard, or a list of a user's projects, so no caller should wait on a reload once a value exists. Only the very first call per key waits. A background reload that fails is ignored and the old value stays; concurrent reloads of one key share a request.
signatures: export function staleWhileRevalidate<T>( load: (key: string) => Promise<T>, options: StaleWhileRevalidateOptions, ): (key: string) => Promise<Result<T, StaleWhileRevalidateError>>

assets.name: taggedLoader
assets.summary: Caches an async loader by key, with tags on each entry so one write can drop every entry that depends on it.
assets.useWhen: one piece of data feeds many cached things whose keys don't share a shape, such as a team's report, its member list and its billing page, and a change to the team must drop them all. Each `load` names the tags its value depends on, like `team:7`; `invalidateTag('team:7')` drops every entry tagged with it. A key keeps the tags from its latest `load` call.
signatures: export function taggedLoader<T>(load: (key: string) => Promise<T>, options: TaggedLoaderOptions = {}): TaggedLoader<T>

assets.name: ttlLookupTable
assets.summary: Loads a whole reference table at once, keeps it for a while, and answers lookups by key from it.
assets.useWhen: lookups hit small, slow-changing reference data, such as currencies, countries, plans, feature flags or tax rates, and one request for the whole table beats one request per key. The table is indexed by `keyOf` once per load. A key not in the table is `Ok(None)`. Concurrent lookups share one load, and a failed load isn't kept, so the next lookup tries again.
signatures: export function ttlLookupTable<V>( loadAll: () => Promise<readonly V[]>, keyOf: (row: V) => string, options: TtlLookupTableOptions, ): (key: string) => Promise<Result<Option<V>, TtlLookupTableError>>

assets.name: weakDerived
assets.summary: Computes a value derived from an object once per object, and lets the cached value go when the object does.
assets.useWhen: the same object is read many times and something costly is built from it, such as an index by id over a list from the store, a parsed schema, or a lookup table for a config object. Objects are compared by identity, so this suits immutable data: a new array is new data and is derived again. Nothing leaks: once the source object is garbage-collected, so is its derived value.
signatures: export function weakDerived<S extends object, T>(derive: (source: S) => T): (source: S) => T

assets.name: writeThroughCache
assets.summary: Caches reads from a store, and sends writes to the store first, caching the new value only once the save succeeds.
assets.useWhen: a value is read far more than written, such as user settings, a profile or a feature configuration, and a read right after a write must see the write without going back to the database. The cache never holds a value the store rejected. Concurrent reads of one key share a load.
signatures: export function writeThroughCache<K, V>( store: WriteThroughCacheStore<K, V>, options: WriteThroughCacheOptions = {}, ): WriteThroughCache<K, V>

assets.name: bottomNBy
assets.summary: Returns the n items with the lowest score, lowest first, with equal scores kept in input order.
assets.useWhen: finding the cheapest offers, the fastest responses or the least-used features, where equal scores must come out in the same order every time. Unlike `R.takeFirstBy`, ties keep their input order. Asking for more items than there are returns them all, and an `n` of 0 or less returns an empty list.
signatures: export function bottomNBy<T>(items: readonly T[], n: number, score: (item: T) => number): readonly T[]
export function bottomNBy<T>(n: number, score: (item: T) => number): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: buildTree
assets.summary: Nests a flat list of rows with `id` and `parentId` into a tree, and returns the rows it couldn't place.
assets.useWhen: categories, comments, folders or an org chart come from a database as flat rows and the UI needs them nested. A `parentId` of `null` or `undefined` makes a root. Children keep their input order. A row whose parent is missing, or that sits in a cycle, can't hang from a root, so it lands in `orphans` instead of vanishing or looping forever. Ids compare as strings, so a `parentId` of `'1'` finds the row with `id: 1`.
signatures: export function buildTree<T extends BuildTreeItem>(items: readonly T[]): BuildTreeResult<T>

assets.name: chunkByWeight
assets.summary: Splits a list into chunks whose total weight stays under a limit, keeping the items in order.
assets.useWhen: batching rows into requests under a payload size, inserts under a parameter limit, or messages under a token budget. Items fill the current chunk until the next one would push it past `maxWeight`, then a new chunk starts. An item heavier than the limit on its own gets a chunk to itself instead of being dropped, so check for those if the limit is hard. For a limit on the number of items, use `R.chunk`.
signatures: export function chunkByWeight<T>( items: readonly T[], maxWeight: number, weight: (item: T) => number, ): readonly (readonly T[])[]
export function chunkByWeight<T>( maxWeight: number, weight: (item: T) => number, ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly (readonly T[])[]

assets.name: competitionRankBy
assets.summary: Ranks items by score, highest first, the way sports tables do: ties share a rank, then places are skipped (1, 1, 3).
assets.useWhen: showing a leaderboard, exam results or a sales contest where "3rd" should mean two people scored higher. Items with equal scores keep their input order. For ranks without gaps (1, 1, 2), use `denseRankBy`.
signatures: export function competitionRankBy<T>( items: readonly T[], score: (item: T) => number, ): readonly CompetitionRankByEntry<T>[]
export function competitionRankBy<T>( score: (item: T) => number, ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly CompetitionRankByEntry<T>[]

assets.name: dedupeByKeepBest
assets.summary: Keeps one item per key, the one that sorts first by a comparator, and returns what it dropped.
assets.useWhen: several records share a key and a rule picks the winner, such as the cheapest offer per product, the highest version per package or the best score per player. Build the rule from `@ontologyio/receta/compare`: `descending(...)` keeps the largest. On a tie the copy that came first wins. Kept items stay where they stood in the input. Keys compare as strings, so `1` and `'1'` are the same key.
signatures: export function dedupeByKeepBest<T>( items: readonly T[], key: (item: T) => string | number, compare: Comparator<T>, ): DedupeByKeepBestResult<T>
export function dedupeByKeepBest<T>( key: (item: T) => string | number, compare: Comparator<T>, ): (items: readonly T[]) => DedupeByKeepBestResult<T>

assets.name: dedupeByKeepFirst
assets.summary: Removes items whose key was already seen, keeping the first, and returns what it dropped.
assets.useWhen: importing rows from a CSV or a form where a repeated email, SKU or id should be skipped and reported, as in "2 duplicate rows were skipped". Keys compare as strings, so `1` and `'1'` are the same key. Normalize the key yourself if case or spaces should not matter, such as `(row) => row.email.trim().toLowerCase()`.
signatures: export function dedupeByKeepFirst<T>( items: readonly T[], key: (item: T) => string | number, ): DedupeByKeepFirstResult<T>
export function dedupeByKeepFirst<T>( key: (item: T) => string | number, ): (items: readonly T[]) => DedupeByKeepFirstResult<T>

assets.name: dedupeByKeepLast
assets.summary: Removes items whose key comes again later, keeping the last copy, and returns what it dropped.
assets.useWhen: a later row should override an earlier one, as when a spreadsheet is uploaded again with corrections, or a change feed sends several versions of one record. Each kept item sits where its last copy stood. Keys compare as strings, so `1` and `'1'` are the same key.
signatures: export function dedupeByKeepLast<T>( items: readonly T[], key: (item: T) => string | number, ): DedupeByKeepLastResult<T>
export function dedupeByKeepLast<T>( key: (item: T) => string | number, ): (items: readonly T[]) => DedupeByKeepLastResult<T>

assets.name: denseRankBy
assets.summary: Ranks items by score, highest first, where ties share a rank and no numbers are skipped: 1, 1, 2.
assets.useWhen: labelling tiers or levels, such as "gold, silver, bronze" for the three best distinct scores, or grouping equal results under one place number. Items with equal scores keep their input order. For sports-style ranks that skip after a tie (1, 1, 3), use `competitionRankBy`.
signatures: export function denseRankBy<T>(items: readonly T[], score: (item: T) => number): readonly DenseRankByEntry<T>[]
export function denseRankBy<T>(score: (item: T) => number): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly DenseRankByEntry<T>[]

assets.name: diffById
assets.summary: Compares two versions of a list by `id`: what was added, removed, changed (and which fields), and kept.
assets.useWhen: syncing a local copy with the server, writing an audit log ("price changed"), or turning a form's list into create, update and delete calls. Each part keeps the order of the list it comes from. Ids are expected to be unique in each list; a repeated id counts once, with its last copy. Ids compare as strings, so `1` and `'1'` are the same id.
signatures: export function diffById<T extends { readonly id: string | number }>( before: readonly T[], after: readonly NoInfer<T>[], ): DiffByIdResult<T>
export function diffById<T extends { readonly id: string | number }>( after: readonly T[], ): (before: readonly T[]) => DiffByIdResult<T>

assets.name: duplicatesBy
assets.summary: Finds the keys that more than one item shares, with all the items that share each one.
assets.useWhen: validating an import or a form list before saving, to tell the user "these 3 rows use the same email", or auditing data for repeated SKUs or slugs. Groups come in the order their key first appears. Keys compare as strings, so `1` and `'1'` are the same key; trim or lowercase in `key` when that should count too.
signatures: export function duplicatesBy<T>(items: readonly T[], key: (item: T) => string | number): readonly DuplicatesByGroup<T>[]
export function duplicatesBy<T>( key: (item: T) => string | number, ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly DuplicatesByGroup<T>[]

assets.name: findTreePath
assets.summary: Finds the first node that matches and returns the path to it, from its root down to the node itself.
assets.useWhen: building breadcrumbs for the page a user is on, expanding the ancestors of a selected node in a tree view, or showing where a file lives. Nodes are searched depth-first, so with several matches the one met first wins. Returns `None` when nothing matches.
signatures: export function findTreePath<T>( roots: readonly T[], children: (node: T) => readonly T[], isTarget: (node: T) => boolean, ): Option<readonly T[]>
export function findTreePath<T>( children: (node: T) => readonly T[], isTarget: (node: T) => boolean, ): (roots: readonly T[]) => Option<readonly T[]>

assets.name: frequencyTable
assets.summary: Counts items per key and lists each key with its count and share of the total, most common first.
assets.useWhen: filling facet counts in a search sidebar ("Red (12)"), showing traffic by browser, or summarizing survey answers. Keys with equal counts come in natural order, so `'v2'` comes before `'v10'`. Shares are fractions; format them with `toPercent` from `@ontologyio/receta/number`.
signatures: export function frequencyTable<T>(items: readonly T[], key: (item: T) => string): readonly FrequencyTableRow[]
export function frequencyTable<T>(key: (item: T) => string): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly FrequencyTableRow[]

assets.name: groupConsecutiveWithin
assets.summary: Groups runs of neighbouring items that share a key and follow each other within a time gap.
assets.useWhen: stacking chat bubbles from one sender, collapsing an activity feed into "Ana made 3 edits", or grouping log lines into bursts. A new group starts when the key changes or when more than `maxGapMs` passed since the previous item. Pass `Infinity` to group by key alone. Items should already be in time order; this doesn't sort them.
signatures: export function groupConsecutiveWithin<T>( items: readonly T[], key: (item: T) => string | number, at: (item: T) => Date | number, maxGapMs: number, ): readonly GroupConsecutiveWithinGroup<T>[]
export function groupConsecutiveWithin<T>( key: (item: T) => string | number, at: (item: T) => Date | number, maxGapMs: number, ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly GroupConsecutiveWithinGroup<T>[]

assets.name: indexByIdStrict
assets.summary: Builds an id-to-item lookup, and fails with every repeated id when ids aren't unique.
assets.useWhen: normalizing API data into a lookup by id, or loading seed data or a config list where a repeated id is a bug that must not be hidden by "last one wins". The error lists all repeated ids at once, so one run shows every row to fix. Ids compare as strings, so `1` and `'1'` count as the same id.
signatures: export function indexByIdStrict<T extends { readonly id: string | number }>( items: readonly T[], ): Result<Readonly<Record<T['id'], T>>, IndexByIdStrictError>

assets.name: insertSorted
assets.summary: Inserts an item into a list that is already sorted, at the place that keeps it sorted.
assets.useWhen: a new message, event or score arrives for a list kept in order, and sorting the whole list again would be wasteful or would reshuffle equal items. The position is found by binary search. The new item goes after any items it ties with, so arrival order holds among equals. The list must already be sorted by the same comparator.
signatures: export function insertSorted<T>( items: readonly NoInfer<T>[], item: NoInfer<T>, compare: Comparator<T>, ): readonly T[]
export function insertSorted<T>( item: NoInfer<T>, compare: Comparator<T>, ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: latestBy
assets.summary: Keeps the newest item per key and lists them newest first.
assets.useWhen: building an inbox with the last message per conversation, the current status per order from an event log, or the latest reading per sensor. When two items of one key share a timestamp, the later one in the input wins, as in an append-only log. Keys compare as strings, so `1` and `'1'` are the same key. Timestamps are `Date`s or epoch numbers; parse ISO strings first.
signatures: export function latestBy<T>( items: readonly T[], key: (item: T) => string | number, timestamp: (item: T) => Date | number, ): readonly T[]
export function latestBy<T>( key: (item: T) => string | number, timestamp: (item: T) => Date | number, ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: leftJoinBy
assets.summary: Pairs each item of one list with the matching item of another, by keys that can differ on each side.
assets.useWhen: showing orders with their customer, line items with their product, or events with their user, when the two lists came from separate requests. Every left item comes back, in order, with `None` when nothing matches, as in a SQL left join. When several right items match, the first one wins. Keys compare as strings, so `7` and `'7'` match.
signatures: export function leftJoinBy<TLeft, TRight>( left: readonly TLeft[], right: readonly TRight[], leftKey: (item: TLeft) => string | number, rightKey: (item: TRight) => string | number, ): readonly LeftJoinByRow<TLeft, TRight>[]

export function leftJoinBy<TLeft, TRight>( right: readonly TRight[], leftKey: (item: TLeft) => string | number, rightKey: (item: TRight) => string | number, ): (left: readonly TLeft[]) => readonly LeftJoinByRow<TLeft, TRight>[]

assets.name: limitPerGroup
assets.summary: Keeps at most `max` items per key, dropping the rest, and leaves the survivors in input order.
assets.useWhen: diversifying search results to at most 2 products per seller, showing 3 posts per author in a feed, or capping notifications per type. Within each key the earliest items stay, so sort the list by relevance first. A `max` of 0 or less returns an empty list.
signatures: export function limitPerGroup<T>(items: readonly T[], key: (item: T) => string | number, max: number): readonly T[]
export function limitPerGroup<T>(key: (item: T) => string | number, max: number): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: mergeById
assets.summary: Applies partial patches to a list by `id`, and returns the patches that matched no item.
assets.useWhen: an API answers a bulk edit with only the changed fields, or a form edits a few columns of many rows, and the list should take those fields without replacing whole items. Several patches for one id apply in order, so a later field wins. A patch with an unknown id can't become an item, since it lacks fields, so it comes back in `unmatched` to report or refetch. Patches are shallow: a nested object in a patch replaces the whole nested object.
signatures: export function mergeById<T extends { readonly id: string | number }>( items: readonly T[], patches: readonly MergeByIdPatch<NoInfer<T>>[], ): MergeByIdResult<T>
export function mergeById<T extends { readonly id: string | number }>( patches: readonly MergeByIdPatch<T>[], ): (items: readonly T[]) => MergeByIdResult<T>

assets.name: moveItemById
assets.summary: Moves the item with an `id` to a new position, as a drag and drop reorder does.
assets.useWhen: a user drags a card, a playlist track or a menu entry and drops it at a position. `toIndex` is where the item ends up. A drop past either end lands at that end, so `-5` means first and `99` means last. A missing id is an error, since the list the user saw is no longer the list being changed.
signatures: export function moveItemById<T extends { readonly id: string | number }>( items: readonly T[], id: T['id'], toIndex: number, ): Result<readonly T[], MoveItemByIdError>
export function moveItemById<T extends { readonly id: string | number }>( id: T['id'], toIndex: number, ): (items: readonly T[]) => Result<readonly T[], MoveItemByIdError>

assets.name: movingAverage
assets.summary: Smooths a series with a trailing moving average: each output is the mean of `size` values in a row.
assets.useWhen: drawing a 7-day average over daily sign-ups, smoothing latency samples, or damping noise before spotting a trend. The result is `size - 1` values shorter than the input, and its first value averages the first `size` inputs. A series shorter than `size`, or a `size` below 1, gives `[]`. A fractional `size` is rounded down.
signatures: export function movingAverage(values: readonly number[], size: number): readonly number[]
export function movingAverage(size: number): (values: readonly number[]) => readonly number[]

assets.name: pageNumbers
assets.summary: Lists the page buttons for a pager, with gaps for the hidden pages: 1 … 5 6 7 … 20.
assets.useWhen: rendering numbered pagination under a table or search results. The first and last pages always show, with `siblings` pages on each side of the current one. The list keeps the same length on every page, so the buttons don't jump around as the user clicks, and a gap that would hide a single page near either end shows that page instead.
signatures: export function pageNumbers(options: PageNumbersOptions): readonly PageNumbersItem[]

assets.name: paginateClamped
assets.summary: Cuts one page out of a list, clamping a page number that is out of range, with the numbers a pager needs.
assets.useWhen: a table or list reads the page from the URL, where `?page=99`, `?page=0` or `?page=abc` must show a real page instead of an empty one. A page past the end shows the last page, and anything below 1 or not a number shows page 1. `from` and `to` fill "Showing 21–40 of 95". A `pageSize` below 1 counts as 1.
signatures: export function paginateClamped<T>(items: readonly T[], options: PaginateClampedOptions): PaginateClampedPage<T>
export function paginateClamped<T>(options: PaginateClampedOptions): (items: readonly T[]) => PaginateClampedPage<T>

assets.name: paginateCursorStrict
assets.summary: Returns the page after a cursor, and fails when the cursor matches no item instead of starting over.
assets.useWhen: serving "load more" or infinite scroll from a list, where a cursor can go stale because its item was deleted. Receta's `paginateCursor` quietly returns the first page for an unknown cursor, which shows the user the same items again; this returns an error to answer with a 400 or a reload. Cursors compare with `===`, so use strings or numbers.
signatures: export function paginateCursorStrict<T, C extends string | number>( items: readonly T[], getCursor: (item: T) => C, options: PaginateCursorStrictOptions<NoInfer<C>>, ): Result<CursorPaginatedResult<T, C>, PaginateCursorStrictError<C>>

export function paginateCursorStrict<T, C extends string | number>( getCursor: (item: T) => C, options: PaginateCursorStrictOptions<NoInfer<C>>, ): (items: readonly T[]) => Result<CursorPaginatedResult<T, C>, PaginateCursorStrictError<C>>

assets.name: pairwiseDeltas
assets.summary: Pairs each item with the next one and gives the difference between them, absolute and relative.
assets.useWhen: showing month-over-month revenue, the growth between releases, or how much a price moved since the last reading. A list of n items gives n - 1 pairs. The relative change is measured against the size of the starting value, so a move from -10 to -5 is +50%. It is `None` when the starting value is 0, where a percentage has no meaning.
signatures: export function pairwiseDeltas<T>( items: readonly T[], value: (item: T) => number, ): readonly PairwiseDeltasEntry<T>[]
export function pairwiseDeltas<T>(value: (item: T) => number): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly PairwiseDeltasEntry<T>[]

assets.name: reconcileById
assets.summary: Matches the records of two sources by `id`: those only on the left, only on the right, and paired in both.
assets.useWhen: checking two systems against each other, such as users in the database against customers in Stripe, or an export against an import, to find what is missing on each side. The two sides can hold different shapes, since only `id` is compared. When a side repeats an id, its last copy is the one paired. Ids compare as strings, so `1` and `'1'` match.
signatures: export function reconcileById< TLeft extends { readonly id: string | number }, TRight extends { readonly id: string | number }, >(left: readonly TLeft[], right: readonly TRight[]): ReconcileByIdResult<TLeft, TRight>

export function reconcileById<TRight extends { readonly id: string | number }>( right: readonly TRight[], ): <TLeft extends { readonly id: string | number }>(left: readonly TLeft[]) => ReconcileByIdResult<TLeft, TRight>

assets.name: removeById
assets.summary: Removes the item with an `id` and hands it back, so an optimistic delete can be undone.
assets.useWhen: deleting a row in the UI before the server confirms. Keep `removed` and put it back with `insertAt` if the request fails. A missing id leaves the list as it was and gives `None`, never removing another item. Only the first item with the id is removed.
signatures: export function removeById<T extends { readonly id: string | number }>( items: readonly T[], id: T['id'], ): RemoveByIdResult<T>
export function removeById<T extends { readonly id: string | number }>( id: T['id'], ): (items: readonly T[]) => RemoveByIdResult<T>

assets.name: sampleEvenly
assets.summary: Picks `count` items spread evenly across a list, always keeping the first and the last.
assets.useWhen: thinning 1,000 points to 50 for a sparkline, choosing which dates to label on a chart axis, or taking preview frames from a long recording. Picks keep their input order. Asking for as many items as the list has, or more, returns the whole list, and a `count` of 1 returns the first item. It doesn't look at values, so a short spike between picks can be lost; use a peak-preserving method when that matters.
signatures: export function sampleEvenly<T>(items: readonly T[], count: number): readonly T[]
export function sampleEvenly(count: number): <T>(items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: splitEvenly
assets.summary: Splits a list into a given number of parts whose sizes differ by at most one, keeping the order.
assets.useWhen: dividing work among n workers, laying out items in n columns, or sharding a batch across n requests, where `R.chunk` would fix the size of each part instead of how many parts there are. Bigger parts come first. There are never more parts than items, so 2 items split into 3 parts give 2 parts of one. A `parts` below 1 gives `[]`.
signatures: export function splitEvenly<T>(items: readonly T[], parts: number): readonly (readonly T[])[]
export function splitEvenly(parts: number): <T>(items: readonly T[]) => readonly (readonly T[])[]

assets.name: tagChanges
assets.summary: Compares two lists of tags, roles or ids and says which were added, removed and kept.
assets.useWhen: a user edits the tags on a post, the roles of a member or the labels of an issue, and the app must send one "add" and one "remove" call per change, or log them for an audit trail. Each value counts once, however often it repeats. Values compare exactly, so trim and lowercase them first if `'Urgent'` and `'urgent'` are the same tag.
signatures: export function tagChanges<T extends string | number>( before: readonly T[], after: readonly T[], ): TagChangesResult<T>
export function tagChanges<T extends string | number>( after: readonly T[], ): (before: readonly T[]) => TagChangesResult<T>

assets.name: topNBy
assets.summary: Returns the n items with the highest score, highest first, with equal scores kept in input order.
assets.useWhen: showing a leaderboard, the top 5 products by revenue or the slowest endpoints, where equal scores must come out in the same order every time. Unlike `R.takeFirstBy`, ties keep their input order. Asking for more items than there are returns them all, and an `n` of 0 or less returns an empty list.
signatures: export function topNBy<T>(items: readonly T[], n: number, score: (item: T) => number): readonly T[]
export function topNBy<T>(n: number, score: (item: T) => number): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: totalsBy
assets.summary: Groups items by a key, adds up a number per group, and lists the groups largest first.
assets.useWhen: building a report row per category, such as hours per team, revenue per product or errors per endpoint, where the biggest group should come first.
signatures: export function totalsBy<T>( items: readonly T[], key: (item: T) => string, value: (item: T) => number, ): readonly GroupTotal[]
export function totalsBy<T>( key: (item: T) => string, value: (item: T) => number, ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly GroupTotal[]

assets.name: treeToRows
assets.summary: Turns a tree into the rows a tree table or file explorer shows, skipping the children of collapsed nodes.
assets.useWhen: rendering nested folders, comments or categories as a flat list with indentation, where the user opens and closes nodes. Rows come in depth-first order: a node, then its open children, then its next sibling. `depth` is the indent level, `hasChildren` says whether to draw an expand arrow, and `expanded` whether it points down.
signatures: export function treeToRows<T>( roots: readonly T[], children: (node: T) => readonly T[], isExpanded: (node: T) => boolean, ): readonly TreeToRowsRow<T>[]
export function treeToRows<T>( children: (node: T) => readonly T[], isExpanded: (node: T) => boolean, ): (roots: readonly T[]) => readonly TreeToRowsRow<T>[]

assets.name: updateById
assets.summary: Applies a change to the item with an `id`, or says the id is missing instead of doing nothing.
assets.useWhen: an edit targets one row and a missing row means the screen is stale, so the caller should refetch or show an error rather than silently drop the edit. The updated item keeps its position. Only the first item with the id is changed.
signatures: export function updateById<T extends { readonly id: string | number }>( items: readonly T[], id: T['id'], update: (item: T) => T, ): Result<readonly T[], UpdateByIdError>
export function updateById<T extends { readonly id: string | number }>( id: T['id'], update: (item: T) => T, ): (items: readonly T[]) => Result<readonly T[], UpdateByIdError>

assets.name: upsertById
assets.summary: Replaces the item with the same `id` where it stands, or appends the item when the id is new.
assets.useWhen: a form saves a record, a websocket pushes one, or an optimistic update lands, and the cached list should show it without a refetch. The list's order doesn't change for an edit. When the list holds the id twice, only the first copy is replaced. Returns a new list and leaves the input alone.

assets.name: upsertManyById
assets.summary: Merges a batch of fresh items into a list by `id`: known ids are replaced in place, new ids appended.
assets.useWhen: a refresh, a websocket batch or the next page of a feed brings items the cached list may already hold, and the list should show the fresh copies without losing its order. New items are appended in the order they first appear in the batch. When the batch holds an id twice, its last copy wins.

assets.name: variantCombinations
assets.summary: Lists every combination of product options, such as each size with each colour, as one record per variant.
assets.useWhen: generating the SKUs or variant rows for a product with options, a test matrix of browsers and screen sizes, or every price plan with every billing period. The first option changes slowest. An option with no values means no variant can exist, so the result is `[]`. A product without options has exactly one variant, `{}`.
signatures: export function variantCombinations<const O extends VariantCombinationsOptions>( options: O, ): readonly VariantCombinationsVariant<O>[]

assets.name: allMatchingRules
assets.summary: Checks every named rule against one value and returns all that match, in rule order.
assets.useWhen: several outcomes can apply at once, such as badges on a profile, warnings on a checkout, labels on a support ticket or flags on a transaction, and each needs its rule's name for display or audit. Every rule runs, so rules must not depend on each other. No match gives an empty list.

assets.name: applyEnabledSteps
assets.summary: Runs a list of flagged steps in order, applying each one only when its feature flag is on.
assets.useWhen: a payload, a price or a page model passes through several optional stages, each behind its own flag, such as tax rules, a new ranking and a promo banner that roll out independently. Steps run in list order and each sees the previous step's output. Only the value `true` turns a flag on; a missing flag, `'true'` or `1` leave the step out.

assets.useWhen: a step in a pipeline sits behind a feature flag, such as a new price calculation, a redesigned payload or an experimental ranking, and flags come from remote config or the environment. Only the value `true` turns a flag on: a missing flag, `false`, `'true'`, `1` or a prototype key such as `constructor` all leave it off, so a typo in config fails closed.

assets.name: assignVariant
assets.summary: Assigns a user to one arm of an A/B test by weight, always the same arm for the same user and experiment.
assets.useWhen: splitting users between a control and one or more variants, on the server or the client, without storing assignments. The user id and the experiment key are hashed to a point along the arms' combined weight, and the arm covering that point wins. Keep the arms and their order fixed while the test runs: changing a weight moves some users to another arm. `None` when there are no arms or every weight is 0.

export function assignVariant<V extends string>( experiment: AssignVariantExperiment<V>, ): (subjectId: string) => Option<V>

assets.name: authorizeAction
assets.summary: Checks that someone may perform an action: signed in, not suspended, and holding the permission.
assets.useWhen: an API handler, a server action or a UI button needs a yes or a reason before it acts. The checks run in that order, so the error code maps straight to a response: `NOT_SIGNED_IN` is a 401, `SUSPENDED` and `FORBIDDEN` are 403s. A granted `posts:*` covers every `posts:` permission and `*` covers all. The `Ok` holds the actor, typed as passed in.

assets.name: bandOf
assets.summary: Labels a number with the band it falls in, where each band starts at a threshold and runs to the next.
assets.useWhen: turning a number into a level, such as a score into a grade, yearly spend into a loyalty tier, a count into a size, or a latency into a rating. The band with the highest `from` at or below the value wins, so bands can be listed in any order. The top band has no upper limit. `None` when the value is below every band or is `NaN`, so add a band from `-Infinity` when every number needs a label.

export function bandOf<L>(bands: readonly BandOfBand<L>[]): (value: number) => Option<L>

assets.useWhen: a SaaS app gates creating a project, inviting a seat or adding an integration by the customer's plan, and the UI needs an upgrade prompt with a reason. `NOT_IN_PLAN` when the plan doesn't list the feature or lists 0; `QUOTA_EXCEEDED` when `used + adding` would pass the limit. Use `Infinity` for unlimited. The `Ok` holds what remains once the action is done.

assets.name: classifyHttpStatus
assets.summary: Names the class of an HTTP status code: informational, success, redirect, client or server error.
assets.useWhen: a fetch wrapper, a logger or a metrics label needs to branch on the kind of response instead of listing codes. A number outside 100–599, or one that isn't whole, comes back as `None`, so a corrupted status can't pass for a success.
signatures: export function classifyHttpStatus(status: number): Option<ClassifyHttpStatusClass>

assets.name: cvssSeverity
assets.summary: Turns a CVSS base score into its severity: none, low, medium, high or critical.
assets.useWhen: a vulnerability scanner, a dependency audit or an advisory feed gives a numeric score and a report, a badge or a CI gate needs the word. Uses the CVSS v3 and v4 bands: 0 none, 0.1–3.9 low, 4.0–6.9 medium, 7.0–8.9 high, 9.0–10.0 critical. A score outside 0–10, or not a number, is an error rather than a guess.
signatures: export function cvssSeverity(score: number): Result<CvssSeverityLabel, CvssSeverityError>

assets.name: decisionTable
assets.summary: Looks up an outcome in a table of rows, each a set of field conditions, and falls back to a default.
assets.useWhen: a business rule is a table someone could write in a spreadsheet, such as shipping rates by country and weight, approval levels by amount and department, or SLA targets by plan and severity. Rows are read top to bottom and the first row whose conditions all hold wins. `otherwise` is required, so every input gets an outcome.
signatures: export function decisionTable<T extends object, U>( input: T, rows: readonly DecisionTableRow<T, U>[], otherwise: U, ): U
export function decisionTable<T extends object, U>( rows: readonly DecisionTableRow<T, U>[], otherwise: U, ): (input: T) => U

assets.name: dispatchCommand
assets.summary: Runs the handler registered under a command's name, or says the command is unknown.
assets.useWhen: a CLI, a chat bot's slash commands, a job queue or an RPC endpoint maps a name that arrives as text to a function. Only the table's own keys count, so a name such as `constructor` or `toString` is unknown instead of reaching `Object.prototype`. Names match exactly, case included. The handler's return value comes back in `Ok`.
signatures: export function dispatchCommand<A, U>( command: DispatchCommandInput<A>, handlers: Readonly<Record<string, (args: A) => U>>, ): Result<U, DispatchCommandError>

assets.name: fileKind
assets.summary: Sorts a MIME type into a kind of file, such as image, spreadsheet or archive, for icons and previews.
assets.useWhen: a file list, an attachment chip or an upload queue shows an icon or picks a previewer by the file's `type`. Parameters such as `; charset=utf-8` and letter case are ignored. CSV counts as a spreadsheet; JSON, XML and YAML count as text. `None` for anything else, such as `application/octet-stream`, so the caller shows a generic icon.
signatures: export function fileKind(mimeType: string): Option<FileKindLabel>

assets.name: firstMatchingRule
assets.summary: Checks named rules in order and returns the first one that matches, with its outcome and name.
assets.useWhen: a decision such as a discount, a routing queue or a risk flag comes from an ordered list of rules, and you need to record which rule decided. Order matters: put the specific rules before the broad ones. `None` when no rule matches, so add a last rule with `when: () => true` if there must always be an outcome.
signatures: export function firstMatchingRule<T, U>( value: T, rules: readonly FirstMatchingRuleEntry<T, U>[], ): Option<FirstMatchingRuleHit<U>>
export function firstMatchingRule<T, U>( rules: readonly FirstMatchingRuleEntry<T, U>[], ): (value: T) => Option<FirstMatchingRuleHit<U>>

assets.name: guardInput
assets.summary: Runs checks in order and stops at the first that fails, returning its code and message.
assets.useWhen: an action needs a gate before it runs, such as a command's arguments, a request about to be queued or a value about to be saved, and only the first reason matters. Each check is `[test, code, message]`, where the message can be a function of the value. Checks after the failing one don't run, so a later check can rely on the earlier ones. To report every failing check at once, use a Validation instead.
signatures: export function guardInput<T, C extends string>( value: T, checks: readonly GuardInputCheck<T, C>[], ): Result<T, GuardInputError<T, C>>
export function guardInput<T, C extends string>( checks: readonly GuardInputCheck<T, C>[], ): (value: T) => Result<T, GuardInputError<T, C>>

assets.name: guardUpload
assets.summary: Checks an uploaded file against a size limit and an accept list before it is stored or sent on.
assets.useWhen: a server receives a file, or a browser is about to send one, and must refuse it with a reason the user can act on. The accept list works like the HTML `accept` attribute, so the same list can guard the input and the server. Checks run in order: not empty, not over `maxBytes`, then an accepted type. Sizes in messages use 1024-byte units.
signatures: export function guardUpload<F extends GuardUploadFile>( file: F, options: GuardUploadOptions, ): Result<F, GuardUploadError>
export function guardUpload<F extends GuardUploadFile>( options: GuardUploadOptions, ): (file: F) => Result<F, GuardUploadError>

assets.name: guardWithdrawal
assets.summary: Approves a withdrawal or transfer only if the amount is valid, covered by the balance and within today's limit.
assets.useWhen: money is about to leave an account, a wallet or a prepaid balance, and the caller needs one reason to show when it can't. Checks run in order: the amount must be a whole, positive number of minor units (cents), then no more than the balance, then no more than what is left of the daily limit. The `Ok` holds the request unchanged, for the next step.
signatures: export function guardWithdrawal( request: GuardWithdrawalRequest, ): Result<GuardWithdrawalRequest, GuardWithdrawalError>

assets.name: inRollout
assets.summary: Decides whether a user is in a percentage rollout, the same way every time, with no stored state.
assets.useWhen: turning a feature on for 5%, then 25%, then 100% of users, or sampling a share of requests or tenants, and the answer must not flicker between page loads or servers. The user and the flag name are hashed into one of 10,000 buckets, so the same pair always gets the same answer, raising the percentage only adds users, and two flags at 10% pick mostly different users. Not a security boundary: anyone who knows the ids can compute the answer.
signatures: export function inRollout(subjectId: string, plan: InRolloutPlan): boolean
export function inRollout(plan: InRolloutPlan): (subjectId: string) => boolean

assets.name: isRetryableStatus
assets.summary: Says whether an HTTP request that got this status is safe and worth sending again.
assets.useWhen: deciding whether a failed call goes back to the retry loop. 408, 425, 429 and 503 are retried for any method, because the server didn't act on the request. 500, 502 and 504 are retried only for idempotent methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT, DELETE), because a POST or PATCH may already have taken effect. Every other status, 2xx included, is `false`. The method is compared without regard to case.
signatures: export function isRetryableStatus(status: number, method: string): boolean
export function isRetryableStatus(method: string): (status: number) => boolean

assets.name: logLevelForResponse
assets.summary: Picks the log level for a finished HTTP request from its status and how long it took.
assets.useWhen: an access-log middleware, a fetch wrapper or a tracing hook writes one line per request and the noise level matters: 5xx is `error`, 4xx or a response at or over `slowMs` is `warn`, everything else is `info`. Status wins over time, so a slow 500 is still an error.
signatures: export function logLevelForResponse( entry: LogLevelForResponseEntry, options: LogLevelForResponseOptions, ): LogLevelForResponseLevel
export function logLevelForResponse( options: LogLevelForResponseOptions, ): (entry: LogLevelForResponseEntry) => LogLevelForResponseLevel

assets.name: mapNonBlank
assets.summary: Trims an optional text value and transforms it only when something is left, otherwise `None`.
assets.useWhen: an optional form field, query parameter or CSV cell arrives as `null`, `undefined`, `''` or spaces when the user left it empty, and only real content should be processed, such as a coupon code to uppercase or a middle name to capitalize. The transform gets the trimmed text and never runs for blank input.
signatures: export function mapNonBlank<U>( text: string | null | undefined, transform: (trimmed: string) => U, ): Option<U>
export function mapNonBlank<U>( transform: (trimmed: string) => U, ): (text: string | null | undefined) => Option<U>

assets.name: matchPath
assets.summary: Matches a URL path against a pattern such as `/users/:id`, returning the named parts it captured.
assets.useWhen: a server, a service worker or a client-side router must tell whether a path belongs to a route and read its parameters, without pulling in a router. `:name` captures one segment and a final `*` captures the rest, under the key `*`. Captured values are URL-decoded. The query and the fragment are ignored, and so are repeated and trailing slashes. Literal segments compare exactly, case included. `None` when the path doesn't fit or holds a malformed escape.
signatures: export function matchPath(path: string, pattern: string): Option<Readonly<Record<string, string>>>
export function matchPath(pattern: string): (path: string) => Option<Readonly<Record<string, string>>>

assets.name: negotiateLanguage
assets.summary: Picks the best supported locale for an `Accept-Language` header, honoring its quality weights.
assets.useWhen: a server, an edge function or a middleware chooses the language of a page, an email or an API message from what the browser asks for. Preferences are tried from the highest `q` down, in header order on ties; for each, an exact tag wins, then the same language with another region (`fr-CH` finds `fr`, `en` finds `en-US`). `q=0` means "not this one". The locale comes back as spelled in `supported`. `None` when nothing fits, so the caller picks the default.
signatures: export function negotiateLanguage( header: string | null | undefined, supported: readonly string[], ): Option<string>
export function negotiateLanguage( supported: readonly string[], ): (header: string | null | undefined) => Option<string>

assets.name: nextInCycle
assets.summary: Returns the value after the current one in a fixed cycle, wrapping from the last back to the first.
assets.useWhen: a control steps through a short list of states, such as a sort header going asc → desc → none, a theme toggle going light → dark → system, ArrowDown moving through menu items, or a carousel's next button. A current value that isn't in the cycle restarts at the first, so stale state recovers. Values compare with `===`. `None` only for an empty cycle.
signatures: export function nextInCycle<T>(current: T, cycle: readonly T[]): Option<T>
export function nextInCycle<T>(cycle: readonly T[]): (current: T) => Option<T>

assets.name: normalizeThenGuard
assets.summary: Builds a function that cleans a value up first, then checks it in order and stops at the first failure.
assets.useWhen: users type a value in many forms and the checks should see one, such as a username, a coupon code, a tag or an SKU that is trimmed and lowercased before its rules run. The `Ok` holds the normalized value, ready to store. The error keeps both the raw input and the normalized value, so a message can quote either. A message can be a function of the value.
signatures: export function normalizeThenGuard<I, T, C extends string>( normalize: (input: I) => T, checks: readonly NormalizeThenGuardCheck<T, C>[], ): (input: I) => Result<T, NormalizeThenGuardError<I, T, C>>

assets.name: previousInCycle
assets.summary: Returns the value before the current one in a fixed cycle, wrapping from the first back to the last.
assets.useWhen: stepping backwards through a short list, such as ArrowUp in a menu or listbox, a carousel's back button, or shift-clicking a toggle to reverse it. A current value that isn't in the cycle starts from the last, so ArrowUp with nothing selected lands on the bottom item. Values compare with `===`. `None` only for an empty cycle.
signatures: export function previousInCycle<T>(current: T, cycle: readonly T[]): Option<T>
export function previousInCycle<T>(cycle: readonly T[]): (current: T) => Option<T>

assets.name: pullRequestSize
assets.summary: Labels a pull request XS to XXL by the lines it changes, for size labels and review routing.
assets.useWhen: a bot or a CI step labels pull requests, asks for a second reviewer on big ones, or nudges authors to split them. Takes the `additions` and `deletions` the GitHub and GitLab APIs report and adds them up. Bands follow the Kubernetes size labels: XS under 10, S under 30, M under 100, L under 500, XL under 1000, XXL from 1000.
signatures: export function pullRequestSize(changes: { readonly additions: number readonly deletions: number }): PullRequestSizeLabel

assets.name: responsiveValue
assets.summary: Picks the value for a screen width from a mobile-first map such as `{ base: 1, md: 2, lg: 4 }`.
assets.useWhen: code outside CSS needs a value per breakpoint, such as grid columns for a virtualized list, chart ticks, page size or image width, and should follow the same breakpoints as the stylesheet. Breakpoints are Tailwind's defaults (sm 640, md 768, lg 1024, xl 1280, 2xl 1536), each a minimum width. The largest breakpoint the width reaches that has a value wins; `base` covers everything below and any gap.

assets.name: routeEvent
assets.summary: Sends an event to the handler registered for its `type`, or returns `None` when nothing handles it.
assets.useWhen: processing webhooks (Stripe, GitHub, Slack), queue messages or UI actions where you handle some event types and must acknowledge the rest without failing. Each handler receives the event narrowed to its type. Only the table's own keys count, so an event typed `constructor` from an untrusted sender is unhandled. Reach for `dispatchCommand` instead when an unknown name is a mistake the caller should hear about.
