assets.name: routePath
assets.summary: Finds the first route in a table whose pattern matches a URL path, with the parameters it captured.
assets.useWhen: dispatching requests in a small server, a worker or an edge function, or choosing a screen in a client, without a router library. Routes are tried in the table's order, so list `/users/new` before `/users/:id`. Patterns use `:name` for one segment and a final `*` for the rest; values are URL-decoded, and the query, the fragment and extra slashes are ignored. `None` when no route matches, which is the 404.

export function routePath<K extends string>( routes: Readonly<Record<K, string>>, ): (path: string) => Option<RoutePathMatch<K>>

assets.name: safeCall
assets.summary: Wraps a function that may throw so it returns a Result, with the arguments and a readable message on failure.
assets.useWhen: calling synchronous code you don't control that signals failure by throwing, such as `decodeURIComponent`, `new URL`, `atob`, a parser or a third-party SDK, and the caller should branch on a value instead. The wrapped function takes the same arguments. Whatever was thrown is kept in `cause`; `message` is its message, the string itself, or a description.
signatures: export function safeCall<Args extends readonly unknown[], T>( fn: (...args: Args) => T, ): (...args: Args) => Result<T, SafeCallError<Args>>

assets.name: safeCallAsync
assets.summary: Wraps an async function so it resolves to a Result instead of rejecting, keeping the arguments on failure.
assets.useWhen: calling an SDK, a database client or `fetch`-based helper you don't control, and every call site would otherwise need its own `try`. The wrapped function takes the same arguments and never rejects. A synchronous throw inside the function is caught too. Whatever it rejected with is kept in `cause`; `message` is its message, the string itself, or a description.
signatures: export function safeCallAsync<Args extends readonly unknown[], T>( fn: (...args: Args) => Promise<T>, ): (...args: Args) => Promise<Result<T, SafeCallAsyncError<Args>>>

assets.name: slaStatus
assets.summary: Says whether an item opened at a given time is on track, at risk or past its deadline, and how much time is left.
assets.useWhen: a support ticket, an incident, an approval or an order has a response or resolution target, and a queue, a badge or an alert needs its state. Takes the open time in epoch milliseconds and `now` from the caller, so the result is testable. An open time in the future, from clock skew, counts as on track.
signatures: export function slaStatus(openedAt: number, policy: SlaStatusPolicy): SlaStatusResult
export function slaStatus(policy: SlaStatusPolicy): (openedAt: number) => SlaStatusResult

assets.name: summarizeNumbers
assets.summary: Computes count, sum, min, max and mean of a list of numbers in one call, skipping values that aren't finite.
assets.useWhen: a dashboard tile, a report footer or a log line needs the usual figures for a column, such as response times, order totals or scores. `NaN`, `Infinity` and `-Infinity` are left out, so one bad reading doesn't poison every figure, and `count` says how many were used. `None` when no finite number is left, rather than a mean of `NaN`. Safe for long lists, unlike `Math.min(...values)`.
signatures: export function summarizeNumbers(values: readonly number[]): Option<SummarizeNumbersSummary>

assets.name: transitionState
assets.summary: Moves a state machine one step: the next state for an event, or an error naming what is allowed.
assets.useWhen: a record has a lifecycle, such as an order, a ticket, a subscription or a document review, and a request asks to apply an event to it. The table lists each state's accepted events; anything missing is refused, so a shipped order can't be paid twice. A state with no entry is final. The event is a plain string, so it can come straight from a request body.

assets.name: webVitalRating
assets.summary: Rates a Core Web Vitals measurement as good, needs-improvement or poor, using Google's thresholds.
assets.useWhen: real-user monitoring or a lab run reports metrics and a dashboard, an alert or a CI budget needs the rating. Takes the `{ name, value }` shape the `web-vitals` library reports; times are in milliseconds and CLS has no unit. Thresholds: LCP 2500/4000, INP 200/500, CLS 0.1/0.25, FCP 1800/3000, TTFB 800/1800. A value equal to a threshold gets the better rating.

assets.summary: Builds a predicate that keeps items where at least one of the named fields passes a test.
assets.useWhen: the same kind of value sits in several fields and any of them should count, such as a work email in `email` or `backupEmail`, a city in a billing or shipping address, or a flag set on any of three checks. Missing and `null` fields are skipped, so the test only sees real values.

assets.name: combineFilters
assets.summary: Joins optional filters with AND, skipping the ones that are absent, so unset filters don't filter.
assets.useWhen: a list screen builds its filter from controls that may be empty, such as a search box, a status picker and a date range, and writing `query ? matches(query) : undefined` for each is natural. `undefined`, `null` and `false` entries are skipped, so `cond && filter` works too. With nothing left, every item is kept.

assets.name: excludeIds
assets.summary: Builds a predicate that drops items whose `id` is in a list, checking each id in constant time.
assets.useWhen: a feed or suggestion list must hide what the person dismissed, blocked, already saw or already has, and the id list may hold thousands of entries. The ids go into a `Set` once, so filtering stays fast where `oneOf` would scan the list for every item; a `Set` you already hold works as it is. Ids match exactly: `7` and `'7'` are different.
signatures: export function excludeIds<Id>(ids: Iterable<Id>): Predicate<{ readonly id: Id }>

assets.name: facetFilter
assets.summary: Builds the predicate behind a faceted search sidebar: any picked value per facet, all facets together.
assets.useWhen: a catalog, job board or log viewer has checkbox groups such as brand, color and size, and the list must keep items matching any checked value in each group and every group that has a check. A group with nothing checked doesn't filter. For a field holding a list, such as `sizes`, an item matches when any of its values is checked. Values match exactly; normalize case before if your data needs it.
signatures: export function facetFilter<T extends object>(selection: FacetFilterSelection<T>): Predicate<T>

assets.name: filterFromQuery
assets.summary: Builds a list filter from URL query parameters: repeated values joined with OR, parameters with AND.
assets.useWhen: a list page keeps its filters in the URL, like `?status=open&status=pending&q=db`, so links can be shared and the back button works. You say how each supported parameter's value becomes a predicate. Blank values are skipped, and parameters without a builder, such as `page` or `utm_source`, are ignored. With no filter in the query, every item is kept. Pass `URLSearchParams` or an already parsed object.
signatures: export function filterFromQuery<T>( params: FilterFromQueryParams | URLSearchParams, builders: FilterFromQueryBuilders<T>, ): Predicate<T>

assets.name: hasAllTags
assets.summary: Builds a predicate that keeps items carrying every one of the selected tags, ignoring case.
assets.useWhen: each picked tag should narrow the list, as in "show recipes that are both `vegan` and `quick`", or skills a candidate must all have. Name the field that holds the item's tags. Extra tags on the item don't matter. An empty selection keeps everything. Items without the field, or with `null` there, are dropped once something is selected.
signatures: export function hasAllTags<K extends PropertyKey>( key: K, selected: readonly string[], ): Predicate<{ readonly [P in K]?: readonly string[] | null | undefined }>
assets.output: Predicate<{ readonly [P in K]?: readonly string[] | null | undefined }>

assets.name: hasAnyTag
assets.summary: Builds a predicate that keeps items carrying at least one of the selected tags, ignoring case.
assets.useWhen: a tag cloud, label picker or category chips should widen the list with each pick, so choosing `react` and `vue` shows items tagged with either. Name the field that holds the item's tags. An empty selection keeps everything, as a filter with nothing picked should. Items without the field, or with `null` there, are dropped once something is selected.
signatures: export function hasAnyTag<K extends PropertyKey>( key: K, selected: readonly string[], ): Predicate<{ readonly [P in K]?: readonly string[] | null | undefined }>
assets.output: Predicate<{ readonly [P in K]?: readonly string[] | null | undefined }>

assets.name: hasExtension
assets.summary: Builds a predicate for file names or paths that end in one of the given extensions, ignoring case.
assets.useWhen: picking images out of an upload, source files out of a directory listing, or keys out of an object-storage listing. Extensions may be written with or without the dot, and may have several parts, such as `tar.gz`. A name must have something before the dot, so `.png` alone, a hidden file, isn't a PNG.
signatures: export function hasExtension(extensions: readonly string[]): Predicate<string>

assets.name: hasFilledField
assets.summary: Builds a predicate that keeps items whose field holds something: not empty, blank or missing.
assets.useWhen: listing records ready for a step that needs a field, such as products with a photo, contacts with a phone number or posts with a summary. `null`, `undefined`, a blank or whitespace-only string and an empty array count as empty; `0` and `false` count as filled.
signatures: export function hasFilledField<K extends PropertyKey>(key: K): Predicate<{ readonly [P in K]?: unknown }>

assets.name: isActiveWithin
assets.summary: Builds a predicate that keeps items whose last-activity timestamp falls within a recent window.
assets.useWhen: counting or listing active users, live sessions, recently seen devices or fresh listings, such as "active in the last 30 days". Name the timestamp field, in milliseconds. The window includes its start and runs up to `now`; a timestamp after `now` still counts, since clocks drift. Items never active, with the field missing or `null`, are dropped.
signatures: export function isActiveWithin<K extends PropertyKey>( key: K, window: IsActiveWithinWindow, ): Predicate<{ readonly [P in K]?: number | null | undefined }>
assets.output: Predicate<{ readonly [P in K]?: number | null | undefined }>

assets.name: isAdultAt
assets.summary: Builds a predicate that keeps people who have reached an age on a given day, from their birth date.
assets.useWhen: an audience, guest list or report must include only people old enough on a date, such as 18 on the event day or 21 today. Name the birth-date field, in milliseconds. Ages are whole years in UTC, and a birthday counts from the start of that day. People without a birth date are dropped.
signatures: export function isAdultAt<K extends PropertyKey>( key: K, rules: IsAdultAtRules, ): Predicate<{ readonly [P in K]?: number | null | undefined }>
assets.output: Predicate<{ readonly [P in K]?: number | null | undefined }>

assets.name: isDueWithin
assets.summary: Builds a predicate that keeps unfinished items due between now and the end of a window ahead.
assets.useWhen: sending "due in 3 days" reminders, showing an "upcoming" column, or warning about renewals, certificates or trials that end soon. Both ends of the window are included, and items already late are left out. If you name a `done` field, finished items are left out too. Items without a due time are never due.
signatures: export function isDueWithin<Due extends PropertyKey, Done extends PropertyKey = never>( rules: IsDueWithinRules<Due, Done>, ): Predicate<IsDueWithinItem<Due, Done>>

assets.name: isEmailLike
assets.summary: Keeps values that are strings shaped like an email address, and types them as strings.
assets.useWhen: picking addresses out of untyped data, such as a pasted list, an imported column or a JSON field, before sending invites or deduplicating contacts. The shape is `something@domain.tld` with no spaces anywhere, so an address with stray spaces is dropped: trim first if you want those kept. It doesn't check that the mailbox exists.
signatures: export function isEmailLike(value: unknown): value is string

assets.name: isInBoundingBox
assets.summary: Builds a predicate that keeps points inside a map's visible rectangle, also when it crosses the date line.
assets.useWhen: a map view shows only the markers or listings in view, refreshed as the person pans and zooms, from bounds such as Mapbox's or Google Maps' `getBounds()`. Edges count as inside. When `west` is greater than `east`, the box crosses the 180° meridian, as over the Pacific, and longitudes on either side of it are kept.
signatures: export function isInBoundingBox(bounds: IsInBoundingBoxBounds): Predicate<IsInBoundingBoxPoint>

assets.name: isLiveAt
assets.summary: Builds a predicate for scheduled content that is live at a moment: started, and not yet ended.
assets.useWhen: showing banners, promotions, announcements, job posts or prices that have a publish and an expiry time, and some leave one of them open. The start is included and the end is not, so a sale ending at midnight is over at midnight. An empty start means already live; an empty end means it never expires.
signatures: export function isLiveAt<Start extends PropertyKey, End extends PropertyKey>( rules: IsLiveAtRules<Start, End>, ): Predicate<IsLiveAtItem<Start, End>>

assets.name: isMissingField
assets.summary: Builds a predicate that keeps items whose field is empty: missing, `null`, blank or an empty list.
assets.useWhen: finding records that need attention, such as products without images, users without a verified email or articles without tags, for a cleanup list or a data-quality report. `null`, `undefined`, a blank or whitespace-only string and an empty array count as empty; `0` and `false` don't.
signatures: export function isMissingField<K extends PropertyKey>(key: K): Predicate<{ readonly [P in K]?: unknown }>

assets.name: isNonBlankString
assets.summary: Keeps strings with something besides whitespace, and tells TypeScript the value is a string.
assets.useWhen: cleaning untyped input, such as a CSV column, a JSON array or form values, where numbers, `null`, empty strings and stray spaces should all be dropped and the result typed `string[]`. Whitespace includes tabs and newlines. It doesn't trim what it keeps.
signatures: export function isNonBlankString(value: unknown): value is string

assets.name: isOverdue
assets.summary: Builds a predicate that keeps unfinished items whose due time has passed, with an optional grace period.
assets.useWhen: listing late invoices, overdue tasks, expired trials awaiting action or library loans not returned, for a dashboard, a reminder job or a dunning email. An item is overdue when its due time plus the grace is before `now` and, if you name a `done` field, that field is empty. Items without a due time are never overdue.
signatures: export function isOverdue<Due extends PropertyKey, Done extends PropertyKey = never>( rules: IsOverdueRules<Due, Done>, ): Predicate<IsOverdueItem<Due, Done>>

assets.name: isUnderPath
assets.summary: Builds a predicate for paths at or below any of the given folders, matching whole segments only.
assets.useWhen: deciding which routes a middleware guards, which files a tool touches, or which storage keys belong to a tenant, where `/admin` must cover `/admin/users` but not `/administrator`. Trailing slashes are ignored on both sides. Matching is case-sensitive, as URLs and most file systems are. The prefix `/` covers every absolute path.
signatures: export function isUnderPath(folders: readonly string[]): Predicate<string>

assets.name: isVisibleTo
assets.summary: Builds a predicate for the items a person may see: public ones, their own, and their teams' shared ones.
assets.useWhen: a list of documents, boards, dashboards or files mixes public, team-shared and private items, and each person should see only theirs. An owner always sees their item, whatever its visibility. A `team` item is seen by members of its team, and one without a team only by its owner. Run the same rule in the database query or API too: a filter in the browser hides items, it doesn't protect them.
signatures: export function isVisibleTo(viewer: IsVisibleToViewer): Predicate<IsVisibleToItem>

assets.name: isWithinDistance
assets.summary: Builds a predicate that keeps points within a radius of a center, measured along the Earth's surface.
assets.useWhen: a store locator, delivery-area check or "near me" list must keep places within so many kilometres of a person. Distance is the great-circle distance, so it is right across the date line and near the poles, but it is as the crow flies, not by road. The edge counts as inside. For points nested in an object, wrap it with `by`.
signatures: export function isWithinDistance(center: IsWithinDistancePoint, radiusKm: number): Predicate<IsWithinDistancePoint>

assets.name: isWithinTimeRange
assets.summary: Builds a predicate for timestamps in a half-open range, `from` included and `to` left out.
assets.useWhen: a log viewer, activity feed or report shows events "from Monday to Sunday" or "in March", and back-to-back ranges must not count an event at midnight twice. Name the timestamp field, in milliseconds. Either bound may be absent. Items without a timestamp are dropped once a bound is set.
signatures: export function isWithinTimeRange<K extends PropertyKey>( key: K, bounds: IsWithinTimeRangeBounds, ): Predicate<{ readonly [P in K]?: number | null | undefined }>
assets.output: Predicate<{ readonly [P in K]?: number | null | undefined }>

assets.name: matchesAnyFilter
assets.summary: Joins optional filters with OR, skipping absent ones; with none left, every item is kept.
assets.useWhen: several saved views, quick filters or alert rules may each claim an item, as in "mine OR mentioning me OR overdue", and some of those rules are switched off. `undefined`, `null` and `false` entries are skipped. With no filter switched on, everything is kept, as a filter bar with nothing selected should, rather than nothing as a bare OR would.
signatures: export function matchesAnyFilter<T>(filters: readonly (Predicate<T> | false | null | undefined)[]): Predicate<T>

assets.name: matchesAnyTerm
assets.summary: Builds a predicate that keeps items where any word of the query appears in a chosen field.
assets.useWhen: the query is a list of alternatives rather than a narrowing search, such as `bug crash error` over ticket titles, or a pasted list of names or SKUs to pick out. Matching ignores case and accents and finds words inside longer ones. Number fields and lists of strings are searched too. A blank query keeps everything.
signatures: export function matchesAnyTerm<T extends object>(query: string, keys: readonly (keyof T)[]): Predicate<T>

assets.name: matchesSearch
assets.summary: Builds a search-box predicate: every word of the query must appear in at least one chosen field.
assets.useWhen: a list, table or command menu has a search box, and typing `ada london` should keep the people whose name or city holds both words. Matching ignores case and accents and finds words inside longer ones, so `lon` finds `London`. Number fields and lists of strings, such as tags, are searched too. A blank query keeps everything.
signatures: export function matchesSearch<T extends object>(query: string, keys: readonly (keyof T)[]): Predicate<T>

assets.name: matchesSubsequence
assets.summary: Builds a fuzzy predicate: the query's letters must appear in the text in order, gaps allowed.
assets.useWhen: a command palette, file picker or quick switcher should find `GitHub Settings` from `ghs`, the way editors do. Matching ignores case. Spaces in the query are ignored, and any character, including `.` or `(`, is matched as itself. It only says yes or no; sort the matches yourself if closer ones should come first. A blank query keeps everything.
signatures: export function matchesSubsequence<T>(query: string, select: (item: T) => string): Predicate<T>

assets.name: numberFilterFromText
assets.summary: Turns a number filter typed as text, like `>= 10`, `< 5`, `!= 0` or `3..8`, into a predicate.
assets.useWhen: a data table, admin search or spreadsheet-like grid lets people type a condition into a column filter instead of picking an operator from a menu. A bare number means equal, and a range includes both ends. A blank filter keeps everything. Text that isn't a filter gives `NOT_A_FILTER` with a hint, and a range written high to low gives `REVERSED_RANGE`.
signatures: export function numberFilterFromText(input: string): Result<Predicate<number>, NumberFilterFromTextError>

assets.name: withinRange
assets.summary: Builds a predicate for a number range where either end may be left open, as range filters allow.
assets.useWhen: a shop, listing or report has "min" and "max" inputs, such as price, rating, size or year, and either input may be empty. Both ends are inclusive. Items whose value is missing, `NaN` or infinite are dropped once any bound is set; with no bounds, everything is kept. Pass the bounds you already parsed from the form or query.
signatures: export function withinRange<T>(select: (item: T) => number | null | undefined, bounds: WithinRangeBounds): Predicate<T>

assets.name: averageBy
assets.summary: Averages one number from each item, skipping items where it is missing or not a number.
assets.useWhen: computing an average rating, score or duration over records where some values are `null`, `undefined` or `NaN`, such as unrated reviews or unfinished runs. Skipped items don't count toward the average, so they don't drag it down to zero. Returns `None` when no item has a value, so an empty list can't show `NaN`.
signatures: export function averageBy<T>(items: readonly T[], value: (item: T) => number | null | undefined): Option<number>
export function averageBy<T>(value: (item: T) => number | null | undefined): (items: readonly T[]) => Option<number>

assets.name: discountedPrice
assets.summary: Applies a percentage or fixed discount to a price in minor units, never going below zero.
assets.useWhen: a cart, a coupon or a sale price takes `15%` or `$5` off. A percentage is clamped to 0–100 and its amount rounded to a whole minor unit, halves up. The price never drops below zero, so a $20 coupon on a $15 item gives 0, and a negative discount never raises the price.
signatures: export function discountedPrice(price: number, discount: DiscountedPriceDiscount): number
export function discountedPrice(discount: DiscountedPriceDiscount): (price: number) => number

assets.name: formatCompactCount
assets.summary: Shortens a count the way social apps do: `1.2K`, `12K`, `123K`, `1.5M`, and `999` as is.
assets.useWhen: showing followers, views, likes or downloads in a tight spot such as a badge or a button. A decimal is shown only while the leading number is a single digit, so the text stays short: `1.2K` but `12K`, never `12.3K`. Values round to the nearest shown digit, so `9,999` reads `10K`. The locale sets the suffixes, such as `1,2 k` in French.
signatures: export function formatCompactCount(count: number, locale: string): string
export function formatCompactCount(locale: string): (count: number) => string

assets.name: formatDelta
assets.summary: Formats a difference with an explicit sign and separators: `+1,234`, `−56`, `0`.
assets.useWhen: showing how a count or amount changed since the last period, such as new signups, stock movement or a score difference. Positive values get `+`, negative ones the typographic minus `−`, and a value that rounds to zero gets no sign. `decimals` sets how many decimals to show.
signatures: export function formatDelta(delta: number, decimals: number): string
export function formatDelta(decimals: number): (delta: number) => string

assets.name: formatDuration
assets.summary: Formats milliseconds as a short duration with its two largest units: `1h 5m`, `45s`, `850ms`.
assets.useWhen: showing how long a job, a request, a call or a video took, in a table cell or a log line. Units are days, hours, minutes and seconds; units that are zero are skipped, and smaller ones are cut off, not rounded, so `1h 59m 59s` reads `1h 59m`. Under a second it shows whole milliseconds. A negative duration, from clock skew, reads `0ms`.
signatures: export function formatDuration(ms: number): string

assets.name: formatDurationLong
assets.summary: Formats milliseconds as words with its two largest units: `1 hour 5 minutes`, `45 seconds`.
assets.useWhen: a sentence or a screen reader says how long something took or will take, such as "Estimated time: 2 hours 10 minutes" or an accessible label for a timer. Units that are zero are skipped, and smaller ones are cut off, not rounded. Anything under a second, including negative values from clock skew, reads `less than a second`. English only.
signatures: export function formatDurationLong(ms: number): string

assets.name: formatFileSize
assets.summary: Formats a byte count the way macOS and storage vendors do, in powers of 1000: `1.5 MB`.
assets.useWhen: showing upload limits, attachment sizes or download progress to people. One decimal at most, and a trailing `.0` is dropped, so `1000000` reads `1 MB`, not `1.0 MB`. Counts below 1000 read as bytes, such as `999 B`. For sizes in powers of 1024, as Windows and most Linux tools show them, use `formatFileSizeBinary`.
signatures: export function formatFileSize(bytes: number): string

assets.name: formatFileSizeBinary
assets.summary: Formats a byte count in powers of 1024 with IEC units, so nobody mistakes them: `1.5 MiB`.
assets.useWhen: showing memory, disk quotas or sizes next to tools that count in 1024s, such as Windows Explorer, `ls -h` or a container's memory limit. Units are `KiB`, `MiB`, `GiB`, `TiB` and `PiB`, one decimal at most, and a trailing `.0` is dropped. Counts below 1024 read as bytes. For powers of 1000, as macOS shows sizes, use `formatFileSize`.
signatures: export function formatFileSizeBinary(bytes: number): string

assets.name: formatPercentChange
assets.summary: Formats a change ratio as a signed percentage: `0.125` → `+12.5%`, `-0.03` → `−3.0%`.
assets.useWhen: a dashboard, report or price ticker shows how much a metric went up or down. The input is a ratio, so `0.125` means 12.5%. The sign is decided after rounding, so a change too small to show reads `0.0%`, never `-0.0%` or `+0.0%`. Negatives use the typographic minus `−`, which lines up with `+` in tables. Large values get separators.
signatures: export function formatPercentChange(ratio: number, decimals: number): string
export function formatPercentChange(decimals: number): (ratio: number) => string

assets.name: formatPrice
assets.summary: Formats an amount stored in minor units, such as cents, as a price: `1999` → `$19.99`.
assets.useWhen: prices come from a database, Stripe or another payment API as integers in the currency's smallest unit. The number of minor digits comes from the currency, so `1999` yen stays `¥1,999` and `1999` cents become `$19.99`. The locale decides symbol position, separators and spacing; some locales put a no-break space (` `) before the symbol.
signatures: export function formatPrice(minorUnits: number, options: FormatPriceOptions): string
export function formatPrice(options: FormatPriceOptions): (minorUnits: number) => string

assets.name: formatPriceRange
assets.summary: Formats a price range from minor units: `$10 – $25`, or one price when both ends match.
assets.useWhen: a product with variants, a plan with tiers or a search filter shows "from–to" prices. When both ends are whole amounts the decimals are dropped (`$10 – $25`); otherwise both ends show them (`$9.99 – $25.00`), so the two always match. Ends given in the wrong order are swapped. The dash is an en dash with spaces.
signatures: export function formatPriceRange(range: FormatPriceRangeBounds, options: FormatPriceRangeOptions): string
export function formatPriceRange(options: FormatPriceRangeOptions): (range: FormatPriceRangeBounds) => string

assets.name: formatRating
assets.summary: Formats an average rating with one decimal against its scale: `4.5 / 5`.
assets.useWhen: showing a product, app or restaurant rating next to stars or in a review summary. The rating rounds to one decimal, always shown, so ratings line up in a list (`4.0 / 5`, not `4 / 5`). A rating outside `0` to `outOf` is clamped, so a bad average can't read `5.3 / 5`.
signatures: export function formatRating(rating: number, outOf: number): string
export function formatRating(outOf: number): (rating: number) => string

assets.name: formatShare
assets.summary: Formats a share of a whole as a whole percent that never rounds to a misleading 0% or 100%.
assets.useWhen: labelling a slice of a chart, a progress share or a market share where `0%` would claim nothing and `100%` would claim everything. A share above zero but under 1% reads `<1%`; one above 99% but not all reads `>99%`. The input is a ratio between 0 and 1; values outside that range are clamped.
signatures: export function formatShare(ratio: number): string

assets.name: growthRate
assets.summary: Computes the change from a previous value to a current one as a ratio: 200 → 250 is `0.25`.
assets.useWhen: a dashboard compares this month with last month, or a price with yesterday's. Returns `None` when the previous value is zero, where growth has no meaning, instead of `Infinity` or `NaN`, and when either value isn't a finite number. The change is divided by the size of the previous value, so going from −100 to −50 counts as growth (`0.5`).
signatures: export function growthRate({ previous, current }: GrowthRatePeriods): Option<number>

assets.name: histogramBuckets
assets.summary: Counts numbers into equal-width buckets for a histogram, including the empty buckets between.
assets.useWhen: drawing a distribution of order values, response times, ages or scores. Each bucket covers `from` up to but not including `to`. Buckets start at a multiple of `size`, so edges are round numbers, and empty buckets in the middle are kept so the chart's bars line up with its axis. `NaN` and infinite values are skipped. No values, or a size of zero or less, give `[]`. Whole-number sizes keep the edges exact.
signatures: export function histogramBuckets(values: readonly number[], size: number): readonly HistogramBucketsEntry[]
export function histogramBuckets(size: number): (values: readonly number[]) => readonly HistogramBucketsEntry[]

assets.name: median
assets.summary: Finds the middle value of a list of numbers, or the mean of the two middle ones.
assets.useWhen: a typical value matters more than the mean because a few outliers would skew it, such as house prices, response times or salaries. `NaN` and infinite values are skipped. Returns `None` for an empty list. The input isn't changed.
signatures: export function median(values: readonly number[]): Option<number>

assets.name: minMax
assets.summary: Finds the smallest and the largest number of a list in one pass.
assets.useWhen: setting a chart's axis, a price filter's slider bounds or a color scale from data. `NaN` and infinite values are skipped, so one bad reading can't break the range. Returns `None` when no finite number is left, where `Math.min()` would give `Infinity`. Works on lists of any length, unlike `Math.min(...values)`.
signatures: export function minMax(values: readonly number[]): Option<MinMaxRange>

assets.name: monthlyPayment
assets.summary: Computes the fixed monthly payment that pays off a loan, in minor units: an annuity.
assets.useWhen: a loan, lease, mortgage or buy-now-pay-later screen shows what each month costs. The principal is in minor units, such as cents, and so is the payment, rounded to the nearest one; lenders adjust the last payment by the few cents rounding leaves. A rate of zero divides the principal evenly. The rate must be a finite number of at least zero and the months a whole number of at least 1, or the terms come back as an error.
signatures: export function monthlyPayment(principal: number, terms: MonthlyPaymentTerms): Result<number, MonthlyPaymentError>
export function monthlyPayment(terms: MonthlyPaymentTerms): (principal: number) => Result<number, MonthlyPaymentError>

assets.name: movingAverage
assets.summary: Smooths a series by averaging each run of `window` consecutive values, such as a 7-day average.
assets.useWhen: a chart of daily signups, sales or errors is too jumpy to read and a rolling average shows the trend. The result has one value per full window, so it is `window - 1` values shorter than the input and its first value covers the first `window` inputs. A series shorter than the window, or a window under 1, gives `[]`.
signatures: export function movingAverage(values: readonly number[], window: number): readonly number[]
export function movingAverage(window: number): (values: readonly number[]) => readonly number[]

assets.name: normalizeScores
assets.summary: Rescales numbers so the smallest becomes 0 and the largest 1, keeping their order and spacing.
assets.useWhen: combining scores on different scales, such as relevance and recency in a search ranking, drawing bars relative to the largest value, or feeding features to a model. When every value is the same, they all become 1, since they all tie for the top. An empty list gives `[]`. Pass finite numbers; a `NaN` makes every result `NaN`.
signatures: export function normalizeScores(values: readonly number[]): readonly number[]

assets.name: percentOfTotal
assets.summary: Turns values into whole percents of their total that always add up to exactly 100.
assets.useWhen: labelling a pie chart, a stacked bar or a survey result, where rounding each share on its own can show 99% or 101% in total. Each share is rounded down, then the points still missing go to the shares that lost the most in rounding (the largest remainder method); ties go to the earlier value. The result is in the same order as the input. Values should not be negative. A total of zero gives zeros.
signatures: export function percentOfTotal(values: readonly number[]): readonly number[]

assets.name: percentile
assets.summary: Finds the value below which a given percent of the numbers fall, such as p95 latency.
assets.useWhen: reporting response-time percentiles, setting a threshold from a distribution, or cutting off outliers. Between two values it interpolates linearly, the way Excel's `PERCENTILE.INC` and NumPy's default do. `p` is from 0 to 100 and is clamped to that range. `NaN` and infinite values are skipped. Returns `None` for an empty list.
signatures: export function percentile(values: readonly number[], p: number): Option<number>
export function percentile(p: number): (values: readonly number[]) => Option<number>

assets.name: priceWithTax
assets.summary: Adds tax to a net price in minor units and returns net, tax and gross that add up exactly.
assets.useWhen: a price is stored before tax, as in US sales tax or B2B prices, and a checkout, invoice or receipt needs every line. `rate` is a fraction, so 20% is `0.2`. The tax is rounded to a whole minor unit, halves away from zero, and the gross is net plus that rounded tax, so the three numbers on the receipt always agree. Negative net prices, such as refunds, get negative tax.
signatures: export function priceWithTax(net: number, rate: number): PriceWithTaxBreakdown
export function priceWithTax(rate: number): (net: number) => PriceWithTaxBreakdown

assets.name: priceWithoutTax
assets.summary: Splits a tax-inclusive price in minor units into net and tax that add up to it exactly.
assets.useWhen: prices are shown with tax included, as with VAT in Europe or GST in Australia, and an invoice or accounting export needs the net and the tax separately. `rate` is a fraction, so 20% is `0.2`. The net is rounded to a whole minor unit, halves away from zero, and the tax is what remains, so net plus tax is always the gross you passed in.
signatures: export function priceWithoutTax(gross: number, rate: number): PriceWithoutTaxBreakdown
export function priceWithoutTax(rate: number): (gross: number) => PriceWithoutTaxBreakdown

assets.name: progressPercent
assets.summary: Turns done-of-total into a whole percent for a progress bar that never misleads: 0 to 100.
assets.useWhen: showing upload, onboarding, import or quiz progress. The percent rounds down, `100` appears only when everything is done and `0` only when nothing is, so a bar never looks finished early or stuck at the start: 999 of 1000 reads `99`, 1 of 1000 reads `1`. Done above total reads `100`; a total of zero or less reads `0`.
signatures: export function progressPercent(done: number, total: number): number
export function progressPercent(total: number): (done: number) => number

assets.name: rankWithTies
assets.summary: Ranks items by a score, best first, giving tied items the same rank: 1st, 1st, 3rd.
assets.useWhen: building a leaderboard, a sales ranking or race results. Ties follow competition ranking: two players tied for first are both `1st` and the next is `3rd`. Pick `highest` when a bigger score wins and `lowest` when a smaller one does. Items with equal scores keep their input order.
signatures: export function rankWithTies<T>( items: readonly T[], score: (item: T) => number, best: RankWithTiesBest, ): readonly RankWithTiesEntry<T>[]
export function rankWithTies<T>( score: (item: T) => number, best: RankWithTiesBest, ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly RankWithTiesEntry<T>[]

assets.name: roundPrice
assets.summary: Rounds a price to the nearest multiple of a step, such as 0.05, without floating-point noise.
assets.useWhen: cash rounding to 5 cents (Switzerland, Canada, Australia), rounding converted prices to tidy steps such as `0.25`, or snapping a slider value to its step. Halves round up. The result has no more decimals than the step, so `1.13` to `0.05` gives `1.15`, not `1.1500000000000001`, and `1.015` to `0.01` gives `1.02`, not `1.01`. A step of zero or less leaves the amount unchanged.
signatures: export function roundPrice(amount: number, step: number): number
export function roundPrice(step: number): (amount: number) => number

assets.name: scoreToGrade
assets.summary: Finds the grade, tier or band a score falls into, from a list of minimum scores.
assets.useWhen: turning a test score into a letter grade, loyalty points into a tier, or a credit or risk score into a label. A score earns the band with the highest `min` that it reaches, and the bands may be listed in any order. Returns `None` when the score is below every band or isn't a number, so a missing band shows up instead of a wrong label.
signatures: export function scoreToGrade<G>(score: number, bands: readonly ScoreToGradeBand<G>[]): Option<G>
export function scoreToGrade<G>(bands: readonly ScoreToGradeBand<G>[]): (score: number) => Option<G>

assets.name: splitByWeights
assets.summary: Splits an amount in minor units in proportion to weights, with parts that add up exactly.
assets.useWhen: allocating a discount across order lines, revenue across partners or a cost across departments, where rounding each part on its own would lose or invent cents. Each part is rounded down, then the cents still missing go to the parts that lost the most in rounding (the largest remainder method); ties go to the earlier part. A negative amount splits the same way with negative parts. Weights must be finite, not negative, and not all zero.
signatures: export function splitByWeights( amount: number, weights: readonly number[], ): Result<readonly number[], SplitByWeightsError>
export function splitByWeights( weights: readonly number[], ): (amount: number) => Result<readonly number[], SplitByWeightsError>

assets.name: splitEvenly
assets.summary: Splits an amount in minor units into equal parts that add up exactly, spreading the rest.
assets.useWhen: dividing a bill, a refund or a subscription charge between people or months, where `1000 / 3` must not lose or invent a cent. Every part gets the same share, and the cents left over go one each to the first parts, so parts differ by at most one. A negative amount splits the same way with negative parts. The amount must be whole minor units, such as cents, and `parts` a whole number of at least 1.
signatures: export function splitEvenly(amount: number, parts: number): Result<readonly number[], SplitEvenlyError>
export function splitEvenly(parts: number): (amount: number) => Result<readonly number[], SplitEvenlyError>

assets.name: standardDeviation
assets.summary: Measures how spread out numbers are around their mean, for a sample or a whole population.
assets.useWhen: flagging unusual values, showing error bars, or checking how steady a metric is, such as response times or daily sales. Pick `sample` when the numbers are a subset, as Excel's `STDEV.S` does, and `population` when they are every value there is, as `STDEV.P` does. `NaN` and infinite values are skipped. Returns `None` for an empty list, and for a sample of fewer than two values, where the spread isn't defined.
signatures: export function standardDeviation(values: readonly number[], kind: StandardDeviationKind): Option<number>
export function standardDeviation(kind: StandardDeviationKind): (values: readonly number[]) => Option<number>

assets.name: toMinorUnits
assets.summary: Converts an amount in major units, such as dollars, to whole minor units: `19.99` USD → `1999`.
assets.useWhen: sending an amount to Stripe or another payment API, or storing money as an integer, from a number a form or a calculation produced. The minor digits come from the currency: 2 for USD and EUR, 0 for JPY, 3 for KWD. Floating-point noise is settled first, so `0.1 + 0.2` dollars is `30` cents and `19.99` is `1999`, not `1998`. Extra precision rounds to the nearest minor unit, halves up.
signatures: export function toMinorUnits(amount: number, currency: string): number
export function toMinorUnits(currency: string): (amount: number) => number

assets.name: weightedAverage
assets.summary: Averages a number from each item, letting each item count as much as its weight.
assets.useWhen: a grade point average weighted by credits, an average price weighted by quantity, or a rating combined from sources of different sizes. Returns `None` when the weights add up to zero, which includes an empty list, so the result is never `NaN` or `Infinity`.
signatures: export function weightedAverage<T>( items: readonly T[], value: (item: T) => number, weight: (item: T) => number, ): Option<number>
export function weightedAverage<T>( value: (item: T) => number, weight: (item: T) => number, ): (items: readonly T[]) => Option<number>

assets.name: applyPathOverrides
assets.summary: Applies a record of `'dot.path': value` overrides to an object, but only if every path exists and keeps its type.
assets.useWhen: layering overrides from CLI flags, environment-specific files or an admin screen onto a known config, where one bad key must stop the whole set and the user should see every mistake at once, not one per run. It returns `Valid(updated)` when all overrides fit, otherwise `Invalid` with one problem per bad path: `PATH_NOT_FOUND` or `WRONG_TYPE`. A setting that holds `null` takes any value. Nothing is applied unless everything fits, and the input is never changed.
signatures: export function applyPathOverrides<T extends object>( value: T, overrides: Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>, ): Validation<T, ApplyPathOverridesProblem>
export function applyPathOverrides<T extends object>( overrides: Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>, ): (value: T) => Validation<T, ApplyPathOverridesProblem>

assets.name: changedValues
assets.summary: Lists each dot path that differs between two versions of an object, with its old and new value.
assets.useWhen: writing an audit log or activity feed entry such as "price: 10 → 12", showing a review screen before saving, or sending a change event. Nested objects are compared leaf by leaf, an array is one value compared whole, and unchanged paths are left out. A path only in `after` has `from: undefined`, one only in `before` has `to: undefined`. Paths of `after` come first, in its order, then the removed ones.
signatures: export function changedValues(before: object, after: object): ChangedValuesResult

assets.name: checkExactShape
assets.summary: Checks an unknown value against a schema of type guards and refuses any key the schema doesn't name.
assets.useWhen: reading a config file, a feature-flag payload or a strict API request where a misspelled or unexpected key (`timout`, `isAdmin`) is a mistake to report, not something to ignore. Field types are checked first, stopping at the first failure. Then every key the schema doesn't name, at any depth with a nested schema, comes back at once as `UNKNOWN_FIELDS`. A field with a type guard is not looked inside.
signatures: export function checkExactShape<T extends PlainObject>( input: unknown, schema: ObjectSchema<T>, ): Result<T, CheckExactShapeError>
export function checkExactShape<T extends PlainObject>( schema: ObjectSchema<T>, ): (input: unknown) => Result<T, CheckExactShapeError>

assets.name: checkShape
assets.summary: Checks that an unknown value is an object whose fields pass the schema's type guards, and types it.
assets.useWhen: trusting parsed JSON, a message from a queue, `localStorage` or a webhook body enough to use its fields, without a validation library. The schema maps each key to a type guard such as `isString`, or to a nested schema. It stops at the first field that fails and returns `Err` with its dot path, the value found there and a readable message. Keys the schema doesn't mention are allowed and kept.
signatures: export function checkShape<T extends PlainObject>(input: unknown, schema: ObjectSchema<T>): Result<T, CheckShapeError>
export function checkShape<T extends PlainObject>(schema: ObjectSchema<T>): (input: unknown) => Result<T, CheckShapeError>

assets.name: compactFormValues
assets.summary: Trims every string in submitted form values, then drops what is left empty, at any depth.
assets.useWhen: turning raw form or query input into a payload, where an untouched field arrives as `''` or `'   '` and should be left out rather than saved. Strings are trimmed at the ends only. Then `null`, `undefined`, `''`, `[]` and `{}` are removed, and so is an object that only held empty fields. Inside arrays, blank and nullish items are dropped. `0` and `false` are answers, so they stay.
signatures: export function compactFormValues<T extends object>(values: T): DeepPartial<T>

assets.name: createMergePatch
assets.summary: Builds the JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7386) that turns one version of an object into another.
assets.useWhen: an edit form or a client cache holds the original and the edited version, and only what changed should go over the wire in a `PATCH`, be stored as a revision, or be queued for sync. Changed and new keys carry their new value, a removed key (or one set to `undefined`) becomes `null`, and nested objects get a nested patch with only their changes. Arrays and other values are sent whole. No change gives `{}`. Merge patch can't express setting a value to `null`: such a key reads as removed.
signatures: export function createMergePatch(before: object, after: object): PlainObject

assets.name: diffPaths
assets.summary: Lists the dot paths that were added, removed or changed between two versions of an object.
assets.useWhen: deciding what to save, revalidate or announce after an edit, such as "settings changed: theme, notifications.email", or which config keys need a restart. Nested objects are compared leaf by leaf (`address.city`), while an array is one value compared whole. A leaf that turns into an object shows up as the old path removed and the new paths added. `added` and `changed` follow the order of `after`, `removed` the order of `before`.
signatures: export function diffPaths(before: object, after: object): DiffPathsResult

assets.name: envToConfig
assets.summary: Reads the environment variables that share a prefix into a nested, camelCased config object.
assets.useWhen: loading settings such as `APP_DB__HOST` and `APP_DB__POOL_MAX` from `process.env`, Docker or Kubernetes into `{ db: { host, poolMax } }`, the way ASP.NET and many twelve-factor loaders do. The prefix is removed, a double underscore `__` starts a nested level, and each level is camelCased (`POOL_MAX` → `poolMax`). A numeric level makes an array (`APP_HOSTS__0`). Values stay strings and unset variables are skipped: parse and check the result next.
signatures: export function envToConfig(env: Readonly<Record<string, string | undefined>>, prefix: string): PlainObject
export function envToConfig(prefix: string): (env: Readonly<Record<string, string | undefined>>) => PlainObject

assets.name: flattenForCsv
assets.summary: Flattens one nested record into `'a.b'` columns whose cells are all strings, ready for a CSV or a sheet row.
assets.useWhen: exporting an order, user or event with nested fields to CSV, Excel or Google Sheets, where each cell must be one string. Nested objects become dot-path columns (`address.city`). Arrays stay in one cell, items joined with `'; '`. `null` and `undefined` become `''`, dates become ISO strings, and an empty object becomes `''`. It doesn't quote or escape: the CSV writer does that.
signatures: export function flattenForCsv(record: object): Record<string, string>

assets.name: getPathOr
assets.summary: Reads a nested value by a dot path or key list, and returns the fallback when it is missing or of another type.
assets.useWhen: reading parsed JSON, a config file or an API response you don't control, where the value might be absent, `null`, or the wrong type (`"8080"` where a number was expected). The value counts only when it has the fallback's `typeof` and is an array exactly when the fallback is one, so the result really is the fallback's type. A path is `'a.b.0'` or `['a', 'b', 0]`; numeric parts index into arrays.
signatures: export function getPathOr<T>(value: object, path: string | ObjectPath, fallback: T): T
export function getPathOr<T>(path: string | ObjectPath, fallback: T): (value: object) => T

assets.name: mergePatch
assets.summary: Applies a JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7386): nested objects merge, `null` removes a key, anything else replaces.
assets.useWhen: handling a `PATCH` request with `Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json`, syncing partial updates from a client, or layering a stored override on a document. A patch key set to `null` removes that key, a nested object is merged into the old value (or into `{}` when there was none), and every other value, arrays included, replaces the old one whole. Keys the patch doesn't mention stay. Neither input is changed. Because `null` means "remove", a merge patch can't store a `null`, and the type only allows `null` on optional keys.
signatures: export function mergePatch<T extends object>(target: T, patch: NoInfer<MergePatchInput<T>>): T
export function mergePatch<T extends object>(patch: NoInfer<MergePatchInput<T>>): (target: T) => T

assets.name: normalizeHeaders
assets.summary: Lower-cases header names, trims values and merges duplicates into one `Record<string, string>`.
assets.useWhen: comparing, logging, signing or forwarding HTTP headers that came from more than one place, such as Node's `req.headers`, a fetch init and your defaults, where `Content-Type` and `content-type` must be the same header. Names are lower-cased and trimmed. A header that appears twice, or as an array, has its values joined with `', '` in the order seen. Numbers become strings, and `null` and `undefined` values are dropped. Don't use it for `set-cookie`, whose values can't be joined with commas.
signatures: export function normalizeHeaders(headers: NormalizeHeadersInput): Record<string, string>

assets.name: omitByPrefix
assets.summary: Removes every key that starts with one of the given prefixes, at any depth, arrays included.
assets.useWhen: data carries bookkeeping fields that mustn't reach the UI, a cache key, a snapshot or the next API, such as GraphQL's `__typename`, MongoDB's `__v` and `_id`, or your own `$meta` and `_internal` fields. Class instances such as `Date` are left as they are, and the input is not changed. The result type drops the same keys.
signatures: export function omitByPrefix<T, P extends string>(value: T, prefixes: readonly P[]): OmitByPrefixResult<T, P>

export function omitByPrefix

(prefixes: readonly P[]): (value: T) => OmitByPrefixResult

assets.name: omitPaths
assets.summary: Removes the fields at the given dot paths, where `*` stands for every array item or key, and keeps the rest.
assets.useWhen: a record is almost right to send, cache or show, but a few nested fields must go, such as `user.passwordHash` or `orders.*.internalNotes`, and listing every field to keep would be longer. A path that isn't there changes nothing. `*` walks every array item or every key of an object; arrays are reached only through `*`, so their length never changes. The input is not changed. The result type stays `T`, so only remove optional fields if the type matters downstream.
signatures: export function omitPaths<T>(value: T, paths: readonly string[]): T
export function omitPaths(paths: readonly string[]): <T>(value: T) => T

assets.name: pickByPrefix
assets.summary: Keeps the keys that start with a prefix, and removes the prefix from their names.
assets.useWhen: reading one group of settings out of a flat bag, such as `VITE_` or `APP_` from `process.env`, `og:` tags from page metadata, or `utm_` fields from a query. Keys that only match the prefix in another case don't count, and a key equal to the prefix alone is left out, since it would have no name.
signatures: export function pickByPrefix<T extends object, P extends string>(value: T, prefix: P): PickByPrefixResult<T, P>
export function pickByPrefix<T extends object, P extends string>(prefix: P): (value: T) => PickByPrefixResult<T, P>

assets.name: pickDefined
assets.summary: Picks the listed keys and leaves out the ones whose value is `undefined`.
assets.useWhen: building an options object, a query or a PATCH body from values that may be unset, where sending `{ limit: undefined }` would override a default or break `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`. Only `undefined` is dropped: `null`, `0`, `''` and `false` are real values and stay. Keys not on the list are left out too.
signatures: export function pickDefined<T extends object, K extends keyof T & string>( value: T, keys: readonly K[], ): PickDefinedResult<T, K>
export function pickDefined<T extends object, K extends keyof T & string>( keys: readonly K[], ): (value: T) => PickDefinedResult<T, K>

assets.name: pickPaths
assets.summary: Keeps only the fields at the given dot paths, nested as they were, like a GraphQL selection or a projection.
assets.useWhen: an API, cache or log should get a few fields of a large record, such as `['id', 'profile.name', 'orders.*.total']`, without writing the nested shape out by hand. `*` walks every array item or every key of an object, and items keep their positions: an item without the field becomes `{}`. A path that isn't there adds nothing, and a path to an object keeps all of it. Array items are reached only through `*`, not by position.
signatures: export function pickPaths<T extends object>(value: T, paths: readonly string[]): DeepPartial<T>
export function pickPaths(paths: readonly string[]): <T extends object>(value: T) => DeepPartial<T>

assets.name: pickRenamed
assets.summary: Keeps only the keys named in a mapping, and gives each the new name the mapping says.
assets.useWhen: turning a third-party or legacy record into your own shape, such as a Stripe customer into `{ id, email, createdAt }`, where every field you don't map should be left behind rather than leak through. A mapped key missing from the input is missing from the output, and a key can keep its name by mapping it to itself. The result type follows the mapping.
signatures: export function pickRenamed<T extends object, const M extends { readonly [K in keyof T]?: string }>( value: T, mapping: M, ): PickRenamedResult<T, M>
export function pickRenamed<T extends object, const M extends { readonly [K in keyof T]?: string }>( mapping: M, ): (value: T) => PickRenamedResult<T, M>

assets.name: redactKeys
assets.summary: Replaces the value of each field whose name is on your list with `'[REDACTED]'`, at any depth.
assets.useWhen: you know exactly which fields are sensitive, such as `ssn`, `dateOfBirth` or `iban`, and want them out of a log, an export or an error report. Names match whole keys, ignoring case, `-`, `_` and spaces, so `'dateOfBirth'` also hides `date_of_birth`. The whole value under a matching key is replaced, nested objects included. Arrays are walked and the input is not changed. The return type stays `T`, but a redacted field holds the string.
signatures: export function redactKeys<T>(value: T, keys: readonly string[]): T
export function redactKeys(keys: readonly string[]): <T>(value: T) => T

assets.name: redactPaths
assets.summary: Replaces the value at each dot path with `'[REDACTED]'`, where `*` stands for every array item or key.
assets.useWhen: one field must go but the same name is harmless elsewhere, such as `card.number` but not `order.number`, or `users.*.email` in an export. A path that isn't there is skipped: no key is added. Array items are reached by position (`items.0.pin`) or all at once (`items.*.pin`). The input is not changed. The return type stays `T`, but a redacted field holds the string.
signatures: export function redactPaths<T>(value: T, paths: readonly string[]): T
export function redactPaths(paths: readonly string[]): <T>(value: T) => T

assets.name: redactSecrets
assets.summary: Replaces the value of every password, token, secret, API key, cookie or authorization field, at any depth.
assets.useWhen: an object is about to reach a log line, an error report or an analytics event, and it may carry credentials, such as a request body, the headers of a failed call or a config. A key counts as secret when, lower-cased and stripped of `-` and `_`, it contains one of password, passwd, secret, token, apikey, accesskey, privatekey, authorization, cookie or credential. The whole value under such a key becomes `'[REDACTED]'`, nested objects included. It errs toward hiding: `tokenCount` is redacted too. Arrays are walked, class instances such as `Date` are left alone, and the input is not changed. The return type stays `T` so it fits a logger, but a redacted field holds the string `'[REDACTED]'`.
signatures: export function redactSecrets<T>(value: T): T

assets.name: setExistingPath
assets.summary: Sets a value at a dot path only if the path already exists and the new value has the same type as the old one.
assets.useWhen: applying an override that comes from outside the code, such as `--set db.port=5432`, an admin screen or a feature-flag service, where a typo must be refused instead of quietly adding a key nobody reads. It returns `Err` with `PATH_NOT_FOUND` when nothing is there and `WRONG_TYPE` when the kinds differ (string, number, boolean, object, array). A setting that holds `null` takes any value. Numeric parts index into arrays. The input is never changed.
signatures: export function setExistingPath<T extends object>( value: T, path: string, next: unknown, ): Result<T, SetExistingPathError>
export function setExistingPath<T extends object>( path: string, next: unknown, ): (value: T) => Result<T, SetExistingPathError>

assets.name: sortKeysDeep
assets.summary: Returns a copy whose object keys are in sorted order at every depth, so equal data always serializes the same.
assets.useWhen: an object becomes a cache key, a hash, an ETag, a signature payload or a snapshot, and `{ a, b }` must produce the same `JSON.stringify` text as `{ b, a }`. Keys sort by UTF-16 code unit, the same in every locale, so `'B'` comes before `'a'`. Arrays keep their order, while the objects inside them are sorted too. Class instances such as `Date` are left as they are, and the input is not changed.
signatures: export function sortKeysDeep<T>(value: T): T

assets.name: toCamelCaseKeys
assets.summary: Renames every key to camelCase at any depth, arrays included, for data that came from a snake_case API.
assets.useWhen: an API, database row or webhook sends `snake_case` or `kebab-case` keys and the app works in camelCase. Keys already in camelCase stay as they are, PascalCase becomes camelCase, and all-caps names become lower-case (`ID` → `id`). Keys that start with `_` or `$`, such as `_id`, `__typename` and `$ref`, are kept as they are. Values are untouched, and class instances such as `Date` are not walked into.
signatures: export function toCamelCaseKeys(value: PlainObject): PlainObject

assets.name: toCsv
assets.summary: Turns a list of nested records into CSV text, with a header row covering every field any record has.
assets.useWhen: offering a "download as CSV" of orders, users or events, where records are nested and don't all have the same fields. Nested fields become dot-path columns, in the order they first appear. A record without a column gets an empty cell. Arrays share one cell, joined with `'; '`; dates become ISO strings. Cells with a comma, quote or line break are quoted as RFC 4180 says, and lines end in `\r\n`. An empty list gives `''`. It doesn't defuse spreadsheet formulas: a cell starting with `=` stays as it is.
signatures: export function toCsv(records: readonly object[]): string

assets.name: toQueryString
assets.summary: Turns a params object into an encoded query string, skipping empty values and nesting with brackets.
assets.useWhen: building the query of a search, filter or paginated list request from state, where unset filters must disappear instead of showing up as `?status=undefined`. `null` and `undefined` are skipped, `''` is kept. Arrays repeat the key (`tag=a&tag=b`), which `URLSearchParams.getAll`, Express, FastAPI and Go read as a list. Nested objects use brackets (`filter[status]=open`), as `qs`, Rails and PHP expect, encoded as `%5B` and `%5D`. Dates become ISO strings. It returns no leading `?`. Lists of objects don't survive the trip: send those as a JSON body.
signatures: export function toQueryString(params: object): string

assets.name: toSnakeCaseKeys
assets.summary: Renames every key to snake_case at any depth, arrays included, for a payload bound for a snake_case API.
assets.useWhen: sending a camelCase object to a backend, database or third-party API that expects `snake_case`, such as a Rails, Django or Postgres row. Acronyms stay one word (`userID` → `user_id`, `HTTPStatus` → `http_status`). Keys that start with `_` or `$`, such as `_id`, `__typename` and `$ref`, are kept as they are. Values are untouched, and class instances such as `Date` are not walked into.
signatures: export function toSnakeCaseKeys(value: PlainObject): PlainObject

assets.name: unflattenFormFields
assets.summary: Turns flat form field names such as `address.city` or `items[0][name]` into one nested object.
assets.useWhen: reading `FormData`, a urlencoded body or a query string whose field names carry the structure, as HTML forms, PHP and Rails do. Dots and brackets both nest, and a numeric part makes an array (`tags[1]` puts a value at index 1). Values stay as they came, usually strings. A name such as `__proto__` becomes an ordinary key, so untrusted field names can't reach a prototype. An empty bracket pair (`tags[]`) is not a list append: pass repeated fields as an array under one key instead.
signatures: export function unflattenFormFields(fields: Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>): PlainObject

assets.name: withDefaults
assets.summary: Fills in every missing setting from a defaults object, at any depth, where `null` and `undefined` count as missing.
assets.useWhen: merging user, file or environment config over defaults, or completing a partial options argument, where a nested default must survive a partial override and an explicit `undefined` must not wipe it out (a plain spread or `deepMerge` lets it). Nested plain objects merge key by key. Arrays and everything else are replaced whole by the given value: `[]` and `''` are kept, because someone chose them. Neither input is changed.
signatures: export function withDefaults<T extends object>(value: WithDefaultsInput<T>, defaults: T): T
export function withDefaults<T extends object>(defaults: T): (value: WithDefaultsInput<T>) => T

assets.name: parseAcceptLanguage
assets.summary: Reads an `Accept-Language` header into language tags ordered by preference, such as `['fr-CH', 'fr', 'en']`.
assets.useWhen: choosing the locale for a page, an email or an API response from what the browser asks for, before matching against the locales you support. Tags are ordered by their `q` weight, highest first, keeping the header's order between equal weights. Tags with `q=0` mean "not this one" and are dropped, malformed parts are skipped, and `*` is kept where it ranks. A missing or empty header is an empty list.
signatures: export function parseAcceptLanguage(header: string | null | undefined): readonly string[]

assets.name: parseBasicAuth
assets.summary: Reads the username and password from an `Authorization: Basic …` header, as Some(credentials) or None.
assets.useWhen: protecting a staging site, an admin route, a metrics endpoint or a webhook with HTTP Basic auth, where any malformed header should lead to the same 401 with a `WWW-Authenticate` challenge. The scheme ignores case, the credentials are decoded as UTF-8, and the password may contain colons. Bad Base64, bad UTF-8 or a missing colon is None. Compare the password in constant time when you check it.
signatures: export function parseBasicAuth( header: string | null | undefined, ): Option<ParseBasicAuthCredentials>

assets.name: parseBearerToken
assets.summary: Takes the token out of an `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header, as Some(token) or None.
assets.useWhen: an API route, middleware or edge function authenticates with a bearer token and a missing, empty or differently-schemed header should all lead to the same 401. The scheme ignores case and extra spaces, as HTTP allows. The token isn't checked; verify it next, for example as a JWT or against a session store.
signatures: export function parseBearerToken(header: string | null | undefined): Option<string>

assets.name: parseBoolean
assets.summary: Reads a yes-or-no answer such as `true`, `yes`, `on` or `1` from text, ignoring case and spaces.
assets.useWhen: a boolean arrives as text, from an environment variable, a query parameter, a CSV cell or a form, and people write it in different ways. `true`, `yes`, `y`, `on` and `1` are true; `false`, `no`, `n`, `off` and `0` are false. Anything else, the empty string included, is an `Err`, so a typo never turns into `false` without anyone noticing.
signatures: export function parseBoolean(input: string): Result<boolean, ParseBooleanError>

assets.name: parseByteSize
assets.summary: Parses a size such as `512`, `10MB` or `1.5 GiB` into a whole number of bytes.
assets.useWhen: an upload limit, a cache size, a disk quota or a body-size cap is set in config as text. `KB`, `MB`, `GB`, `TB` and `PB` are powers of 1000 and `KiB`, `MiB`, `GiB`, `TiB` and `PiB` are powers of 1024, as the units are defined; units ignore case, and a bare number is bytes. Negative sizes and unknown units are an `Err`. The result is rounded to a whole byte.
signatures: export function parseByteSize(input: string): Result<number, ParseByteSizeError>

assets.name: parseCommaList
assets.summary: Splits text on commas and line breaks into trimmed items, dropping the empty ones.
assets.useWhen: someone pastes a list into one field or variable, such as allowed origins, recipient emails or SKUs, and writes it comma-separated, one per line, or both. Order and duplicates are kept; blank input gives an empty list. It never fails, so check each item afterwards if the items have a format.
signatures: export function parseCommaList(input: string): readonly string[]

assets.name: parseContentType
assets.summary: Parses a `Content-Type` header such as `application/json; charset=utf-8` into its media type and parameters.
assets.useWhen: an HTTP handler, a webhook receiver or an upload step must decide how to read a body, check for `application/json` before parsing, or find a multipart `boundary` or a `charset`. Type and subtype are lowercased, as they are case-insensitive; quoted parameter values are unquoted, and malformed parameters are skipped. A header without `type/subtype` is an `Err`, which usually means 415 Unsupported Media Type.
signatures: export function parseContentType( header: string, ): Result<ParseContentTypeMedia, ParseContentTypeError>

assets.name: parseCookieHeader
assets.summary: Reads a `Cookie` request header into a record of names and decoded values, skipping anything malformed.
assets.useWhen: a server, middleware or edge function needs one cookie, such as a session id, a theme or a consent flag, without a cookie library. Values are percent-decoded when they can be and kept as sent when they can't, surrounding double quotes are removed, and parts without `=` are ignored, as browsers do. When a name appears twice, the first wins, since browsers send the cookie with the more specific path first. A missing header is `{}`.
signatures: export function parseCookieHeader(header: string | null | undefined): Readonly<Record<string, string>>

assets.name: parseCoordinates
assets.summary: Parses a `latitude, longitude` pair such as `51.5072, -0.1276` and checks both are on the globe.
assets.useWhen: a location is pasted from a map app, typed into a form, read from a CSV column or passed as `?near=51.5,-0.12`. The numbers may be separated by a comma, spaces, or both. Latitude comes first, as map apps copy it. A latitude past ±90 usually means the pair was swapped, and gets its own code so the message can say so.
signatures: export function parseCoordinates(input: string): Result<ParseCoordinatesPoint, ParseCoordinatesError>

assets.name: parseCsvLine
assets.summary: Splits one CSV line into its fields, honouring quotes, so `a,"b, c","say ""hi"""` gives `['a', 'b, c', 'say "hi"']`.
assets.useWhen: reading lines of a CSV or TSV export, a spreadsheet paste or a log, where fields may contain the delimiter or quotes and a plain split would cut them apart. Pass `','`, `';'` or `'\t'`. A quote only opens a field as its first character, `""` inside quotes is one quote, spaces are kept as written, and a trailing `\r` from Windows line endings is dropped. A quoted field that runs past the end of the line is an `Err`: split the file with a full CSV parser if fields can contain line breaks.
signatures: export function parseCsvLine(line: string, delimiter: string): Result<readonly string[], ParseCsvLineError>
export function parseCsvLine(delimiter: string): (line: string) => Result<readonly string[], ParseCsvLineError>

assets.name: parseDurationMs
assets.summary: Parses a human duration such as `90s`, `5m`, `1h30m` or `1.5d` into milliseconds.
assets.useWhen: a timeout, TTL, cache lifetime, polling interval or session length is set in config or by a person, and `CACHE_TTL=15m` is easier to get right than `900000`. Units are `ms`, `s`, `m`, `h`, `d` and `w`, in any case, and parts add up, with or without spaces: `1h 30m`. A bare number is milliseconds. Negative values, unknown units and leftover text are an `Err`. The total is rounded to a whole millisecond.
signatures: export function parseDurationMs(input: string): Result<number, ParseDurationMsError>

assets.name: parseEmailAddress
assets.summary: Splits an address such as `Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com>` into an optional display name and a checked email.
assets.useWhen: reading `From`, `To` or `Reply-To` style values, a contact pasted from a mail client, or an invite field where people paste whole addresses. Plain `ada@example.com`, `<ada@example.com>`, `Ada <ada@example.com>` and `"Lovelace, Ada" <ada@example.com>` are understood. The email is checked with Receta's practical `isEmail` rule; the name has its spaces tidied and is None when absent or blank.
signatures: export function parseEmailAddress( input: string, ): Result<ParseEmailAddressMailbox, ParseEmailAddressError>

assets.name: parseEnum
assets.summary: Matches text against a fixed list of allowed values, ignoring case and spaces, and returns the value as listed.
assets.useWhen: a status, role, sort order, log level or plan name comes in as text and the code needs the exact literal type, such as `'asc' | 'desc'`. `' Published '` matches `'published'` and comes back spelled as the list spells it. Anything else is an `Err` that lists what was allowed, ready to show the caller.
signatures: export function parseEnum<const A extends string>( input: string, allowed: readonly A[], ): Result<A, ParseEnumError<A>>
export function parseEnum<const A extends string>( allowed: readonly A[], ): (input: string) => Result<A, ParseEnumError<A>>

assets.name: parseEnvFlag
assets.summary: Reads an on/off feature flag such as `DEBUG=1`, falling back to a default when it is unset or blank.
assets.useWhen: a boolean environment variable or setting may be missing, and missing should mean the default rather than an error. `true`, `yes`, `y`, `on` and `1` turn it on; `false`, `no`, `n`, `off` and `0` turn it off, in any case. A value that is set but unreadable, like `DEBUG=enabled`, is an `Err`, so a typo never flips the flag silently.
signatures: export function parseEnvFlag( value: string | undefined, fallback: boolean, ): Result<boolean, ParseEnvFlagError>
export function parseEnvFlag( fallback: boolean, ): (value: string | undefined) => Result<boolean, ParseEnvFlagError>

assets.name: parseHexColor
assets.summary: Parses a CSS hex color such as `#fc0`, `#ffcc00` or `#ffcc0080` into red, green, blue and alpha numbers.
assets.useWhen: a theme, a brand color setting or a user-picked color arrives as hex and the code needs the channels, to compute contrast, mix colors, build an `rgba()` string or pass it to a canvas or chart. The `#` is optional and case doesn't matter. Three, six and eight digits are accepted; anything else, including four-digit `#fc08`, is an `Err`.
signatures: export function parseHexColor(input: string): Result<ParseHexColorRgba, ParseHexColorError>

assets.name: parseHostPort
assets.summary: Splits an address such as `db.internal:5432` or `[::1]:6379` into a host and a numeric port.
assets.useWhen: a database, cache, broker or upstream address is configured as one `host:port` string, such as `REDIS_ADDR`, and a missing or bad port must stop startup with a clear reason. IPv6 hosts need brackets, as in URLs, and come back without them. The port must be digits only, from 1 to 65535, so `80abc` and `1e3` are refused.
signatures: export function parseHostPort(input: string): Result<ParseHostPortAddress, ParseHostPortError>

assets.name: parseHttpUrl
assets.summary: Parses an absolute `http` or `https` URL from text into a `URL`, refusing other schemes and relative paths.
assets.useWhen: a person or a config supplies a link the server will call or redirect to, such as a webhook endpoint, a callback URL, an avatar URL or `API_BASE_URL`. `new URL` throws on bad input and happily accepts `javascript:`, `file:` and `ftp:`; this returns an `Err` for all of them. Surrounding spaces are trimmed. It doesn't check which host the URL points to, so add an allow-list when calling user-supplied URLs from a server.
signatures: export function parseHttpUrl(input: string): Result<URL, ParseHttpUrlError>

assets.name: parseIdList
assets.summary: Parses a comma-separated list of numeric ids such as `?ids=4,8,15`, stopping at the first item that isn't one.
assets.useWhen: a query parameter, a CLI argument or a bulk-action field carries several positive integer ids and one bad item should reject the whole request. Spaces and empty items (`4,,8,`) are ignored, and blank input is an empty list. An id is digits only, so `12abc`, `1e3` and `-1` are refused. The error names the first bad item and its position.
signatures: export function parseIdList(input: string): Result<readonly number[], ParseIdListError>

assets.name: parseIntInRange
assets.summary: Parses a whole number from text and checks it lies between a minimum and a maximum, both included.
assets.useWhen: a count, limit, age, retry total or page size comes in as text and a value outside its range must be refused with a reason, not clamped. Only digits with an optional minus sign count: decimals, blanks, `1e3`, `0x10` and trailing junk such as `12abc` are `NOT_AN_INTEGER`.
signatures: export function parseIntInRange( input: string, bounds: ParseIntInRangeBounds, ): Result<number, ParseIntInRangeError>
export function parseIntInRange( bounds: ParseIntInRangeBounds, ): (input: string) => Result<number, ParseIntInRangeError>

assets.name: parseJsonArrayOf
assets.summary: Parses JSON text that must be an array whose every item passes a type guard, such as a list of ids or tags.
assets.useWhen: a list arrives as JSON, in an environment variable like `ALLOWED_IDS=[1,2,3]`, a `localStorage` entry or a request field, and the code needs `T[]`, not `unknown`. Pass a guard such as `isString` or `isNumber`, or your own `(value: unknown) => value is T`. The error names the first item that failed and where it is.
signatures: export function parseJsonArrayOf<T>( input: string, isItem: (value: unknown) => value is T, ): Result<readonly T[], ParseJsonArrayOfError>
export function parseJsonArrayOf<T>( isItem: (value: unknown) => value is T, ): (input: string) => Result<readonly T[], ParseJsonArrayOfError>

assets.name: parseJsonAs
assets.summary: Parses JSON text and checks it against a schema of type guards, returning a typed object or the first field that's wrong.
assets.useWhen: JSON from outside the program, such as a request body, a queue message, a file or `localStorage`, has to become a typed value without a cast. The schema maps each field to a guard such as `isString` or `isNumber`, or to a nested schema; fields not in the schema are kept as they are. The error says which path failed, so it can go straight into a 400 response or a log line.
signatures: export function parseJsonAs<T extends PlainObject>( input: string, schema: ObjectSchema<T>, ): Result<T, ParseJsonAsError>
export function parseJsonAs<T extends PlainObject>( schema: ObjectSchema<T>, ): (input: string) => Result<T, ParseJsonAsError>

assets.name: parseJsonObject
assets.summary: Parses JSON text that must hold an object, such as a settings blob, a webhook body or a cached record.
assets.useWhen: the code is about to read fields from parsed JSON, where an array, a number or `null` would slip past `JSON.parse` and fail later as "cannot read property". Broken JSON is `INVALID_JSON`, with the parser's reason in the message; valid JSON that isn't an object is `NOT_AN_OBJECT`. The fields themselves stay `unknown`; check them next.
signatures: export function parseJsonObject(input: string): Result<Record<string, unknown>, ParseJsonObjectError>

assets.name: parseKeyValuePairs
assets.summary: Parses `key=value` pairs joined by a separator, such as `ssl=true;pool=5`, into a record.
assets.useWhen: a single environment variable, connection-string option, header or CLI flag packs several settings, like `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES=service=api,env=prod`.
