Keys and values are trimmed, empty segments are skipped, and a value may contain `=`. A segment without `=`, an empty key or a key given twice is an `Err` naming the segment. Values stay strings; parse them further where their type is known.
signatures: export function parseKeyValuePairs( input: string, separator: string, ): Result<Readonly<Record<string, string>>, ParseKeyValuePairsError>
export function parseKeyValuePairs( separator: string, ): (input: string) => Result<Readonly<Record<string, string>>, ParseKeyValuePairsError>

assets.name: parseMoneyCents
assets.summary: Parses a typed money amount such as `$1,234.50` or `1.234,50 €` into whole cents: 123450.
assets.useWhen: a price, a payment or an invoice line comes in as text, from a form, a CSV export or a bank statement, and the code stores money as integer minor units so sums never drift. Currency symbols and codes, thousands separators and accounting brackets for negatives, `(12.00)`, are understood; a comma followed by exactly two digits is read as the decimal point, and `1,5 €` is refused rather than guessed. More than two decimals is `TOO_MANY_DECIMALS` rather than a silent rounding.
signatures: export function parseMoneyCents(input: string): Result<number, ParseMoneyCentsError>

assets.name: parseNumberLike
assets.summary: Accepts a finite number or numeric text such as `' 12.5 '` from an unknown value, and refuses everything else.
assets.useWhen: a number arrives from JSON, a spreadsheet, a form library or a third-party API that sometimes sends `12` and sometimes `"12"`, and the code needs a plain `number`. Numbers must be finite; text is trimmed and must be a whole numeric string (`12px` and `''` are refused). `NaN`, `Infinity`, booleans, `null`, arrays and objects are an `Err`, never quietly turned into 0 or 1 the way `Number()` would.
signatures: export function parseNumberLike(value: unknown): Result<number, ParseNumberLikeError>

assets.name: parseNumericRange
assets.summary: Parses a range such as `10-50`, `10..50`, `1.5 to 3` or a single `7` into `{ min, max }`.
assets.useWhen: a filter in a URL, a search box or a spreadsheet cell holds a span, such as a price range `?price=10-50`, an age band or a size range. A single number is a range of one. Negative numbers work, so `-5--1` is -5 to -1. A range whose low end is bigger than its high end is `REVERSED_RANGE` instead of being swapped, since it's usually a typo.
signatures: export function parseNumericRange( input: string, ): Result<ParseNumericRangeBounds, ParseNumericRangeError>

assets.name: parseOptionalInt
assets.summary: Parses a whole number that may be left blank: blank is Ok(None), a number is Ok(Some(n)), anything else is Err.
assets.useWhen: an optional numeric field, such as a form input, a CSV cell or a query parameter, may be empty, but a value that is present must be a whole number. Blank and missing mean "not given"; they are never read as 0. Only digits with an optional minus sign count, so `1e3` and `12abc` are an `Err`.
signatures: export function parseOptionalInt( input: string | undefined, ): Result<Option<number>, ParseOptionalIntError>

assets.name: parsePageRanges
assets.summary: Parses a page selection such as `1-3, 5, 8-9` into the sorted list of page numbers, checked against the page count.
assets.useWhen: a print dialog, a PDF splitter, an export or a bulk action lets someone pick pages, slides or rows the way print dialogs do. Pages are whole numbers from 1 to `pageCount`; overlapping parts are merged, and the result is sorted with no duplicates. Blank input is an empty list, so decide yourself whether that means "all pages". The first bad part stops the parse and is named in the error.
signatures: export function parsePageRanges( input: string, pageCount: number, ): Result<readonly number[], ParsePageRangesError>
export function parsePageRanges( pageCount: number, ): (input: string) => Result<readonly number[], ParsePageRangesError>

assets.name: parsePagination
assets.summary: Reads `page` and page-size query parameters into safe numbers and an offset, falling back to defaults instead of failing.
assets.useWhen: a list endpoint or a table view takes `?page=` and `?limit=` from the URL, and a missing, garbled or abusive value should never break the page or ask the database for a million rows. Only digits count, so `2abc` and `1e3` are bad values. A bad or missing page is 1; a bad or missing size is `defaultPerPage`; a size above `maxPerPage` is cut down to it. Use a Result-returning parse instead if the client must be told its parameters were wrong.
signatures: export function parsePagination( query: ParsePaginationQuery, settings: ParsePaginationSettings, ): ParsePaginationPage
export function parsePagination( settings: ParsePaginationSettings, ): (query: ParsePaginationQuery) => ParsePaginationPage

assets.name: parsePercent
assets.summary: Parses a percentage such as `45%` or `12.5` into a fraction: `45%` becomes 0.45.
assets.useWhen: a rate, discount, tax, threshold or progress value is typed as a percentage and the code computes with fractions. The `%` sign is optional and the number always counts as percentage points, so `0.5` means half a percent (0.005), not 50%. Values below 0 or above 100 are kept, because growth and change rates can be anywhere; check the range after if it matters. The result is rounded to 10 decimals to drop float noise.
signatures: export function parsePercent(input: string): Result<number, ParsePercentError>

assets.name: parsePort
assets.summary: Parses a TCP or UDP port number from a string, such as an environment variable.
assets.useWhen: reading `PORT` or the port part of `host:port` from config, where a value outside 1–65535 must stop startup instead of failing later inside `listen`. Only digits count, after trimming: `80abc`, `1e3` and `80.0` are rejected.
signatures: export function parsePort(input: string): Result<number, ParsePortError>

assets.name: parsePortOption
assets.summary: Reads a TCP or UDP port from a string that may be missing, as Some(port) or None.
assets.useWhen: a port is optional and a default should take over when it is missing or unusable, such as `PORT` in development. Blank, out-of-range and non-digit values, such as `80abc` or `1e3`, all come back as None, so pair it with `unwrapOr` for the default. When a bad value must stop startup with a reason, use `parsePort` instead.
signatures: export function parsePortOption(input: string | undefined): Option<number>

assets.name: parseQueryString
assets.summary: Parses a URL query string such as `?tag=a&tag=b&q=red+shoes` into a record of value lists.
assets.useWhen: a query string, a form-urlencoded body or a hash fragment needs reading without a URL object, and repeated keys such as `tag=a&tag=b` must all survive. Every key maps to a list, so its type never depends on how many times it appeared. `+` is a space, a key without `=` gets `''`, and a broken escape like `%E0%A4%A` is an `Err` instead of the exception `decodeURIComponent` throws.
signatures: export function parseQueryString( input: string, ): Result<Readonly<Record<string, readonly string[]>>, ParseQueryStringError>

assets.name: parseRequiredEnv
assets.summary: Reads the environment variables a program can't start without, and lists every one that is missing in a single error.
assets.useWhen: a server, worker or CLI starts up and needs `DATABASE_URL`, `API_KEY` and the like, and a deploy with three missing variables should fail once with all three named, not three times in a row. Blank values count as missing, and values are trimmed, since a stray space or newline from a `.env` file is a common bug. Pass `process.env`, `Bun.env` or `Deno.env.toObject()`. Parse the values further, such as with `parsePort`, after.
signatures: export function parseRequiredEnv<const K extends string>( env: Readonly<Record<string, string | undefined>>, names: readonly K[], ): Result<Readonly<Record<K, string>>, ParseRequiredEnvError<K>>
export function parseRequiredEnv<const K extends string>( names: readonly K[], ): (env: Readonly<Record<string, string | undefined>>) => Result<Readonly<Record<K, string>>, ParseRequiredEnvError<K>>

assets.name: parseRetryAfter
assets.summary: Reads a `Retry-After` header, in seconds or as an HTTP date, into how many milliseconds to wait.
assets.useWhen: an API answered 429 Too Many Requests or 503 Service Unavailable and the client should wait as long as the server asked before trying again. `now` is the current time in milliseconds, such as `Date.now()`, passed in so the function stays pure. A date in the past means no wait, `Some(0)`. A missing or unreadable header is None, so fall back to your own backoff with `unwrapOr`.
signatures: export function parseRetryAfter(header: string | null | undefined, now: number): Option<number>
export function parseRetryAfter(now: number): (header: string | null | undefined) => Option<number>

assets.name: parseSemver
assets.summary: Parses a semantic version such as `v2.1.0-beta.3+build.7` into its numbered parts.
assets.useWhen: comparing app, API, plugin or schema versions, checking a minimum client version, or reading a git tag, where string comparison gets `1.10.0` versus `1.9.0` wrong. A leading `v` and surrounding spaces are allowed. Ranges such as `^1.2` and partial versions such as `1.2` are an `Err`: this reads one exact version.
signatures: export function parseSemver(input: string): Result<ParseSemverVersion, ParseSemverError>

assets.name: parseTagList
assets.summary: Turns typed tags like `React, react ,  Type Script` into a clean list: lowercased, single-spaced, no duplicates.
assets.useWhen: users type tags, labels, keywords or topics into one comma-separated field and `React` and ` react` must count as the same tag. The first spelling's position wins; empty entries are dropped. Spaces inside a tag are kept as one space, so `Type   Script` becomes `type script`; slugify the tags afterwards if they go into URLs.
signatures: export function parseTagList(input: string): readonly string[]

assets.name: validateIdList
assets.summary: Parses a comma-separated list of numeric ids and reports every item that isn't one, not just the first.
assets.useWhen: a person typed or pasted the list, such as order numbers in an admin form or a spreadsheet column, and should fix every mistake in one go. Spaces and empty items are ignored, and an id is digits only, so `12abc` and `1e3` are refused. `Valid` carries the ids in order; `Invalid` lists each bad item with its position.
signatures: export function validateIdList(input: string): Validation<readonly number[], ValidateIdListError>

assets.name: collectAllErrors
assets.summary: Combines a list of Results into Ok with every value, or Err with every error, not just the first.
assets.useWhen: several independent checks or parses have already run, such as one per row, file or field, and the caller should see all the failures at once instead of fixing them one by one. Order is kept on both sides. An empty list is `Ok([])`. Use `collect` from Receta when the first error is enough.
signatures: export function collectAllErrors<T, E>( results: readonly Result<T, E>[], ): Result<readonly T[], readonly E[]>

assets.name: ensure
assets.summary: Keeps an Ok only when its value passes a check, and turns it into an Err built from the value otherwise.
assets.useWhen: a parse or a load succeeded but the value still breaks a rule, such as a number that must be positive, a list that must not be empty, a user who must be active or a date that must be in the future, and the pipe should carry on as one `Result`. An `Err` passes through untouched and the check never runs. With a type guard such as `isString`, the Ok value's type narrows.
signatures: export function ensure<T, S extends T, E, F>( result: Result<T, E>, check: (value: T) => value is S, toError: (value: T) => F, ): Result<S, E | F>
export function ensure<T, E, F>( result: Result<T, E>, check: (value: T) => boolean, toError: (value: T) => F, ): Result<T, E | F>
export function ensure<T, S extends T, F>( check: (value: T) => value is S, toError: (value: T) => F, ): <E>(result: Result<T, E>) => Result<S, E | F>
export function ensure<T, F>( check: (value: T) => boolean, toError: (value: T) => F, ): <E>(result: Result<T, E>) => Result<T, E | F>

assets.name: findOrErr
assets.summary: Finds the first item that matches, as Ok(item), or returns the error you give when none does.
assets.useWhen: looking something up is part of a `Result` pipe and "not there" is a failure with a reason, such as the user for an id, the price for a SKU, the route for a path or the plan for a name. Build the predicate with `where` and `eq` for record lookups. With a type guard, the found item's type narrows.
signatures: export function findOrErr<T, S extends T, E>( items: readonly T[], matches: (item: T) => item is S, error: E, ): Result<S, E>
export function findOrErr<T, E>( items: readonly T[], matches: (item: T) => boolean, error: E, ): Result<T, E>
export function findOrErr<T, S extends T, E>( matches: (item: T) => item is S, error: E, ): (items: readonly T[]) => Result<S, E>
export function findOrErr<T, E>( matches: (item: T) => boolean, error: E, ): (items: readonly T[]) => Result<T, E>

assets.name: firstOk
assets.summary: Tries a list of fallbacks in order and returns the first Ok, calling each one only if everything before it failed.
assets.useWhen: a value can come from several places in order of preference, such as an explicit setting, then an environment variable, then a config file, or several parsers for the formats an input may be in. Attempts are functions, so later ones never run once an earlier one succeeds. When all fail, the `Err` holds every error in order; an empty list is `Err([])`.
signatures: export function firstOk<T, E>( attempts: readonly (() => Result<T, E>)[], ): Result<T, readonly E[]>

assets.name: firstOkAsync
assets.summary: Runs async fallbacks one after another and resolves with the first Ok; later ones never start.
assets.useWhen: a read has a preferred source and slower or costlier backups, such as memory cache, then Redis, then the database, then a third-party API, and each source reports a miss or failure as an `Err`. Attempts run in order, never in parallel, and stop at the first `Ok`. When all fail, the `Err` holds every error in order. A rejected promise is not caught; wrap that source with `tryCatchAsync` if it can throw.
signatures: export async function firstOkAsync<T, E>( attempts: readonly (() => Promise<Result<T, E>>)[], ): Promise<Result<T, readonly E[]>>

assets.name: firstSome
assets.summary: Tries a list of lookups in order and returns the first Some, calling each one only if everything before it was None.
assets.useWhen: a value has several places it may come from and missing is not an error until all of them are empty, such as a locale from the user's setting, then the browser, then the account; or a display name from a nickname, then a full name, then an email. Lookups are functions, so later ones never run once an earlier one finds a value. All None, or an empty list, is None.
signatures: export function firstSome<T>(lookups: readonly (() => Option<T>)[]): Option<T>

assets.name: ifPresent
assets.summary: Runs a step that returns a Result only when a value is present: missing is Ok(None), and a present value is parsed or checked.
assets.useWhen: an optional field still has to be valid when it's given, such as an optional `TIMEOUT` variable, a `?limit=` parameter, a middle name or a coupon code. `null` and `undefined` mean "not given" and succeed as `None`; anything else goes through the step, and its `Err` comes back as is. An empty string counts as present, so trim and check for blank first if it should mean missing.
signatures: export function ifPresent<T, U, E>( value: T | null | undefined, step: (value: T) => Result<U, E>, ): Result<Option<U>, E>
export function ifPresent<T, U, E>( step: (value: T) => Result<U, E>, ): (value: T | null | undefined) => Result<Option<U>, E>

assets.name: isErrWithCode
assets.summary: Checks whether a Result is an Err with a given `code`, and narrows the error to that code's shape when it is.
assets.useWhen: one error code needs its own branch, such as answering 404 for `NOT_FOUND`, asking for a login on `UNAUTHENTICATED`, highlighting a field on `INVALID`, or counting timeouts in a batch. Inside the `if`, TypeScript knows the error's extra fields for that code. Works with `R.filter` in its data-last form.
signatures: export function isErrWithCode<T, E extends { readonly code: string }, const C extends E['code']>( result: Result<T, E>, code: C, ): result is Err<E & { readonly code: C }>
export function isErrWithCode<E extends { readonly code: string }, const C extends E['code']>( code: C, ): <T>(result: Result<T, E>) => result is Err<E & { readonly code: C }>
assets.output: result is Err<E & { readonly code: C }>

assets.name: mapSome
assets.summary: Runs a step that returns an Option on every item and keeps only the Some values, in order.
assets.useWhen: some items don't produce a value and that's fine, such as keeping the valid emails from a pasted list, the numbers that parse from a column, the users that have a phone number, or the routes that match. Receta validators that return an Option, like `isEmail` and `isUrl`, plug straight in.
signatures: export function mapSome<T, U>( items: readonly T[], pick: (item: T, index: number) => Option<U>, ): readonly U[]
export function mapSome<T, U>( pick: (item: T, index: number) => Option<U>, ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly U[]

assets.name: orElse
assets.summary: Replaces an Err with the Result of a fallback that receives the error; an Ok passes through untouched.
assets.useWhen: a failure has a second way to succeed that depends on what went wrong, such as reading a backup file when the main one is missing, using a cached copy after a timeout, or retrying with different settings. The fallback runs only on `Err` and may fail too, with its own error type. To recover with a plain value, return `ok(value)`.
signatures: export function orElse<T, E, U, F>( result: Result<T, E>, fallback: (error: E) => Result<U, F>, ): Result<T | U, F>
export function orElse<E, U, F>( fallback: (error: E) => Result<U, F>, ): <T>(result: Result<T, E>) => Result<T | U, F>

assets.name: recoverWhen
assets.summary: Turns an Err into an Ok only when its `code` is one you list; every other error passes through.
assets.useWhen: some failures are normal outcomes with a sensible value, such as `NOT_FOUND` meaning an empty list, `CACHE_MISS` meaning "load it", or `ALREADY_EXISTS` meaning the work was done, while the rest must still fail loudly. When the error type is a union of codes, the recovered codes leave the error type. Recovering from everything hides real problems; prefer naming the codes.
signatures: export function recoverWhen<T, E extends { readonly code: string }, const C extends E['code'], U>( result: Result<T, E>, codes: readonly C[], recover: (error: E) => U, ): Result<T | U, Exclude<E, { readonly code: C }>>

export function recoverWhen<E extends { readonly code: string }, const C extends E['code'], U>( codes: readonly C[], recover: (error: E) => U, ): <T>(result: Result<T, E>) => Result<T | U, Exclude<E, { readonly code: C }>>
assets.output: Result<T | U, Exclude<E, { readonly code: C }>>

assets.name: renameErrorCodes
assets.summary: Renames error codes using a lookup table, such as `ER_DUP_ENTRY` to `EMAIL_TAKEN`, keeping every other field of the error.
assets.useWhen: errors cross a boundary where their codes stop making sense, such as database or SDK codes reaching an API or a UI that should speak in domain terms, or several providers that call the same failure by different names. Codes not in the table pass through as they are. An `Ok` is untouched.
signatures: export function renameErrorCodes< T, E extends { readonly code: string }, const M extends { readonly [C in E['code']]?: string }, >(result: Result<T, E>, renames: M): Result<T, RenameErrorCodesError<E, M>>

export function renameErrorCodes< E extends { readonly code: string }, const M extends { readonly [C in E['code']]?: string }, >(renames: M): <T>(result: Result<T, E>) => Result<T, RenameErrorCodesError<E, M>>

assets.name: resultFromPredicate
assets.summary: Checks a plain value and returns Ok(value) when it passes, or an Err built from the value when it doesn't.
assets.useWhen: a value of unknown or loose type has to enter a `Result` pipe, such as a field of a parsed body, a function argument or a value read from storage, and the check is a predicate or a type guard. With a guard such as `isString` or `R.isArray`, the Ok value gets the narrowed type, so no cast is needed afterwards.
signatures: export function resultFromPredicate<T, S extends T, E>( value: T, check: (value: T) => value is S, toError: (value: T) => E, ): Result<S, E>
export function resultFromPredicate<T, E>( value: T, check: (value: T) => boolean, toError: (value: T) => E, ): Result<T, E>
export function resultFromPredicate<T, S extends T, E>( check: (value: T) => value is S, toError: (value: T) => E, ): (value: T) => Result<S, E>
export function resultFromPredicate<T, E>( check: (value: T) => boolean, toError: (value: T) => E, ): (value: T) => Result<T, E>

assets.name: sequenceOptionRecord
assets.summary: Turns a record of Options into Some of a record when every field has a value, or None when any is missing.
assets.useWhen: an object only makes sense with all its parts, such as an address that needs street, city and postcode, a connection that needs host, user and password, or a price that needs amount and currency. Field names and types carry over, so `{ city: Option<string> }` becomes `Option<{ city: string }>`.
signatures: export function sequenceOptionRecord<const Os extends Readonly<Record<string, Option<unknown>>>>( options: Os, ): Option<SequenceOptionRecordValues<Os>>

assets.name: sequenceRecord
assets.summary: Turns a record of Results into one Result of a record: Ok with every field's value, or the first field's Err.
assets.useWhen: several values are parsed or loaded separately, such as the fields of a request, the settings of a config or the parts of a page, and the code needs one typed object or a reason to stop. Field names and types carry over, so `{ port: Result<number, E> }` becomes `Result<{ port: number }, E>`. Fields are checked in the order they were written.
signatures: export function sequenceRecord<const Rs extends Readonly<Record<string, Result<unknown, unknown>>>>( results: Rs, ): Result<SequenceRecordValues<Rs>, SequenceRecordError<Rs>>

assets.name: sequenceRecordAll
assets.summary: Turns a record of Results into Ok with every field's value, or Err with the error of every field that failed, by name.
assets.useWhen: a form, a request body or a config has several fields parsed separately, and the caller should get every field's problem at once, keyed by field so it can sit next to the right input or be listed in a startup error. Field names and types carry over.
signatures: export function sequenceRecordAll<const Rs extends Readonly<Record<string, Result<unknown, unknown>>>>( results: Rs, ): Result<SequenceRecordAllValues<Rs>, SequenceRecordAllErrors<Rs>>

assets.name: settleResults
assets.summary: Runs a step that returns a Result on every item and splits the outcome into what succeeded and what failed, with the inputs.
assets.useWhen: a batch should do as much as it can and report the rest, such as sending a newsletter, importing contacts or resizing images, where the failures go to a retry queue, a report or a "3 rows were skipped" message. Unlike an all-or-nothing `Result`, the successes are kept even when some items fail. Each failure keeps its item and index.
signatures: export function settleResults<T, U, E>( items: readonly T[], step: (item: T, index: number) => Result<U, E>, ): SettleResultsOutcome<T, U, E>
export function settleResults<T, U, E>( step: (item: T, index: number) => Result<U, E>, ): (items: readonly T[]) => SettleResultsOutcome<T, U, E>

assets.name: summarizeResults
assets.summary: Counts a batch's Results: how many succeeded, how many failed, and how many failures had each error code.
assets.useWhen: a job, an import or a fan-out finished and needs a one-line report, a metric or an alert rule, such as "sent 120, failed 3 (BOUNCED 2, TIMEOUT 1)", without keeping the values. Errors must have a `code`. An empty batch is all zeros.
signatures: export function summarizeResults<T, E extends { readonly code: string }>( results: readonly Result<T, E>[], ): SummarizeResultsSummary

assets.name: toHttpResponse
assets.summary: Turns a Result into an HTTP status and JSON body, mapping error codes to statuses and hiding unmapped errors behind a 500.
assets.useWhen: a route handler ends with a `Result` and must answer, in Express, Hono, Next.js route handlers or a Lambda. An `Ok` becomes `okStatus` with the value as the body. A listed error code gets its status and `{ error: { code, message } }`. Any other code becomes a 500 with a generic body, so internal messages such as SQL errors never reach the client; log the original error yourself.
signatures: export function toHttpResponse<T, E extends { readonly code: string; readonly message: string }>( result: Result<T, E>, options: ToHttpResponseOptions<E>, ): ToHttpResponseReply<T>
export function toHttpResponse<T, E extends { readonly code: string; readonly message: string }>( options: ToHttpResponseOptions<E>, ): (result: Result<T, E>) => ToHttpResponseReply<T>

assets.name: toUserMessage
assets.summary: Turns a Result into the sentence to show a person: a success text from the value, or the text for the error's code.
assets.useWhen: an action's outcome becomes a toast, a banner, a CLI line or a chat reply, and error codes must turn into friendly words without leaking internals like stack traces or SQL. Codes you didn't list get the fallback, so a new error code never shows up raw. The error's own `message` is never shown; put that in your logs.
signatures: export function toUserMessage<T, E extends { readonly code: string }>( result: Result<T, E>, texts: ToUserMessageTexts<T, E>, ): string
export function toUserMessage<T, E extends { readonly code: string }>( texts: ToUserMessageTexts<T, E>, ): (result: Result<T, E>) => string

assets.name: traverseResults
assets.summary: Runs a step that returns a Result on each item and stops at the first Err, so later items are never touched.
assets.useWhen: each item goes through a parse, a check or a write that can fail, and one failure should stop the batch, such as applying migrations in order, importing rows into a transaction, or parsing a list where any bad entry rejects the request. The step is never called after the first `Err`, which matters when it has effects. On success the values keep the input's order.
signatures: export function traverseResults<T, U, E>( items: readonly T[], step: (item: T, index: number) => Result<U, E>, ): Result<readonly U[], E>
export function traverseResults<T, U, E>( step: (item: T, index: number) => Result<U, E>, ): (items: readonly T[]) => Result<readonly U[], E>

assets.name: traverseResultsAll
assets.summary: Runs a step that returns a Result on every item and reports every failure with its index, or all the values.
assets.useWhen: a person will fix the input, such as rows of a CSV upload, lines of a pasted list or entries of a bulk form, and should see each problem with where it is in one pass. Every item runs, even after a failure. On success the values keep the input's order.
signatures: export function traverseResultsAll<T, U, E>( items: readonly T[], step: (item: T, index: number) => Result<U, E>, ): Result<readonly U[], readonly TraverseResultsAllFailure<E>[]>
export function traverseResultsAll<T, U, E>( step: (item: T, index: number) => Result<U, E>, ): (items: readonly T[]) => Result<readonly U[], readonly TraverseResultsAllFailure<E>[]>

assets.name: traverseResultsAsync
assets.summary: Runs an async step that resolves to a Result on every item, a few at a time, and returns all values or the first Err.
assets.useWhen: each item needs an async call that reports failure as an `Err`, such as loading users by id, checking stock per SKU or validating addresses against an API, and the caller needs all of them or a reason why not. `concurrency` caps the calls in flight so a list of 500 ids doesn't open 500 connections. Every item runs; the first `Err` in input order wins. A step that rejects instead of resolving shows up as Receta's `MapAsyncError`.
signatures: export async function traverseResultsAsync<T, U, E>( items: readonly T[], step: (item: T, index: number) => Promise<Result<U, E>>, options: TraverseResultsAsyncOptions = {}, ): Promise<Result<readonly U[], E | MapAsyncError>>

assets.name: withErrorContext
assets.summary: Wraps an Err with a note about what was being done, so the message reads `loading config: file not found`.
assets.useWhen: an error crosses a layer and its own message no longer says where it happened, such as `ENOENT` from deep inside a config loader or `timeout` from one of several API calls. Wrapping again adds another layer in front, like a stack trace written for people. The original error stays in `cause` for code that needs its fields. An `Ok` passes through.
signatures: export function withErrorContext<T, E>( result: Result<T, E>, context: string, ): Result<T, WithErrorContextError<E>>
export function withErrorContext( context: string, ): <T, E>(result: Result<T, E>) => Result<T, WithErrorContextError<E>>

assets.name: latestVersion
assets.summary: Picks the newest stable version from a list of version strings, ignoring pre-releases.
assets.useWhen: deciding what to show as "latest", whether an upgrade is available, or which release a "stable" channel points to. Pre-releases like '2.0.0-rc.1' and strings that aren't versions are skipped. A leading `v` is allowed and kept in the result. Returns `None` when no stable version is in the list.
signatures: export function latestVersion(versions: readonly string[]): Option<string>

assets.name: pinnedFirst
assets.summary: Puts pinned items first, then lists each group newest first.
assets.useWhen: ordering notes, chats, announcements or saved searches where users pin a few items to the top and expect everything else by recency. Pinned items are also ordered newest first among themselves. Items with the same pin state and date keep their input order. Dates are `Date`s or epoch numbers.
signatures: export function pinnedFirst<T>( items: readonly T[], isPinned: (item: T) => boolean, date: (item: T) => Date | number, ): readonly T[]
export function pinnedFirst<T>( isPinned: (item: T) => boolean, date: (item: T) => Date | number, ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: sectionsByInitial
assets.summary: Sorts items by name and splits them into A–Z sections by first letter, with '#' last for digits and symbols.
assets.useWhen: building a contacts list, a glossary, a brand directory or any long list with an alphabet index on the side. Accents are folded, so 'Émile' files under E and 'Ålesund' under A. Names starting with a digit or symbol share a '#' section at the end. Inside a section, names are in natural order, case ignored. Letters from other scripts get sections of their own.
signatures: export function sectionsByInitial<T>( items: readonly T[], name: (item: T) => string, ): readonly SectionsByInitialSection<T>[]
export function sectionsByInitial<T>( name: (item: T) => string, ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly SectionsByInitialSection<T>[]

assets.name: sortByClosestTo
assets.summary: Sorts items by how close a number of theirs is to a target, closest first, with the lower value first on a tie.
assets.useWhen: suggesting the products nearest a budget, the shoe sizes next to the one that's out of stock, the time slots nearest a requested time, or the plans closest to a usage figure. When two items are equally far above and below the target, the lower one comes first.
signatures: export function sortByClosestTo<T>(items: readonly T[], target: number, value: (item: T) => number): readonly T[]
export function sortByClosestTo<T>(target: number, value: (item: T) => number): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: sortByColumn
assets.summary: Sorts table rows by a column and direction the user picked, comparing each cell by its type, blanks last.
assets.useWhen: a data table sorts on a header click, or reads `?sort=price&dir=desc` from the URL, and the columns hold a mix of numbers, text, dates and booleans. Numbers compare as numbers, dates by time, booleans with false first, and text naturally ('Item 2' before 'item 10', case ignored). Blank cells (`null`, `undefined`, `''` and `NaN`) go last in both directions. Two cells of different types compare as text. Equal cells keep their input order.
signatures: export function sortByColumn<T>(rows: readonly T[], options: SortByColumnOptions<NoInfer<T>>): readonly T[]
export function sortByColumn<T>(options: SortByColumnOptions<T>): (rows: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: sortByCustomOrder
assets.summary: Sorts items by where their value appears in a given list, with values not in the list last.
assets.useWhen: the order is a business rule rather than alphabetical, such as statuses in workflow order (todo, doing, done), sizes (S, M, L, XL), severities, or a saved manual order of ids. Values missing from the list go last, in their input order, so a new status never breaks the page. Items with the same value keep their input order.
signatures: export function sortByCustomOrder<T, V>(items: readonly T[], order: readonly V[], value: (item: T) => V): readonly T[]
export function sortByCustomOrder<T, V>(order: readonly V[], value: (item: T) => V): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: sortByDate
assets.summary: Sorts by a date that may be a `Date`, an ISO string, epoch milliseconds or missing, with bad and missing dates last.
assets.useWhen: sorting API data whose dates arrive as strings like '2024-05-01T10:00:00Z', where some rows have `null`, an empty string or an unparseable value. Those rows go last in both directions instead of landing at a random spot, since an invalid `Date` makes ordinary comparators return `NaN`. Strings are parsed with `new Date(text)`, so prefer ISO 8601. Equal dates keep their input order.
signatures: export function sortByDate<T>( items: readonly T[], date: (item: T) => Date | string | number | null | undefined, direction: 'asc' | 'desc', ): readonly T[]
export function sortByDate<T>( date: (item: T) => Date | string | number | null | undefined, direction: 'asc' | 'desc', ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

inputs.name: date
inputs.type: (item: T) => Date | string | number | null | undefined

assets.name: sortByDateDescThenId
assets.summary: Sorts newest first and breaks equal timestamps by id, so the order is total and the same on every run.
assets.useWhen: paging a feed, an audit log or orders with a cursor, where many rows share a timestamp (bulk imports, second-precision clocks) and a page boundary falling between them would repeat or skip rows. Pair it with a cursor of `(date, id)`. Ids compare as numbers or by code unit, so use one id type per list.
signatures: export function sortByDateDescThenId<T>( items: readonly T[], date: (item: T) => Date | number, id: (item: T) => string | number, ): readonly T[]
export function sortByDateDescThenId<T>( date: (item: T) => Date | number, id: (item: T) => string | number, ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: sortByDistanceFrom
assets.summary: Sorts places by distance from a point, nearest first, and gives each one its distance in kilometres.
assets.useWhen: listing stores near the user, the closest drivers to a pickup, or venues around a map pin. Distances follow the curve of the Earth (the haversine formula), which is accurate to well under 1% for this purpose; it is not road distance. Coordinates are in degrees. Places at the same distance keep their input order.
signatures: export function sortByDistanceFrom<T>( items: readonly T[], origin: SortByDistanceFromPoint, location: (item: T) => SortByDistanceFromPoint, ): readonly SortByDistanceFromEntry<T>[]
export function sortByDistanceFrom<T>( origin: SortByDistanceFromPoint, location: (item: T) => SortByDistanceFromPoint, ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly SortByDistanceFromEntry<T>[]

assets.name: sortByDueDate
assets.summary: Sorts tasks the way a to-do list should: open tasks by due date, soonest first, then open tasks with no due date, then done ones.
assets.useWhen: showing a task list, a reading list or follow-ups, where overdue items must surface first and finished items sink. Overdue tasks come first simply because their dates are the earliest. Done tasks follow the same order among themselves. Tasks with the same due date keep their input order. Due dates are `Date`s or epoch numbers, or `null`/`undefined` when unset.
signatures: export function sortByDueDate<T>( items: readonly T[], due: (item: T) => Date | number | null | undefined, isDone: (item: T) => boolean, ): readonly T[]
export function sortByDueDate<T>( due: (item: T) => Date | number | null | undefined, isDone: (item: T) => boolean, ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: sortByFrecency
assets.summary: Sorts items by frecency, a mix of how often and how recently they were used, so habits rise and stale favourites fade.
assets.useWhen: ordering a command palette, recent files, emoji suggestions or "jump to" results, where an item used 50 times last year should drop below one used 5 times today. Each item scores `count × 0.5^(age / halfLifeMs)`. A last use in the future counts as now. Equal scores keep their input order.
signatures: export function sortByFrecency<T>(items: readonly T[], options: SortByFrecencyOptions<NoInfer<T>>): readonly T[]
export function sortByFrecency<T>(options: SortByFrecencyOptions<T>): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: sortByFrequency
assets.summary: Lists each distinct value once, the most frequent first, with ties in the order they first appear.
assets.useWhen: suggesting the most used tags first in an autocomplete, ordering categories by popularity, or showing which errors happen most. Values compare exactly, so normalize case first if 'Bug' and 'bug' are the same tag. For the counts themselves, use `frequencyTable` from the collection assets.
signatures: export function sortByFrequency<T extends string | number>(values: readonly T[]): readonly T[]

assets.name: sortByKeys
assets.summary: Sorts by several fields in turn, each ascending or descending, like SQL's `ORDER BY a, b DESC`.
assets.useWhen: the order comes from data rather than code, such as a saved view, a report definition or a "sort by" menu with a secondary sort, written as `[{ key, direction }]`. Later rules only decide between items the earlier rules found equal, and items equal on every rule keep their input order. An empty list of rules keeps the input order. Fields should hold numbers, strings or dates; strings compare by code unit.
signatures: export function sortByKeys<T>(items: readonly T[], rules: readonly SortByKeysRule<NoInfer<T>>[]): readonly T[]
export function sortByKeys<T>(rules: readonly SortByKeysRule<T>[]): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: sortByLastName
assets.summary: Sorts people by last name, then by the rest of the name, when only a full-name field exists.
assets.useWhen: listing staff, authors, attendees or customers in a directory where the data holds one `name` field like 'Ada Lovelace'. The last word is the last name, after dropping suffixes such as 'Jr.', 'Sr.', 'II' or 'PhD', so 'Martin Luther King Jr.' sorts under King. Names are compared naturally with case ignored. Particles stay with the first name, so 'Ludwig van Beethoven' sorts under Beethoven. It can't know family-name-first orders.
signatures: export function sortByLastName<T>(items: readonly T[], fullName: (item: T) => string): readonly T[]
export function sortByLastName<T>(fullName: (item: T) => string): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: sortByLocale
assets.summary: Sorts text in the alphabetical order of one language, such as Swedish, German or Spanish.
assets.useWhen: showing names, cities or product titles to users of a given locale, where code-unit order is wrong: Swedish puts 'Ä' after 'Z', German files it with 'A', and Spanish puts 'ñ' after 'n'. Case doesn't change the order; when two texts differ only by case, the locale's own tie-break decides, so the result is the same every time. `locale` is a BCP 47 tag like 'sv' or 'de-DE'.
signatures: export function sortByLocale<T>(items: readonly T[], text: (item: T) => string, locale: string): readonly T[]
export function sortByLocale<T>(text: (item: T) => string, locale: string): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: sortByPriorityThenNewest
assets.summary: Sorts by priority number, most urgent first, and within one priority by date, newest first.
assets.useWhen: ordering an issue tracker, a support queue or an alert list where priority 1 beats priority 3, and among equal priorities the most recent item matters most. Items with the same priority and date keep their input order. Dates are `Date`s or epoch numbers.
signatures: export function sortByPriorityThenNewest<T>( items: readonly T[], priority: (item: T) => number, date: (item: T) => Date | number, ): readonly T[]
export function sortByPriorityThenNewest<T>( priority: (item: T) => number, date: (item: T) => Date | number, ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: sortByRelevance
assets.summary: Sorts search results by score, best first, and breaks ties by name in natural order.
assets.useWhen: showing search or autocomplete results, where many results share a score and an unstable order would make the list jump between keystrokes. Equal scores fall back to the name, compared naturally ('Plan 2' before 'plan 10', case ignored), so the order is the same every time.
signatures: export function sortByRelevance<T>( items: readonly T[], score: (item: T) => number, name: (item: T) => string, ): readonly T[]
export function sortByRelevance<T>( score: (item: T) => number, name: (item: T) => string, ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: sortByWeightedScore
assets.summary: Ranks items by a weighted mix of numeric fields, each scaled to 0–1 first, and gives every item its score.
assets.useWhen: ranking products by rating and price, candidates by several criteria, or servers by load and latency, where fields have different units. Each field is min-max scaled across the list, so a price in dollars can't drown a rating out of 5. Give a field a negative weight when lower is better. A field where every item has the same value adds nothing. Equal scores keep their input order. Scores are relative to this list, so they change when the list does.
signatures: export function sortByWeightedScore<T>( items: readonly T[], weights: SortByWeightedScoreWeights<NoInfer<T>>, ): readonly SortByWeightedScoreEntry<T>[]
export function sortByWeightedScore<T>( weights: SortByWeightedScoreWeights<T>, ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly SortByWeightedScoreEntry<T>[]

assets.name: sortNatural
assets.summary: Sorts text the way people expect: numbers by value, so 'file2' comes before 'file10', and case ignored.
assets.useWhen: listing file names, invoice numbers, chapter titles or hostnames where embedded numbers should count as numbers. Case and accents are ignored for the order, and when two texts differ only by case, a fixed tie-break by code unit puts uppercase first, so the result is the same on every run.
signatures: export function sortNatural<T>(items: readonly T[], text: (item: T) => string): readonly T[]
export function sortNatural<T>(text: (item: T) => string): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: sortNullsFirst
assets.summary: Sorts by a field that may be `null` or `undefined`, with the missing values first in both directions.
assets.useWhen: the missing value is the one to act on, such as leads never contacted, invoices without a sent date, or records never reviewed, as SQL's `NULLS FIRST` does. Reversing an ordinary comparator would move the missing values to the end; this keeps them at the front either way. Equal values, and the missing ones, keep their input order.
signatures: export function sortNullsFirst<T, V extends number | string | Date>( items: readonly T[], value: (item: T) => Nullable<V>, direction: 'asc' | 'desc', ): readonly T[]
export function sortNullsFirst<T, V extends number | string | Date>( value: (item: T) => Nullable<V>, direction: 'asc' | 'desc', ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: sortNullsLast
assets.summary: Sorts by a field that may be `null` or `undefined`, with the missing values last in both directions.
assets.useWhen: sorting customers by last order date where some never ordered, tasks by an optional estimate, or products by a price that isn't set yet, as SQL's `NULLS LAST` does. Reversing an ordinary comparator would move the missing values to the front; this keeps them at the end either way. Equal values, and the missing ones, keep their input order. Strings compare by code unit; use `sortByColumn` for natural text order.
signatures: export function sortNullsLast<T, V extends number | string | Date>( items: readonly T[], value: (item: T) => Nullable<V>, direction: 'asc' | 'desc', ): readonly T[]
export function sortNullsLast<T, V extends number | string | Date>( value: (item: T) => Nullable<V>, direction: 'asc' | 'desc', ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: sortTopologically
assets.summary: Orders items so each comes after everything it depends on, or reports the missing or circular dependencies.
assets.useWhen: running database migrations, build steps, setup tasks or plugin initialisation in dependency order. Items that become ready together keep their input order, so the output is stable. A dependency on an id that isn't in the list fails with `MISSING_DEPENDENCY`. Items that wait on each other fail with `CYCLE`, listing every item left unplaced, including those that only depend on the cycle.
signatures: export function sortTopologically<T, K extends string | number>( items: readonly T[], id: (item: T) => K, dependsOn: (item: T) => readonly K[], ): Result<readonly T[], SortTopologicallyError<K>>
export function sortTopologically<T, K extends string | number>( id: (item: T) => K, dependsOn: (item: T) => readonly K[], ): (items: readonly T[]) => Result<readonly T[], SortTopologicallyError<K>>

assets.name: sortVersions
assets.summary: Sorts version strings oldest first by semantic versioning, so '1.10.0' comes after '1.9.0'.
assets.useWhen: listing releases, package versions, API versions or firmware builds. A leading `v` is allowed, and a missing minor or patch counts as 0. A pre-release sorts before its release ('1.0.0-beta.2' < '1.0.0-beta.11' < '1.0.0'), and build metadata after `+` is ignored for the order. Strings that aren't versions, like 'latest', go last. Reverse the result for newest first.
signatures: export function sortVersions(versions: readonly string[]): readonly string[]

assets.name: cartAddItem
assets.summary: Adds a line to a cart, or adds its quantity to the line with the same id, so a product appears once.
assets.useWhen: an "Add to cart" button, a reorder or a cart merge after login adds products to the cart in state. A new id is appended at the end with the given line. An id already in the cart keeps its line and position and only its quantity grows, so a price or note on the existing line wins. A quantity of 0 or less adds nothing and returns the same array. Give each variant its own id (`'shirt-m-blue'`) when variants must be separate lines.
signatures: export function cartAddItem<L extends CartAddItemLine>(lines: readonly L[], line: L): readonly L[]
export function cartAddItem<L extends CartAddItemLine>(line: L): (lines: readonly L[]) => readonly L[]

assets.name: cartSetQuantity
assets.summary: Sets the quantity of the cart line with an id, and removes the line when the quantity is 0 or less.
assets.useWhen: the quantity input, the "−" button or a "remove" link of a cart row changes one line. Removing is just setting 0, so one handler covers all three. The line keeps its position and other fields. An id that isn't in the cart changes nothing and returns the same array: use `cartAddItem` to add a product.
signatures: export function cartSetQuantity<L extends CartSetQuantityLine>( lines: readonly L[], id: L['id'], quantity: number, ): readonly L[]
export function cartSetQuantity<L extends CartSetQuantityLine>( id: L['id'], quantity: number, ): (lines: readonly L[]) => readonly L[]

assets.name: formResetField
assets.summary: Puts one form field back to its initial value, and forgets that it was touched or had an error.
assets.useWhen: a field has an "undo" or "reset" button, an edit is cancelled, or a dependent field must go back to its default when another one changes, such as the state when the country changes. The form state is `{ values, initial, touched, errors }`, with extra fields kept. The rest of the form is untouched, and the field name is checked against `values`.
signatures: export function formResetField<F extends FormResetFieldState<object>, K extends keyof F['values'] & string>( form: F, field: K, ): F
export function formResetField<F extends FormResetFieldState<object>, K extends keyof F['values'] & string>( field: K, ): (form: F) => F

assets.name: formSetField
assets.summary: Sets one form field's value, marks it touched and clears its error, in one immutable update.
assets.useWhen: a hand-rolled form in React, Vue, Svelte or a reducer handles an input's change, and the field should stop showing its old error while the user fixes it. The form state is `{ values, touched, errors }`, with extra fields kept. The field name and value are checked against the type of `values`. Validate again on blur or submit to bring errors back.
signatures: export function formSetField<F extends FormSetFieldState<object>, K extends keyof F['values'] & string>( form: F, field: K, value: F['values'][K], ): F
export function formSetField<F extends FormSetFieldState<object>, K extends keyof F['values'] & string>( field: K, value: F['values'][K], ): (form: F) => F

assets.name: formShowErrors
assets.summary: Replaces a form's errors with a new set, and marks every field that has one as touched so it shows.
assets.useWhen: a submit fails validation on the client or the server answers 422 with field errors, and each message must appear under its field even if the user never visited it. Errors from before are dropped, so pass every current error, and an empty message counts as no error. Touched flags of other fields stay. The form state is `{ values, touched, errors }`, with extra fields kept, and the error keys are checked against `values`.
signatures: export function formShowErrors<F extends FormShowErrorsState<object>>( form: F, errors: Readonly<Partial<Record<keyof F['values'], string>>>, ): F
export function formShowErrors<F extends FormShowErrorsState<object>>( errors: Readonly<Partial<Record<keyof F['values'], string>>>, ): (form: F) => F

assets.name: historyPush
assets.summary: Records a new present state in an undo history, keeping at most `limit` past states and clearing redo.
assets.useWhen: an editor, canvas, form builder or spreadsheet needs undo and redo, and each committed change goes through here. The old present moves to the end of `past`, the oldest past states beyond `limit` are dropped, and `future` empties because a new change ends the redo trail. A `next` deep-equal to the present is not a change: the same history comes back.
signatures: export function historyPush<T>(history: HistoryPushState<T>, next: T, limit: number): HistoryPushState<T>
export function historyPush<T>(next: T, limit: number): (history: HistoryPushState<T>) => HistoryPushState<T>

assets.name: historyRedo
assets.summary: Steps an undo history forward one state after an undo: the first redo state becomes present.
assets.useWhen: handling Ctrl+Shift+Z or a redo button in an editor whose history `historyPush` records and `historyUndo` steps back. The current present goes to the end of `past`. With nothing in `future`, either because nothing was undone or because a new change cleared it, the same history comes back.
signatures: export function historyRedo<T>(history: HistoryRedoState<T>): HistoryRedoState<T>

assets.name: historyUndo
assets.summary: Steps an undo history back one state: the last past state becomes present, and the present goes to redo.
assets.useWhen: handling Ctrl+Z or an undo button in an editor whose history `historyPush` records. The current present is put at the front of `future`, so `historyRedo` can bring it back. With nothing in `past`, the same history comes back, which also tells a button to show as disabled: `history.past.length === 0`.
signatures: export function historyUndo<T>(history: HistoryUndoState<T>): HistoryUndoState<T>

assets.name: incrementAt
assets.summary: Returns new state with the number at a dot path increased by an amount, where a missing count starts at 0.
assets.useWhen: counting in state, such as unread messages, likes, a page number, a retry count or `'stats.byDay.mon'`, and the counter may not exist yet. Pass a negative amount to decrease. The path must lead to a number in the state's type, or the call doesn't compile. There are no bounds: use `incrementClampedAt` for a stepper that must stay in a range.
signatures: export function incrementAt<S, P extends string>(state: S, at: IncrementAtPath<S, P>, by: number): S
export function incrementAt<S, P extends string>(at: IncrementAtPath<S, P>, by: number): (state: S) => S

assets.name: incrementClampedAt
assets.summary: Returns new state with the number at a dot path stepped by an amount and kept between a minimum and a maximum.
assets.useWhen: a stepper, slider or keyboard shortcut moves a bounded number, such as a quantity from 1 to the stock level, a zoom level, a volume or a page index, and pressing "+" at the top must stay at the top. A missing value starts at `min`. The result is clamped even if the stored value was already out of range. The path must lead to a number in the state's type, or the call doesn't compile.
signatures: export function incrementClampedAt<S, P extends string>( state: S, at: IncrementClampedAtPath<S, P>, by: number, range: IncrementClampedAtRange, ): S
export function incrementClampedAt<S, P extends string>( at: IncrementClampedAtPath<S, P>, by: number, range: IncrementClampedAtRange, ): (state: S) => S

assets.name: mergeAt
assets.summary: Returns new state with some fields of the object at a dot path replaced, keeping its other fields.
assets.useWhen: a form section, a server response or a settings panel updates several fields of one nested object at once, such as `'profile.address'` or `'filters'`, and the rest of that object must survive. The merge is one level deep: a nested object inside the patch replaces the old one whole. A missing object is created from the patch. The patch is checked against the object's type, and the input is never changed.
signatures: export function mergeAt<S, P extends string>(state: S, at: P, patch: MergeAtPatch<S, P>): S
export function mergeAt<S, P extends string>(at: P, patch: MergeAtPatch<S, P>): (state: S) => S

assets.name: moveBetweenLists
assets.summary: Moves one item from a position in one list to a position in another, as a kanban drag and drop does.
assets.useWhen: handling the drop of a card between kanban columns, a task between sprints, a file between folders or a player between teams, where the lists live in one record by id. The item leaves `from` and is inserted at `to`, and items after it shift. A `to.index` past the end appends. Moving within one list works too. If either list is missing or nothing is at `from`, the same board comes back. Lists that weren't touched are the same arrays.
signatures: export function moveBetweenLists<T>( board: MoveBetweenListsBoard<T>, from: MoveBetweenListsSpot, to: MoveBetweenListsSpot, ): MoveBetweenListsBoard<T>
export function moveBetweenLists( from: MoveBetweenListsSpot, to: MoveBetweenListsSpot, ): <T>(board: MoveBetweenListsBoard<T>) => MoveBetweenListsBoard<T>

assets.name: normalizedRemove
assets.summary: Removes entities by id from a normalized `{ ids, byId }` store, from both the order and the lookup.
assets.useWhen: records are deleted, archived or evicted from an entity cache, such as a deleted message, users who left a channel, or rows a bulk action removed. Ids that aren't stored are ignored, and when none of them are, the same state object comes back. The remaining ids keep their order.
signatures: export function normalizedRemove<E extends { readonly id: string | number }>( state: NormalizedRemoveState<E>, ids: readonly E['id'][], ): NormalizedRemoveState<E>
export function normalizedRemove<E extends { readonly id: string | number }>( ids: readonly E['id'][], ): (state: NormalizedRemoveState<E>) => NormalizedRemoveState<E>

assets.name: normalizedUpsert
assets.summary: Adds new entities to a normalized `{ ids, byId }` store and merges updates into the ones it already has.
assets.useWhen: a page of results, a websocket batch or a mutation response must land in an entity cache keyed by id, where the same record can arrive again with only some fields and the list order must not jump. A new id is appended to `ids` and stored whole. A known id keeps its place, and the incoming fields are merged over the stored ones, one level deep. The same id twice in one batch is merged twice. Other entities are the same objects as before.
signatures: export function normalizedUpsert<E extends { readonly id: string | number }>( state: NormalizedUpsertState<E>, entities: readonly E[], ): NormalizedUpsertState<E>
export function normalizedUpsert<E extends { readonly id: string | number }>( entities: readonly E[], ): (state: NormalizedUpsertState<E>) => NormalizedUpsertState<E>

assets.name: patchById
assets.summary: Returns a new list where the item with the given `id` has some fields replaced, keeping its other fields.
assets.useWhen: a server response, a form or a websocket event carries part of a record, such as `{ status: 'shipped' }` for one order, and the list in state must reflect it. The merge is one level deep, and the `id` can't be changed through the patch. When no item has the id, the same array comes back. The other items are the same objects as before.
signatures: export function patchById<T extends { readonly id: unknown }>( items: readonly T[], id: T['id'], patch: Partial<Omit<T, 'id'>>, ): readonly T[]
export function patchById<T extends { readonly id: unknown }>( id: T['id'], patch: Partial<Omit<T, 'id'>>, ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: pushAt
assets.summary: Returns new state with an item added to the end of the array at a dot path, creating the array if missing.
assets.useWhen: a reducer appends to a nested list, such as a message to `'chat.messages'`, a toast to `'ui.toasts'` or a line to `'orders.0.lines'`. The path must lead to an array in the state's type and the item must fit it, or the call doesn't compile. Objects off the path are reused, and the input is never changed. Use `pushCappedAt` when the list must not grow forever.
signatures: export function pushAt<S, P extends string>(state: S, at: P, item: PushAtItem<S, P>): S
export function pushAt<S, P extends string>(at: P, item: PushAtItem<S, P>): (state: S) => S

assets.name: pushCappedAt
assets.summary: Returns new state with an item appended to the array at a dot path, dropping the oldest items beyond a limit.
assets.useWhen: a list in state must stay bounded, such as recent searches, the last 50 log lines, notifications, chat history kept in memory or an activity feed. The newest item goes last, and only the last `max` items are kept, so the oldest go first. A missing array starts empty. The path must lead to an array in the state's type and the item must fit it.
signatures: export function pushCappedAt<S, P extends string>(state: S, at: P, item: PushCappedAtItem<S, P>, max: number): S
export function pushCappedAt<S, P extends string>(at: P, item: PushCappedAtItem<S, P>, max: number): (state: S) => S

assets.name: reduceRequest
assets.summary: Moves a remote-data state (idle, loading, success, error) on by one event, keeping the last data while it reloads.
assets.useWhen: a reducer, store or hook tracks a fetch by hand and the screen must show stale data with a spinner during a refresh, and keep it with an error banner when the refresh fails. `start` clears the error but keeps the data, `success` stores the new data, `failure` stores the error and keeps the data, and `reset` goes back to idle with nothing. A first load and a refresh both say `loading`: `isSome(state.data)` tells them apart.
signatures: export function reduceRequest<T, E>(state: ReduceRequestState<T, E>, event: ReduceRequestEvent<T, E>): ReduceRequestState<T, E>
export function reduceRequest<T, E>(event: ReduceRequestEvent<T, E>): (state: ReduceRequestState<T, E>) => ReduceRequestState<T, E>

assets.name: removeWhereAt
assets.summary: Returns new state without the items of the array at a dot path that match a predicate.
assets.useWhen: clearing completed todos, dismissing read notifications, removing an item by id from `'cart.lines'`, or dropping expired entries from a nested list. Pass a Receta predicate such as `where({ done: eq(true) })`. Items keep their order. A missing array stays missing, and objects off the path are reused. The path must lead to an array in the state's type, and the predicate gets its item type.
signatures: export function removeWhereAt<S, P extends string>( state: S, at: RemoveWhereAtPath<S, P>, predicate: (item: RemoveWhereAtItem<S, P>) => boolean, ): S
export function removeWhereAt<S, P extends string>( at: RemoveWhereAtPath<S, P>, predicate: (item: RemoveWhereAtItem<S, P>) => boolean, ): (state: S) => S

assets.name: reorderAt
assets.summary: Returns new state with one item of the array at a dot path moved from one position to another.
assets.useWhen: handling the drop of a drag-and-drop list, such as reordering playlist tracks, form fields, dashboard widgets or the cards of one kanban column. The item is taken out at `from` and put at `to`, and the others shift to make room. Negative positions count from the end. If either position is outside the array, or the array is missing, the state comes back unchanged.
signatures: export function reorderAt<S, P extends string>(state: S, at: ReorderAtPath<S, P>, from: number, to: number): S
export function reorderAt<S, P extends string>(at: ReorderAtPath<S, P>, from: number, to: number): (state: S) => S

assets.name: setAt
assets.summary: Returns new state with one value replaced at a dot path, copying only the objects on the way to it.
assets.useWhen: a reducer, a `setState` callback or a store update must change one nested field, such as `'settings.theme'` or `'todos.2.title'`, without spreading every level by hand. The path is checked against the state's type, and so is the value. Numeric parts index into arrays. Objects off the path are reused, so memoized components that read them don't re-render. A missing object on the way is created as `{}`. The input is never changed.
signatures: export function setAt<S, P extends string>(state: S, at: P, value: SetAtValue<S, P>): S
export function setAt<S, P extends string>(at: P, value: SetAtValue<S, P>): (state: S) => S

assets.name: setManyAt
assets.summary: Returns new state with a value written at each dot path of a record, as one update.
assets.useWhen: one event changes fields in several places, such as a login response filling `'session.user'` and `'session.token'` and clearing `'ui.error'`, or a "reset filters" button. Paths are written in the record's order, so a later path wins over an earlier one that overlaps it. Each path and value is checked against the state's type. Objects off the paths are reused, and the input is never changed.
signatures: export function setManyAt<S, U extends Record<string, unknown>>(state: S, updates: SetManyAtUpdates<S, U>): S
export function setManyAt<S, U extends Record<string, unknown>>(updates: SetManyAtUpdates<S, U>): (state: S) => S

assets.name: swapAt
assets.summary: Returns new state with two items of the array at a dot path exchanged, leaving the others in place.
assets.useWhen: a "move up" or "move down" button swaps neighbours, a puzzle or seating chart swaps two cells, or a comparison view swaps the left and right item. If either position is outside the array, or the array is missing, the state comes back unchanged. Use `reorderAt` for drag and drop, where the items between should shift.
signatures: export function swapAt<S, P extends string>(state: S, at: SwapAtPath<S, P>, first: number, second: number): S
export function swapAt<S, P extends string>(at: SwapAtPath<S, P>, first: number, second: number): (state: S) => S

assets.name: toggleAt
assets.summary: Returns new state with the boolean at a dot path flipped, where a missing flag counts as false.
assets.useWhen: a click flips one nested flag, such as a modal's `open`, a sidebar's `collapsed`, a todo's `done` (`'todos.3.done'`) or an optional `'flags.beta'` that may not be set yet. The path must lead to a boolean in the state's type, or the call doesn't compile. Objects off the path are reused, and the input is never changed.
signatures: export function toggleAt<S, P extends string>(state: S, at: ToggleAtPath<S, P>): S
export function toggleAt<S, P extends string>(at: ToggleAtPath<S, P>): (state: S) => S

assets.name: toggleById
assets.summary: Returns a new list where a boolean field of the item with the given `id` is flipped.
assets.useWhen: a checkbox or switch in a list row flips one flag, such as a todo's `done`, an email's `starred`, a feature's `enabled` or a row's `selected`. The field must be a boolean in the item type, or the call doesn't compile. When no item has the id, the same array comes back. The other items are the same objects as before.
signatures: export function toggleById<T extends { readonly id: unknown }>( items: readonly T[], id: T['id'], field: KeysOfType<T, boolean>, ): readonly T[]
export function toggleById<T extends { readonly id: unknown }>( id: T['id'], field: KeysOfType<T, boolean>, ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: toggleMembershipAt
assets.summary: Returns new state where a value is removed from the array at a dot path if present, or appended if not.
assets.useWhen: a checkbox list, a tag picker, a filter chip or a multi-select table toggles one id in `'selection.ids'` or `'filters.colors'`. Values compare with `===`, so use ids or strings, not objects. Every copy of the value is removed when present. A missing array becomes `[value]`. The path must lead to an array in the state's type and the value must fit it.
signatures: export function toggleMembershipAt<S, P extends string>(state: S, at: P, value: ToggleMembershipAtItem<S, P>): S
export function toggleMembershipAt<S, P extends string>(at: P, value: ToggleMembershipAtItem<S, P>): (state: S) => S

assets.name: unsetAt
assets.summary: Returns new state with the key at a dot path deleted, not set to `undefined`, or with the array item removed.
assets.useWhen: an entry must disappear from a nested record, such as a closed tab from `'tabs.byId.t3'`, a cleared error from `'form.errors.email'` or a draft from `'drafts.p1'`, so `Object.keys`, `in` and JSON no longer see it. A numeric last part removes that array item and the later ones shift up. A path that isn't there returns the same state object. Only remove optional keys: the type stays `S`.
signatures: export function unsetAt<S, P extends string>(state: S, at: UnsetAtPath<S, P>): S
export function unsetAt<S, P extends string>(at: UnsetAtPath<S, P>): (state: S) => S

assets.name: updateById
assets.summary: Returns a new list where the item with the given `id` is replaced by `update(item)`, and all others are kept.
assets.useWhen: a list in state holds records with an `id`, such as todos, rows, messages or products, and one of them changes: renamed, completed, refreshed from the server. Only the first item with that id is updated, and its position stays. When no item has the id, the same array comes back, so a stale event changes nothing. The other items are the same objects as before.
signatures: export function updateById<T extends { readonly id: unknown }>( items: readonly T[], id: T['id'], update: (item: T) => T, ): readonly T[]
export function updateById<T extends { readonly id: unknown }>( id: T['id'], update: (item: T) => T, ): (items: readonly T[]) => readonly T[]

assets.name: updateIfPresent
assets.summary: Returns new state with `update` applied to the value at a dot path, or the same state when that value is missing.
assets.useWhen: an event refers to something that may already be gone, such as a websocket update for a closed chat, a late response for a removed row, or `'selected.details'` after the selection was cleared. A plain update would create the path and call `update(undefined)`; here `null` and `undefined` mean "nothing to do", the same state object comes back, and `update` never sees a missing value.
signatures: export function updateIfPresent<S, P extends string>( state: S, at: UpdateIfPresentPath<S, P>, update: (value: UpdateIfPresentValue<S, P>) => UpdateIfPresentValue<S, P>, ): S
export function updateIfPresent<S, P extends string>( at: UpdateIfPresentPath<S, P>, update: (value: UpdateIfPresentValue<S, P>) => UpdateIfPresentValue<S, P>, ): (state: S) => S

assets.name: updateWhereAt
assets.summary: Returns new state where each item of the array at a dot path that matches a predicate is replaced by `update(item)`.
assets.useWhen: one action changes many items of a nested list, such as "mark all as read", "archive everything older than a week" or "apply the discount to every line from this vendor". Items that don't match are kept as the same objects, in the same order. A missing array stays missing. The path must lead to an array, and both functions get its item type.
signatures: export function updateWhereAt<S, P extends string>( state: S, at: UpdateWhereAtPath<S, P>, predicate: (item: UpdateWhereAtItem<S, P>) => boolean, update: (item: UpdateWhereAtItem<S, P>) => UpdateWhereAtItem<S, P>, ): S

export function updateWhereAt<S, P extends string>( at: UpdateWhereAtPath<S, P>, predicate: (item: UpdateWhereAtItem<S, P>) => boolean, update: (item: UpdateWhereAtItem<S, P>) => UpdateWhereAtItem<S, P>, ): (state: S) => S

assets.name: avatarInitials
assets.summary: Gets the one or two letters for an avatar from a name or an email: first and last name.
assets.useWhen: a user has no profile picture and the UI draws a circle with their initials. Middle names are skipped, so `Mary Jane Watson` gives `MW`, not `MJ`. An email such as `jane.doe@example.com` gives `JD`. Returns `None` when there is nothing to take letters from, so the caller can fall back to an icon.
signatures: export function avatarInitials(nameOrEmail: string): Option<string>

assets.name: columnName
assets.summary: Turns a spreadsheet header or label into a SQL column name: `Order Total ($)` → `order_total`.
assets.useWhen: importing a CSV or spreadsheet into a database table and the headers become column names. Accents are dropped, symbols separate words, and camelCase splits at its capitals. A name starting with a digit gets `_` in front, since SQL needs quotes for it, and names are cut to 63 characters, PostgreSQL's limit. A header with no letters or digits gives `''`, so check for duplicates and blanks across all headers.
signatures: export function columnName(header: string): string

assets.name: countLabel
assets.summary: Writes a count with its noun in the right form and thousands separators: `1,234 replies`.
assets.useWhen: a badge, heading or summary says how many of something there are, such as `1 item`, `0 files` or `3 people`. Only exactly 1 takes the singular. Regular English plurals are built for you (`reply` gives `replies`); pass `{ one, other }` for irregular ones like `person`/`people`, or for words the rules get wrong. English only.
signatures: export function countLabel(count: number, noun: CountLabelNoun): string
export function countLabel(noun: CountLabelNoun): (count: number) => string

assets.name: displayName
assets.summary: Builds a person's full name from its parts, fixing parts typed all lower or upper case.
assets.useWhen: showing a name from a form, a CRM or an import where parts may be missing, padded with spaces, or typed as `ada` or `LOVELACE`. A part in mixed case such as `McDonald` or `van der Berg` is kept as typed. Hyphenated and apostrophe names work: `jean-luc` gives `Jean-Luc`, `o'brien` gives `O'Brien`. Returns `None` when every part is blank, so the caller can fall back to an email or `Anonymous`.
signatures: export function displayName(parts: DisplayNameParts): Option<string>

assets.name: ellipsizeMiddle
assets.summary: Shortens text to `maxLength` characters by cutting the middle: `0x71C7…d8976F`.
assets.useWhen: the start and the end both identify the value, as with wallet addresses, commit hashes, file paths and file names with versions or extensions, and the column is too narrow for all of it. The `…` counts toward `maxLength`; when the kept characters don't split evenly, the start gets the extra one. Text that fits comes back unchanged.
signatures: export function ellipsizeMiddle(text: string, maxLength: number): string
export function ellipsizeMiddle(maxLength: number): (text: string) => string

assets.name: ensureSentence
assets.summary: Tidies a message into a sentence: one line, a capital first letter and a closing period.
assets.useWhen: showing error or status messages that come from APIs, validators or other teams in mixed styles, such as `could not save,` or `  Invalid email`. A message already ending in `.`, `!`, `?` or `…` keeps its ending; a trailing comma, colon or semicolon is replaced by the period. Only the first letter changes case. An empty message stays `''`.
signatures: export function ensureSentence(message: string): string

assets.name: envVarName
assets.summary: Turns any label or key into an environment variable name: `api url` becomes `API_URL`.
assets.useWhen: generating `.env` entries, CI secrets or config keys from setting names that people typed, or from camelCase keys in a config object. Accents are dropped, anything other than letters and digits separates words, and a name starting with a digit gets a `_` in front so shells accept it. A label with no letters or digits gives `''`.
signatures: export function envVarName(label: string): string

assets.name: excerptByLength
assets.summary: Shortens text to at most `maxLength` characters on one line, cut at a word and ending in `…`.
assets.useWhen: a field has a hard character limit, such as a meta description, a push notification or an SMS, and the text must not end mid-word. Whitespace collapses to single spaces first. The `…` counts toward `maxLength`. A single word longer than the limit is cut inside the word, since there is no space to cut at.
signatures: export function excerptByLength(text: string, maxLength: number): string
export function excerptByLength(maxLength: number): (text: string) => string

assets.name: excerptByWords
assets.summary: Shortens text to its first words as one line, ending in `…` when something was cut.
assets.useWhen: a card, list row or notification previews the start of a post, comment or message. Line breaks, tabs and runs of spaces collapse to single spaces first, so the preview never wraps oddly. Text within the limit comes back whole, trimmed and without `…`. For HTML, run it through `htmlToPlainText` first.
signatures: export function excerptByWords(text: string, maxWords: number): string
export function excerptByWords(maxWords: number): (text: string) => string

assets.name: extractEmails
assets.summary: Finds the email addresses in free text, lowercased, each once, in order of appearance.
assets.useWhen: pulling contacts out of a pasted list, a support ticket, a signature or an import where addresses sit among names, brackets and punctuation. `Ana <ana@x.io>`, `mailto:ana@x.io` and an address ending a sentence all work. Addresses compare without case. Candidates that don't pass `isEmail` are dropped.
signatures: export function extractEmails(text: string): readonly string[]

assets.name: extractHashtags
assets.summary: Finds the hashtags in a post, lowercased, without `#`, each once, in order of appearance.
assets.useWhen: indexing posts, comments or captions by topic, or suggesting tags from text. Tags in any script work (`#café`, `#東京`). A `#` inside a word (`C#`), in an HTML entity (`'`) or in a URL fragment is not a tag, and neither is a tag of digits alone such as `#1`. Tags compare without case, so `#Launch` and `#launch` give one tag.
signatures: export function extractHashtags(text: string): readonly string[]

assets.name: extractMentions
assets.summary: Finds the `@username` mentions in a message, lowercased, without `@`, each once.
assets.useWhen: notifying the people mentioned in a comment, chat message or pull request review. Email addresses aren't mentions, so `ana@example.com` is skipped. Usernames are letters, digits, underscores and inner hyphens, as on GitHub and most chat apps, and trailing punctuation such as `@bob.` or `@cy,` is left out. Names compare without case.
signatures: export function extractMentions(text: string): readonly string[]

assets.name: fieldLabel
assets.summary: Turns a code name such as `firstName`, `created_at` or `apiUrl` into a label: `API URL`.
assets.useWhen: generating form labels, table headers or validation messages from object keys or database columns. camelCase, PascalCase, snake_case and kebab-case all work. Only the first word is capitalized, the way most UIs write labels, and common acronyms such as `id`, `url`, `api` and `vat` are uppercased wherever they appear.
signatures: export function fieldLabel(key: string): string

assets.name: fillTemplate
assets.summary: Fills `{{name}}` placeholders from values, using a fallback for any value that is missing.
assets.useWhen: rendering a notification, email subject or UI string where a missing value should not stop the message, such as `Hi {{name}}` for a user without a name. A key that is absent, `null` or `undefined` renders as `fallback`. Placeholders are `{{word}}`, with no spaces inside the braces. When every value must be there, use `renderTemplate`.
signatures: export function fillTemplate(text: string, values: FillTemplateValues, fallback: string): string
export function fillTemplate(values: FillTemplateValues, fallback: string): (text: string) => string

assets.name: firstSentence
assets.summary: Takes the first sentence of a text as one line, cut at a word with `…` if it is too long.
assets.useWhen: a commit body, a product description or an article lead has to become a one-line summary, a tooltip or a meta description. A sentence ends at `.`, `!` or `?` followed by a capital letter, a digit or the end, so `v2.0` and `e.g. this` don't end it. A text without an ending is treated as one sentence. The `…` counts toward `maxLength`.
signatures: export function firstSentence(text: string, maxLength: number): string
export function firstSentence(maxLength: number): (text: string) => string

assets.name: headingIds
assets.summary: Gives each heading on a page an anchor id, unique within the page: `setup`, `setup-1`.
